title: Core words
description: The everyday verbs, nouns, adjectives and adverbs the other lists don’t teach, chosen by how often people say them.

conventions.romaji: kotoba's stored spelling: modified Hepburn, lowercase, no macrons, long vowels as spelled (sou, daijoubu, kirei), wa/o/e particles, っ before ch = t (kotchi). Leading hyphen = attaches to a word.
conventions.register: romaji = casual form, learned first; polite = desu/masu counterpart, or null when there is no register difference.
conventions.freqRank: rank in jiten.moe drama frequency list (CC BY-SA 4.0); freqNote explains tokenizer-split forms. null = no usable rank.
conventions.contrastGroup: items sharing a group name are learned side by side; their examples share a base sentence.

blocks.label: Walking and running
blocks.rationale: Say how you're getting somewhere on foot and tell someone to hurry.
blocks.interference: isogu is hurrying in general, not running; tobu covers both fly and jump.

items.use: aruite iku = go on foot.

example.ja: 駅まで歩いて行こうか。
example.english: Shall we walk to the station?

examplePolite.romaji: eki made aruite ikimashou ka.
examplePolite.ja: 駅まで歩いて行きましょうか。
examplePolite.english: Shall we walk to the station?

items.notes: aruite gofun = a five-minute walk.

items.use: isoide! is the everyday 'Hurry up!'.

example.ja: 急いで！電車行っちゃうよ。
example.english: Hurry! We'll miss the train.

examplePolite.romaji: isoide kudasai. densha ga demasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 急いでください。電車が出ますよ。
examplePolite.english: Please hurry. The train's about to leave.

items.notes: isoganakute ii yo = no rush.

example.ja: 走れば間に合うよ！
example.english: If we run, we'll make it!

examplePolite.romaji: hashireba ma ni aimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 走れば間に合いますよ。
examplePolite.english: If we run, we'll make it.

items.notes: Also for vehicles running: basu ga hashitte nai (the buses aren't running).

example.ja: 雪で飛行機飛ばないって。
example.english: They say the planes aren't flying because of the snow.

examplePolite.romaji: yuki de hikouki ga tobanai sou desu.
examplePolite.ja: 雪で飛行機が飛ばないそうです。
examplePolite.english: I hear flights are grounded because of the snow.

items.notes: sugu tonde iku = I'll rush right over. A jump on the spot is often janpu suru.

blocks.label: Sitting and lining up
blocks.rationale: Handle seats, queues and crowds: sit, line up, meet up, move aside.
blocks.interference: narabu is joining a line yourself; atsumaru is people gathering as a group.

items.use: The seat takes ni: isu ni suwaru.

example.ja: この席、座ってもいい？
example.english: Can I sit here?

examplePolite.romaji: kono seki, suwatte mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: この席、座ってもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: Is this seat free?

items.notes: Opposite: tatsu (stand up). Hosts say douzo, okake kudasai (please have a seat).

items.english: line up, queue; be in a row

example.romaji: kono mise, itsumo sugoi naranderu ne.
example.ja: この店、いつもすごい並んでるね。
example.english: This place always has a huge line.

examplePolite.romaji: kono mise wa itsumo sugoku narande imasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この店はいつもすごく並んでいますね。
examplePolite.english: There's always a long line at this place.

items.notes: Arranging things in a row is naraberu.

example.ja: 7時に駅前に集まろう。
example.english: Let's meet in front of the station at seven.

examplePolite.romaji: shichiji ni ekimae ni atsumarimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 7時に駅前に集まりましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's meet in front of the station at seven.

items.notes: Collecting things or rounding people up is atsumeru.

items.english: get out of the way, move aside
items.use: doite! (move!) is blunt; with strangers say sumimasen instead.

example.ja: ちょっとどいて、通れないよ。
example.english: Move a sec, I can't get through.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, chotto doite moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: すみません、ちょっとどいてもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, could you move over a little?

items.notes: doke! is the rough command. Moving something else out of the way is dokeru.

blocks.label: Welcoming and guiding
blocks.rationale: Recognise 'come' in respectful, humble and parental speech, and offer to show someone around.
blocks.interference: irassharu raises the other person and mairu lowers yourself; never use irassharu for yourself.

items.use: For what a customer, boss or elder does; never for yourself.

example.romaji: buchou wa mou kaigi ni irasshatta?
example.ja: 部長はもう会議にいらっしゃった？
example.english: Has the boss come to the meeting yet?

examplePolite.romaji: buchou wa mou kaigi ni irasshaimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 部長はもう会議にいらっしゃいましたか？
examplePolite.english: Has the department head arrived at the meeting yet?

items.notes: irasshaimase is the shop greeting; irasshai is a warm 'welcome' at home.

items.english: come here (to a child or pet)
items.use: Warm and parental; to an adult friend say kotchi kite instead.

example.ja: ほら、おいで。こっちおいで。
example.english: Come on, come over here.

items.notes: Also an older person's invitation: asobi ni oide (come and visit).

items.use: mairimasu humbly says you're going or coming, to customers or a boss; maitta (na) is a casual 'ugh, I'm stuck'.

example.ja: 参ったな、鍵なくしちゃった。
example.english: Ugh, I've lost my keys.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita no juuji ni sochira e mairimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 明日の10時にそちらへ参ります。
examplePolite.english: I'll come to you at ten tomorrow.

items.notes: In service speech: sugu mairimasu (I'll be right with you).

items.english: show around, guide; show the way

example.ja: この辺、案内するよ。
example.english: I'll show you around the area.

examplePolite.romaji: kono hen o annai shimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: この辺を案内しますよ。
examplePolite.english: I'll show you around the area.

items.notes: Staff say goannai shimasu (let me show you). annaijo = information desk.

blocks.label: Cooking and clearing up
blocks.rationale: Make a meal and clear up: cut, get things ready, grill, throw out.
blocks.interference: kiru 'cut' (kirimasu) sounds like kiru 'wear' (kimasu); the forms tell them apart.

example.ja: これ、もう捨てていい？
example.english: Can I throw this out?

examplePolite.romaji: kore wa mou sutete mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: これはもう捨ててもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: Is it okay to throw this away?

items.notes: gomi o suteru = throw away rubbish. Also for dumping a person.

items.english: cut; hang up (a phone); switch off

example.ja: あれ、髪切った？似合うね。
example.english: Oh, did you get a haircut? It suits you.

examplePolite.romaji: are, kami o kirimashita ka? niaimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あれ、髪を切りましたか？似合いますね。
examplePolite.english: Oh, did you get your hair cut? It suits you.

items.notes: denwa o kiru = hang up. Not kiru 'wear' (着る): this one goes kirimasu, kitte; that one kimasu, kite.

items.use: Getting things ready, like food, drinks or documents.

example.romaji: nomimono wa watashi ga youi suru ne.
example.ja: 飲み物は私が用意するね。
example.english: I'll sort out the drinks.

examplePolite.romaji: nomimono wa watashi ga youi shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 飲み物は私が用意します。
examplePolite.english: I'll prepare the drinks.

items.notes: youi dekita? = ready? youi, don! = ready, set, go!

items.use: Almost any dry-heat cooking: niku o yaku, pan o yaku.

example.ja: 今日は肉焼こうか。
example.english: Shall we grill some meat today?

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa niku o yakimashou ka.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は肉を焼きましょうか。
examplePolite.english: Shall we grill some meat today?

items.notes: Getting tanned uses yakeru: hi ni yaketa (I got a tan).

blocks.label: On, off, open, close
blocks.rationale: Ask to switch lights and the AC on or off and to open or shut windows and doors.
blocks.interference: Lights and TVs take tsukeru and kesu, never akeru and shimeru.

items.english: turn on (a light, TV, AC); put on, attach
items.use: Switching on: denki o tsukeru. Opposite: kesu.

example.ja: もう暗いから、電気つけて。
example.english: It's getting dark, turn the light on.

examplePolite.romaji: kurai node, denki o tsukete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 暗いので、電気をつけてください。
examplePolite.english: It's dark, so please turn on the light.

items.notes: ki o tsukete = take care. Also attach or apply: namae o tsukeru (give a name).

items.english: turn off (a light, TV); erase, delete
items.use: Opposite of tsukeru.

example.ja: 寝るから電気消して。
example.english: I'm going to bed, turn off the light.

examplePolite.romaji: neru node denki o keshite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 寝るので電気を消してください。
examplePolite.english: I'm going to sleep, so please turn off the light.

items.notes: Also delete: shashin o kesu. Something going out by itself is kieru.

items.use: You open something; something opening by itself is aku.

example.ja: 暑いね。窓開けていい？
example.english: It's hot. Mind if I open the window?

examplePolite.romaji: atsui desu ne. mado o akete mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 暑いですね。窓を開けてもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: It's hot, isn't it. May I open the window?

items.notes: Opposite: shimeru (close).

items.english: close, shut (a door, window); close (a shop)
items.use: You close something; something closing by itself is shimaru.

example.ja: 寒いから窓閉めて。
example.english: It's cold, shut the window.

examplePolite.romaji: samui node mado o shimete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 寒いので窓を閉めてください。
examplePolite.english: It's cold, so please close the window.

items.notes: Opposite: akeru. 締める shimeru, same sound, is fasten or tighten (a seatbelt, a tie).

blocks.label: Morning routine
blocks.rationale: Talk through the start of a day: waking someone, washing, heading out, changing, going to school or work.
blocks.interference: okosu wakes someone else; waking up yourself is okiru.

items.use: Waking someone else; waking up yourself is okiru.

example.ja: 明日7時に起こしてくれる？
example.english: Can you wake me at seven tomorrow?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita shichiji ni okoshite moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日7時に起こしてもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: Could you wake me up at seven tomorrow?

items.notes: Also cause trouble: jiko o okosu (cause an accident).

example.romaji: gohan no mae ni te aratte ne.
example.ja: ご飯の前に手洗ってね。
example.english: Wash your hands before dinner.

examplePolite.romaji: gohan no mae ni te o aratte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: ご飯の前に手を洗ってください。
examplePolite.english: Please wash your hands before the meal.

items.notes: Doing the laundry is sentaku suru; washing up is sara o arau.

items.english: go out (on an outing or errand)

example.ja: ちょっと出かけてくるね。
example.english: I'm popping out for a bit.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto dekakete kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと出かけてきます。
examplePolite.english: I'm going out for a bit.

items.notes: dekakete iru = is out (not home right now).

example.ja: ちょっと着替えてくるね。
example.english: I'm just going to get changed.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto kigaete kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと着替えてきます。
examplePolite.english: I'll just go and get changed.

items.notes: kigae = a change of clothes. Also heard as kikaeru.

items.english: go regularly (to school, work, a gym); commute
items.use: For a place you keep going to, usually as kayotte iru.

example.romaji: ima jimu ni kayotteru n da.
example.ja: 今ジムに通ってるんだ。
example.english: I'm going to a gym these days.

examplePolite.romaji: ima jimu ni kayotte imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今ジムに通っています。
examplePolite.english: I go to a gym these days.

items.notes: A single trip is just iku.

blocks.label: Owning up
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about apologising, admitting, lying and being frank.
blocks.interference: Ayamaru is talking about apologising; the actual words are gomen or sumimasen.

items.use: Talking about apologising; the words themselves are gomen or sumimasen.

example.romaji: hayaku kanojo ni ayamari na yo.
example.ja: 早く彼女に謝りなよ。
example.english: Go apologise to her, quick.

examplePolite.romaji: hayaku kanojo ni ayamatta hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 早く彼女に謝ったほうがいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You should apologise to her soon.

example.romaji: kare, zettai machigai mitomenai n da yo.
example.ja: 彼、絶対間違い認めないんだよ。
example.english: He never admits he's wrong.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa zettai ni machigai o mitomenai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 彼は絶対に間違いを認めないんです。
examplePolite.english: He never admits he's wrong.

items.notes: Also 'accept, approve': oya ni mitomete moraenai = my parents won't accept it.

example.romaji: iitai koto aru nara, hakkiri itte.
example.ja: 言いたいことあるなら、はっきり言って。
example.english: If you've got something to say, say it straight.

examplePolite.romaji: iitai koto ga aru nara, hakkiri itte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 言いたいことがあるなら、はっきり言ってください。
examplePolite.english: If you have something to say, please say it plainly.

items.notes: Hakkiri itte at the start of a sentence = 'frankly, to be honest'.

blocks.label: Read, write, explain
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about reading, writing, explaining and learning from someone.
blocks.interference: Osowaru (be taught) and oshieru (teach) are the same lesson from opposite sides.

example.ja: ここに名前書いてね。
example.english: Write your name here, okay?

examplePolite.romaji: koko ni onamae o kaite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: ここにお名前を書いてください。
examplePolite.english: Please write your name here.

items.notes: Drawing a picture is also kaku: e o kaku.

example.ja: この本、もう読んだ?
example.english: Have you read this book yet?

examplePolite.romaji: kono hon wa mou yomimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: この本はもう読みましたか?
examplePolite.english: Have you read this book yet?

items.notes: Kuuki o yomu = read the room.

items.use: The listener takes ni: tomodachi ni setsumei suru.

example.ja: もう一回説明してくれる?
example.english: Can you explain that again?

examplePolite.romaji: mou ichido setsumei shite itadakemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: もう一度説明していただけますか?
examplePolite.english: Could you explain that again?

items.notes: Also a noun: setsumei ga wakariyasui = the explanation is clear.

items.use: Learning from a person: X ni osowaru.

example.romaji: kono ryouri, haha ni osowatta n da.
example.ja: この料理、母に教わったんだ。
example.english: My mum taught me this dish.

examplePolite.romaji: kono ryouri wa haha ni osowarimashita.
examplePolite.ja: この料理は母に教わりました。
examplePolite.english: My mother taught me this dish.

items.notes: Pairs with oshieru (teach). Narau is close but also covers lessons and classes.

blocks.label: Inviting and introducing
blocks.rationale: Lets you call people over, introduce them, invite them and turn invitations down.
blocks.interference: Yobu (call over, have round) vs sasou (ask along); neither means phoning.

items.english: call (over); invite; send for; call (by a name)
items.use: Not phoning, which is denwa suru.

example.ja: 何て呼べばいい?
example.english: What should I call you?

examplePolite.romaji: nan to yobeba ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 何と呼べばいいですか?
examplePolite.english: What should I call you?

items.notes: Also 'invite': tomodachi o ie ni yobu. Kyuukyuusha yonde! = call an ambulance!

items.use: Introducing people to each other, or pointing someone to a place or service.

example.romaji: dareka ii hito shoukai shite yo.
example.ja: 誰かいい人紹介してよ。
example.english: Introduce me to someone nice.

examplePolite.romaji: dareka ii hito o shoukai shite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 誰かいい人を紹介してください。
examplePolite.english: Please introduce me to someone nice.

items.notes: Jiko shoukai = self-introduction.

items.use: Asking someone to come along, or asking someone on a date.

example.romaji: kanojo, eiga ni sasotte miyou ka na.
example.ja: 彼女、映画に誘ってみようかな。
example.english: Maybe I'll ask her to a movie.

examplePolite.romaji: kanojo o eiga ni sasotte miyou to omoimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 彼女を映画に誘ってみようと思います。
examplePolite.english: I think I'll ask her to a movie.

items.notes: Being invited is sasowareru. Shoutai suru is for formal invitations.

items.use: Declining an invitation, request or offer.

example.ja: 飲み会に誘われたけど、断っちゃった。
example.english: I got invited out drinking but turned it down.

examplePolite.romaji: nomikai ni sasowaremashita ga, kotowarimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 飲み会に誘われましたが、断りました。
examplePolite.english: I was invited out drinking, but I declined.

items.notes: On a sign, okotowari shimasu means 'not allowed'.

blocks.label: Respectful say, know, eat
blocks.rationale: Lets you hear and use the polite-speech words for saying, knowing and eating.
blocks.interference: Ossharu and meshiagaru raise the other person; mousu and moushiageru lower yourself, so never swap them.

items.use: Heard almost only as moushimasu: giving your own name, or staff speaking to customers.

example.ja: はじめまして、田中と申します。
example.english: Nice to meet you, I'm Tanaka.

items.notes: Never for what others say; for that, use ossharu.

items.use: For what a customer, boss or elder says; never for yourself.

example.romaji: shachou ga sou osshatta n da yo.
example.ja: 社長がそうおっしゃったんだよ。
example.english: That's what the boss said.

examplePolite.romaji: shachou ga sou osshaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 社長がそうおっしゃいました。
examplePolite.english: That's what the boss said.

items.notes: The polite form is irregular: osshaimasu. Ossharu toori desu = you're quite right.

items.use: Asking a customer or superior whether they know something: gozonji desu ka?

example.ja: この店、ご存じですか?
example.english: Do you know this place?

items.notes: Your own knowing is humble: zonjimasen = I don't know. Gozonji no toori = as you know.

items.use: Mostly in set business phrases: onegai moushiagemasu, owabi moushiagemasu.

example.ja: 今後ともよろしくお願い申し上げます。
example.english: We look forward to working with you going forward.

items.notes: Heard in speeches, announcements and business email; mousu is the lighter version.

items.use: Said of someone else's eating or drinking — a host to a guest, staff to a customer.

example.romaji: douzo, atsui uchi ni meshiagatte kudasai.
example.ja: どうぞ、熱いうちに召し上がってください。
example.english: Please, eat it while it's hot.

items.notes: Never for yourself: your own eating is itadaku or tabemasu.

blocks.label: Chatting and going quiet
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about chatting, greeting, striking up a conversation and going silent.
blocks.interference: Hanashikakeru (speak to someone first) vs shaberu (just chatting).

items.use: Also 'blab': dare ni mo shaberanaide = don't tell anyone.

example.ja: 昨日ずっと友達としゃべってた。
example.english: I was chatting with friends all day yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou wa zutto tomodachi to shabette imashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日はずっと友達としゃべっていました。
examplePolite.english: I was chatting with friends all day yesterday.

items.notes: More casual than hanasu, and leans toward chatting.

items.english: go quiet; shut up; keep (something) quiet

example.ja: なんでずっと黙ってるの?
example.english: Why have you gone so quiet?

examplePolite.romaji: doushite zutto damatte iru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: どうしてずっと黙っているんですか?
examplePolite.english: Why have you been so quiet?

items.notes: Damatte! alone is a blunt 'shut up!'. Oya ni damatte = without telling your parents.

items.english: greet; say hello; give a short speech
items.use: Saying hello properly, or a formal few words at an event.

example.romaji: tonari no hito ni aisatsu shita?
example.ja: 隣の人に挨拶した?
example.english: Did you say hello to the neighbours?

examplePolite.romaji: tonari no kata ni aisatsu shimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 隣の方に挨拶しましたか?
examplePolite.english: Did you say hello to the neighbours?

items.notes: Aisatsu ni iku = pay a courtesy visit (new neighbours, in-laws).

items.english: talk to; start a conversation with
items.use: Being the one who speaks first: X ni hanashikakeru.

example.romaji: densha de shiranai hito ni hanashikakerareta.
example.ja: 電車で知らない人に話しかけられた。
example.english: A stranger started talking to me on the train.

examplePolite.romaji: densha de shiranai hito ni hanashikakeraremashita.
examplePolite.ja: 電車で知らない人に話しかけられました。
examplePolite.english: A stranger started talking to me on the train.

items.notes: Ima hanashikakenaide = don't talk to me right now.

blocks.label: Getting the message across
blocks.rationale: Lets you pass on messages, report news and check you were understood.
blocks.interference: Tsutaeru (you tell) vs tsutawaru (it gets through).

items.english: tell, pass on (a message); get across
items.use: Passing a message along, or putting feelings into words.

example.ja: 彼によろしく伝えて。
example.english: Say hi to him for me.

examplePolite.romaji: kare ni yoroshiku tsutaete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 彼によろしく伝えてください。
examplePolite.english: Please say hello to him for me.

items.notes: Tsutaeru is you telling; tsutawaru is the message getting through.

items.english: get across; come through; be passed down
items.use: When a message or feeling reaches the other person: tsutawatta? = did that make sense?

example.romaji: kimochi, chanto tsutawatta to omou yo.
example.ja: 気持ち、ちゃんと伝わったと思うよ。
example.english: I think your feelings really came across.

examplePolite.romaji: kimochi wa chanto tsutawatta to omoimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 気持ちはちゃんと伝わったと思います。
examplePolite.english: I think your feelings came across.

items.notes: The person tsutaeru; the message tsutawaru.

items.english: get through; be understood; connect (a call)
items.use: Your meaning, your language, or a phone call getting through.

example.romaji: ryokou de eigo ga zenzen tsuujinakatta.
example.ja: 旅行で英語が全然通じなかった。
example.english: On the trip, nobody understood my English at all.

examplePolite.romaji: ryokou de eigo ga zenzen tsuujimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 旅行で英語が全然通じませんでした。
examplePolite.english: On the trip, my English didn't get through at all.

items.notes: Denwa ga tsuujinai = the call won't go through. Hanashi ga tsuujiru = we understand each other.

items.use: Passing on news or results — to a boss, family or friends.

example.ja: 結果出たら報告するね。
example.english: I'll let you know when the results come out.

examplePolite.romaji: kekka ga detara houkoku shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 結果が出たら報告します。
examplePolite.english: I'll report back when the results come out.

items.notes: The work motto hourensou = houkoku, renraku, soudan (report, keep in touch, consult).

blocks.label: Believe, feel, imagine
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about trusting, sensing and picturing things.
blocks.interference: Kanjiru (to sense) vs the noun kanji (a feeling, vibe) in sonna kanji.

example.ja: 私のこと、信じてよ。
example.english: Come on, trust me.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi no koto o shinjite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 私のことを信じてください。
examplePolite.english: Please trust me.

items.notes: Shinjirarenai! = 'I can't believe it!'

items.use: Feeling a sensation, mood or presence: samusa o kanjiru.

example.ja: 最近、年を感じるな。
example.english: I'm feeling my age lately.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin, toshi o kanjimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 最近、年を感じます。
examplePolite.english: I've been feeling my age lately.

items.notes: The noun kanji = feeling, vibe: sonna kanji = something like that.

example.ja: そんなの、想像もしてなかった。
example.english: I never even imagined that.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna koto wa souzou mo shite imasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: そんなことは想像もしていませんでした。
examplePolite.english: I never even imagined that.

items.notes: Souzou dekinai = I can't imagine. Souzou ijou = beyond what I imagined.

blocks.label: Glad, surprised, calm
blocks.rationale: Lets you describe reactions: calming down, being pleased, shocked or having fun.
blocks.interference: Yorokobu describes someone's visible joy; for your own, say ureshii.

items.english: calm down; settle down; feel at home

example.ja: 大丈夫、落ち着いてゆっくり話して。
example.english: It's okay — calm down and talk slowly.

examplePolite.romaji: daijoubu desu, ochitsuite yukkuri hanashite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 大丈夫です、落ち着いてゆっくり話してください。
examplePolite.english: It's all right — please calm down and speak slowly.

items.notes: Also 'cozy': kono heya, ochitsuku ne. Shigoto ga ochitsuitara = once work quiets down.

items.use: Usually describes someone else's visible joy; for your own, say ureshii.

example.ja: これあげたら、お母さん喜ぶよ。
example.english: Mum will be thrilled if you give her this.

examplePolite.romaji: kore o agetara, okaasan ga yorokobimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: これをあげたら、お母さんが喜びますよ。
examplePolite.english: Your mother will be delighted if you give her this.

items.notes: Yorokonde = gladly: yorokonde tetsudau yo.

example.romaji: kyuu ni koe kakeru kara odoroita yo.
example.ja: 急に声かけるから驚いたよ。
example.english: You surprised me, calling out like that.

examplePolite.romaji: kyuu ni koe o kakerareta node odorokimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 急に声をかけられたので驚きました。
examplePolite.english: I was surprised when you suddenly called out.

items.notes: In speech, bikkuri suru is more common; odoroku sounds a little more serious.

items.use: Takes an object: ryokou o tanoshimu. 'I had fun' is tanoshikatta.

example.romaji: kyou wa minna de omoikkiri tanoshimou!
example.ja: 今日はみんなで思いっきり楽しもう!
example.english: Let's all really enjoy ourselves today!

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa minna de omoikkiri tanoshimimashou!
examplePolite.ja: 今日はみんなで思いっきり楽しみましょう!
examplePolite.english: Let's all really enjoy ourselves today!

items.notes: Tanoshimi = something to look forward to: tanoshimi ni shiteru.

blocks.label: Knowing and remembering
blocks.rationale: Lets you say you don't know, can't remember, got it wrong, or understand.
blocks.interference: Shiranai (no information) vs wakaranai (not sure); omoidasu (recall) vs oboete iru (still remember).

items.use: Means you have no information; for 'I'm not sure', wakaranai is softer.

example.ja: そんな人、知らないよ。
example.english: I don't know anyone like that.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna hito wa shirimasen.
examplePolite.ja: そんな人は知りません。
examplePolite.english: I don't know anyone like that.

items.notes: The negative of shiru; 'I know' is shitte iru (shitteru), never shiru. Shiranai hito = a stranger.

example.ja: あの人の名前、思い出せない。
example.english: I can't remember that person's name.

examplePolite.romaji: ano kata no namae ga omoidasemasen.
examplePolite.ja: あの方の名前が思い出せません。
examplePolite.english: I can't remember that person's name.

items.notes: Omoidasu is the moment it comes back; oboete iru is still having it in memory.

items.english: get the wrong idea; mistake (one thing for another)

example.romaji: gomen, ashita da to kanchigai shiteta.
example.ja: ごめん、明日だと勘違いしてた。
example.english: Sorry, I thought it was tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, ashita da to kanchigai shite imashita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、明日だと勘違いしていました。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I thought it was tomorrow.

items.notes: Kanchigai shinaide = don't get the wrong idea. Machigai is a mistake you make; kanchigai is a wrong belief.

items.use: A step more formal than wakaru; also being understanding toward someone.

example.romaji: oya ga zenzen rikai shite kurenai.
example.ja: 親が全然理解してくれない。
example.english: My parents just don't understand me.

examplePolite.romaji: oya ga zenzen rikai shite kuremasen.
examplePolite.ja: 親が全然理解してくれません。
examplePolite.english: My parents just don't understand me.

items.notes: Day to day, wakaru is the usual 'understand'.

blocks.label: Hopes, worries, regrets
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about hoping, holding on, agonising and regretting.
blocks.interference: Nayamu (torn or troubled) vs shinpai suru (afraid something bad will happen).

items.use: Hoping for something good, or expectations placed on someone.

example.ja: あんまり期待しないでね。
example.english: Don't get your hopes up too much.

examplePolite.romaji: amari kitai shinaide kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: あまり期待しないでくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please don't expect too much.

items.notes: Kitai shiteru yo = I'm counting on you. Kitaihazure = a letdown.

items.english: put up with; hold back; hold it in
items.use: Enduring pain or waiting, or holding back from something you want.

example.ja: もうちょっと我慢して。
example.english: Hang in there a bit longer.

examplePolite.romaji: mou sukoshi gaman shite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: もう少し我慢してください。
examplePolite.english: Please bear with it a little longer.

items.notes: Mou gaman dekinai = I can't take it anymore.

example.romaji: ima yaranai to, zettai koukai suru yo.
example.ja: 今やらないと、絶対後悔するよ。
example.english: If you don't do it now, you'll regret it.

examplePolite.romaji: ima yaranai to, kitto koukai shimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 今やらないと、きっと後悔しますよ。
examplePolite.english: If you don't do it now, you'll regret it.

items.notes: Koukai shitenai = I have no regrets.

items.english: worry about; agonise over; be torn
items.use: Being troubled by something or stuck on a choice: X de nayamu.

example.romaji: dotchi ni suru ka mada nayanderu.
example.ja: どっちにするかまだ悩んでる。
example.english: I still can't decide which one to pick.

examplePolite.romaji: dochira ni suru ka mada nayande imasu.
examplePolite.ja: どちらにするかまだ悩んでいます。
examplePolite.english: I'm still deciding which one to pick.

items.notes: Nayami = a worry, a problem. Shinpai suru is fearing what might happen.

blocks.label: Making sense of things
blocks.rationale: Lets you say something makes sense, make a call, or clear up a misunderstanding or a muddle.
blocks.interference: Nattoku is accepting a reason, not just understanding it (wakaru).

items.english: be convinced, accept; be satisfied (with a reason)
items.use: Mostly 'nattoku dekinai' (I can't accept that) and 'nattoku shita' (Now it makes sense).

example.romaji: sono setsumei ja nattoku dekinai yo.
example.ja: その説明じゃ納得できないよ。
example.english: I can't accept that explanation.

examplePolite.romaji: sono setsumei de wa nattoku dekimasen.
examplePolite.ja: その説明では納得できません。
examplePolite.english: I can't accept that explanation.

items.notes: 'Naruhodo, nattoku' means 'Ah, that explains it'.

items.use: For making a call on the facts: 'Jibun de handan shite' (Use your own judgment).

example.romaji: sore wa jibun de handan shite yo.
example.ja: それは自分で判断してよ。
example.english: You'll have to decide that for yourself.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa jibun de handan shite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: それは自分で判断してください。
examplePolite.english: Please decide that for yourself.

items.notes: The noun is common too: 'ii handan' (a good call), 'handan ga muzukashii' (it's hard to say).

items.use: 'Gokai da yo!' means 'You've got it wrong!'; 'Gokai shinaide' means 'Don't get the wrong idea'.

example.romaji: chigau yo, sore wa gokai da yo.
example.ja: 違うよ、それは誤解だよ。
example.english: No, you've got the wrong idea.

examplePolite.romaji: chigaimasu, sore wa gokai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 違います、それは誤解です。
examplePolite.english: No, that's a misunderstanding.

items.notes: Also gokai suru (misunderstand) and gokai sareru (be misunderstood).

items.use: For a muddled head or a chaotic situation: 'Atama ga konran shiteru' (My head's spinning).

example.romaji: chotto matte, atama ga konran shiteru.
example.ja: ちょっと待って、頭が混乱してる。
example.english: Hang on, my head's all mixed up.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto matte kudasai, atama ga konran shite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと待ってください、頭が混乱しています。
examplePolite.english: Hold on, I'm getting confused.

items.notes: Also public chaos, as with traffic or markets. For a light 'I'm lost', wakaranaku natta is more everyday.

blocks.label: Helping out
blocks.rationale: Lets you offer help, thank someone for it and cheer people on.
blocks.interference: Tasukeru is what you do, tasukaru is how it feels to get it; ouen is cheering, sapooto is hands-on.

items.use: Shouted alone as 'Tasukete!' for 'Help!'.

example.romaji: kinou wa tasukete kurete arigatou ne.
example.ja: 昨日は助けてくれてありがとうね。
example.english: Thanks for helping me out yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou wa tasukete itadaite, arigatou gozaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日は助けていただいて、ありがとうございました。
examplePolite.english: Thank you for helping me out yesterday.

items.notes: For help with a chore or task, tetsudau is more natural.

items.english: be a big help; be saved
items.use: Said as thanks: 'Tasukaru!' or 'Tasukatta!' means 'That really helps!'.

example.ja: 本当に助かったよ、ありがとう。
example.english: That was a huge help, thanks.

examplePolite.romaji: hontou ni tasukarimashita, arigatou gozaimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 本当に助かりました、ありがとうございます。
examplePolite.english: That was a huge help, thank you.

items.notes: Pairs with tasukeru: tasukeru is what you do for someone, tasukaru is how it lands on you.

items.use: For rooting for a team, a friend's plans or a favourite idol; 'Ouen shiteru yo' means 'I'm behind you'.

example.ja: ずっと応援してるからね。
example.english: I'll always be rooting for you.

examplePolite.romaji: zutto ouen shite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: ずっと応援しています。
examplePolite.english: I'll always be rooting for you.

items.notes: Mostly moral support; for practical help use tasukeru or tetsudau.

items.use: For chipping in on a shared job; the noun kyouryoku (cooperation) is common too.

example.romaji: minna de kyouryoku shite ganbarou yo.
example.ja: みんなで協力して頑張ろうよ。
example.english: Let's all pull together and do our best.

examplePolite.romaji: minna de kyouryoku shite ganbarimashou.
examplePolite.ja: みんなで協力して頑張りましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's all pull together and do our best.

items.notes: 'Gokyouryoku onegai shimasu' is the set request for cooperation in notices and announcements.

items.use: Hands-on backup at work or in a project; also customer support.

example.romaji: nanika attara sapooto suru kara ne.
example.ja: 何かあったらサポートするからね。
example.english: If anything comes up, I'll back you up.

examplePolite.romaji: nanika attara sapooto shimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 何かあったらサポートしますね。
examplePolite.english: If anything comes up, I'll back you up.

items.notes: Close to ouen, but sapooto is practical help and ouen is mostly cheering.

blocks.label: Meeting and marrying
blocks.rationale: Lets you tell how a couple met, married or divorced.
blocks.interference: Deau is a first or chance meeting, shiriau is getting acquainted; au is meeting up as planned.

items.use: 'Kekkon shite iru' means 'is married'; the partner takes to.

example.romaji: ani ga raigetsu kekkon suru n da.
example.ja: 兄が来月結婚するんだ。
example.english: My brother's getting married next month.

examplePolite.romaji: ani ga raigetsu kekkon suru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 兄が来月結婚するんです。
examplePolite.english: My brother's getting married next month.

items.english: meet (for the first time), come across
items.use: For a first meeting, often a meaningful one.

example.romaji: futari wa doko de deatta no?
example.ja: 二人はどこで出会ったの？
example.english: Where did you two meet?

examplePolite.romaji: futari wa doko de deatta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 二人はどこで出会ったんですか？
examplePolite.english: Where did you two meet?

items.notes: Au is meeting up as planned; deau is meeting for the first time or by chance.

items.use: The ex-partner takes to: 'Kare to rikon shita'.

example.romaji: ryoushin wa mukashi rikon shita n da.
example.ja: 両親は昔離婚したんだ。
example.english: My parents divorced a long time ago.

examplePolite.romaji: ryoushin wa mukashi rikon shita n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 両親は昔離婚したんです。
examplePolite.english: My parents divorced a long time ago.

items.use: Mostly in the past, for how people first met.

example.romaji: kanojo to wa shigoto de shiriatta n da.
example.ja: 彼女とは仕事で知り合ったんだ。
example.english: I met her through work.

examplePolite.romaji: kanojo to wa shigoto de shiriatta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 彼女とは仕事で知り合ったんです。
examplePolite.english: I met her through work.

items.notes: The noun shiriai means an acquaintance.

items.use: The person proposed to takes ni; 'puropoozu sareta' means 'got proposed to'.

example.ja: 昨日彼にプロポーズされた！
example.english: He proposed to me yesterday!

examplePolite.romaji: kinou kare ni puropoozu saremashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日彼にプロポーズされました。
examplePolite.english: He proposed to me yesterday.

items.notes: Only for marriage; a business proposal is teian.

blocks.label: Work and keep going
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about your job, things that go on, and getting used to them.
blocks.interference: Tsuzuku is 'it goes on' while tsuzukeru is 'keep doing it'.

example.ja: どこで働いてるの？
example.english: Where do you work?

examplePolite.romaji: doko de hataraite imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: どこで働いていますか？
examplePolite.english: Where do you work?

items.notes: Shigoto suru also works for 'work'. For a machine 'working', use ugoku.

items.use: Things going on by themselves: rain, a streak, a story; on screen it means 'to be continued'.

example.romaji: kono ame, itsu made tsuzuku n darou.
example.ja: この雨、いつまで続くんだろう。
example.english: I wonder how long this rain will keep up.

examplePolite.romaji: kono ame wa itsu made tsuzuku n deshou ne.
examplePolite.ja: この雨はいつまで続くんでしょうね。
examplePolite.english: I wonder how long this rain will keep up.

items.notes: Tsuzukeru is 'keep doing it' (you continue something): benkyou o tsuzukeru.

items.use: Takes ni (shigoto ni nareru); mostly heard as nareta (got used to it) or narete iru (am used to it).

example.ja: 新しい仕事、もう慣れた？
example.english: Used to the new job yet?

examplePolite.romaji: atarashii shigoto ni wa mou naremashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 新しい仕事にはもう慣れましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you got used to the new job yet?

items.notes: Same sound as nareru, 'can become' (the potential of naru).

blocks.label: Choose and decide
blocks.rationale: Lets you pick, settle plans and change them.
blocks.interference: Kimaru (it's decided) vs kimeru (I decide); henkou (change you make) vs henka (change that happens).

example.ja: どっちか選んで。
example.english: Pick one.

examplePolite.romaji: dochira ka erande kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: どちらか選んでください。
examplePolite.english: Please choose one.

items.notes: When ordering, 'X ni suru' is more natural: kore ni suru (I'll have this).

items.use: For plans, dates and orders once they're settled; who decided stays unsaid.

example.ja: 何食べるか決まった？
example.english: Have you decided what to eat?

examplePolite.romaji: nani o taberu ka kimarimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 何を食べるか決まりましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you decided what you'll have?

items.notes: Kimeru is the 'I decide it' partner. Waiters ask 'gochuumon wa okimari desu ka?' (ready to order?).

items.use: Sounds official; casually it's mostly the cry 'kettei!' (that's settled) or 'X ni kettei' (we'll go with X).

example.ja: じゃあ、ラーメンに決定！
example.english: Right, ramen it is!

examplePolite.romaji: jaa, raamen ni kettei desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: じゃあ、ラーメンに決定ですね。
examplePolite.english: Right, so ramen it is.

items.notes: Kettei suru is formal; in conversation say kimeru (decide) or kimaru (be decided).

items.use: Changing something already set; a little formal, common with staff and at work.

example.ja: 予約の時間、変更できる？
example.english: Can I change the booking time?

examplePolite.romaji: yoyaku no jikan o henkou dekimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 予約の時間を変更できますか？
examplePolite.english: Could I change the time of my booking?

items.notes: Casually, kaeru also works: yotei o kaeru. Henka is change that happens; henkou is change you make.

blocks.label: Borrow, return, hand over
blocks.rationale: Lets you borrow things, give them back, hand them over and bring them.
blocks.interference: Kariru (borrow) gets swapped with kasu (lend); kaesu (give back) sounds like kaeru (go home).

items.use: Takes kara or ni for the person you borrow from.

example.ja: ペン、ちょっと借りていい？
example.english: Can I borrow your pen a sec?

examplePolite.romaji: pen o chotto karite mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ペンをちょっと借りてもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: May I borrow your pen for a moment?

items.notes: Kasu is the opposite, lend; the two are easy to swap. 'Toire karite ii?' = can I use your bathroom?

items.english: give back; return; reply (to a message)
items.use: Returning borrowed things or money; also replying: henji o kaesu.

example.ja: この本、明日返すね。
example.english: I'll give this book back tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: kono hon, ashita kaeshimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この本、明日返しますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll return this book tomorrow.

items.notes: Kaesu (give back) sounds close to kaeru (go home). Kaette kuru = come back.

items.use: Physically handing something to someone: a gift, papers, a key.

example.ja: これ、彼に渡しといて。
example.english: Can you give this to him for me?

examplePolite.romaji: kore o kare ni watashite oite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: これを彼に渡しておいてください。
examplePolite.english: Please give this to him.

items.notes: Ageru is giving as a gift or favour; watasu is the physical handing over.

items.use: For bringing a person, use tsurete kuru.

example.ja: 傘持ってきた？
example.english: Did you bring an umbrella?

examplePolite.romaji: kasa o motte kimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 傘を持ってきましたか？
examplePolite.english: Did you bring an umbrella?

items.notes: Motte iku = take it there. Kuru points towards the speaker, iku away.

blocks.label: Left over and kept
blocks.rationale: Lets you say what's left and leave things with someone for safekeeping.
blocks.interference: Two mirror pairs: nokoru (be left) vs nokosu (leave it), and azukaru (keep it for someone) vs azukeru (leave it with someone).

items.use: For food, money, time or people still there after the rest has gone.

example.ja: ケーキ、まだ残ってる？
example.english: Is there any cake left?

examplePolite.romaji: keeki wa mada nokotte imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ケーキはまだ残っていますか？
examplePolite.english: Is there any cake left?

items.notes: Nokosu is 'leave it' (you do it). Kaisha ni nokoru = stay late at the office.

items.use: You leave some: food on the plate, a note, money for later.

example.ja: ごめん、ちょっと残しちゃった。
example.english: Sorry, I couldn't finish it.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, sukoshi nokoshite shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、少し残してしまいました。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I left a little.

items.notes: Nokoru is 'be left' (by itself). Messeeji o nokosu = leave a message.

items.english: look after (for someone); keep; take charge of
items.use: You hold something for someone: keys, bags, a pet, a child.

example.ja: 鍵、預かっとくね。
example.english: I'll hold on to the keys.

examplePolite.romaji: kagi wa watashi ga azukatte okimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 鍵は私が預かっておきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll keep the keys for you.

items.notes: Azukeru is the other side: you leave it with someone. Cashiers say 'sen'en oazukari shimasu' when taking your money.

items.use: Handing something over to be kept: a coat, luggage, a child, money at the bank.

example.ja: 荷物、フロントに預けよう。
example.english: Let's leave our bags at the front desk.

examplePolite.romaji: nimotsu o furonto ni azukemashou.
examplePolite.ja: 荷物をフロントに預けましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's leave our bags at the front desk.

items.notes: Azukaru is the other side, the person who keeps it.

blocks.label: Send and deliver
blocks.rationale: Lets you send things, ask if they've arrived, and carry or deliver them.
blocks.interference: Todoku is 'it arrives', todokeru is 'deliver it'; okuru (send) sounds like okureru (be late).

items.use: Messages, parcels and photos; also walking or driving someone home or to the station.

example.ja: 後で写真送るね。
example.english: I'll send you the photos later.

examplePolite.romaji: ato de shashin o okurimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 後で写真を送りますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll send you the photos later.

items.notes: Okutte iku yo = I'll take you home. Don't confuse with okureru, be late.

items.use: Things sent arriving; also being able to reach something high.

example.ja: 荷物、届いた？
example.english: Did the package arrive?

examplePolite.romaji: nimotsu wa todokimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 荷物は届きましたか？
examplePolite.english: Has the package arrived?

items.notes: Todokeru is 'deliver it' (you do it). Te ga todokanai = can't reach.

items.english: deliver; take (something) to someone; hand in
items.use: You take something to a person or place, like lost property to the police.

example.ja: 忘れ物、家まで届けるよ。
example.english: I'll bring what you left to your place.

examplePolite.romaji: wasuremono wa ie made todokemasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 忘れ物は家まで届けますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll bring what you left to your house.

items.notes: Todoku is 'arrive, reach' (by itself). Keisatsu ni todokeru = hand it in to the police.

items.use: Moving things, often heavy, from one place to another.

example.ja: これ、一緒に運んでくれる？
example.english: Can you help me carry this?

examplePolite.romaji: kore, issho ni hakonde moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: これ、一緒に運んでもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: Could you help me carry this?

items.notes: Motsu is 'hold, have on you'; hakobu is taking things somewhere.

blocks.label: Humble give and receive
blocks.rationale: Lets you receive and give politely, the way staff and guests do.
blocks.interference: Itadaku and sashiageru are humble; with friends, use morau and ageru.

items.use: Polite 'receive' from someone above you, and the modest way to say you'll eat or drink.

example.ja: じゃあ、遠慮なくいただくね。
example.english: Well, don't mind if I do.

examplePolite.romaji: dewa, enryo naku itadakimasu.
examplePolite.ja: では、遠慮なくいただきます。
examplePolite.english: Well then, I'll gladly accept.

items.notes: 'Itadakimasu' before a meal is the set phrase. After a te-form, -te itadaku is the politer -te morau, 'have someone do it'.

items.english: receive; accept; pick up (a parcel, tickets)
items.use: Taking something handed or sent to you; a bit more formal than morau.

example.ja: チケット、もう受け取った？
example.english: Have you picked up the tickets yet?

examplePolite.romaji: chiketto wa mou uketorimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: チケットはもう受け取りましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you received the tickets yet?

items.notes: Morau is the everyday 'get'; uketoru stresses taking it in hand: parcels, payments, gifts.

items.use: The humble 'give' toward customers or superiors; mostly heard from shop staff.

example.ja: 後ほど、こちらからお電話差し上げます。
example.english: We'll call you back later.

items.notes: Ageru is the everyday 'give'. Said to a friend, sashiageru sounds stiff or joking.

blocks.label: Find and lose
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about finding, losing, dropping, picking up and hiding things.
blocks.interference: Nakusu is losing an object, not a game (makeru); otosu (drop) and hirou (pick up) are a pair.

example.romaji: eki no chikaku de ii mise mitsuketa yo.
example.ja: 駅の近くでいい店見つけたよ。
example.english: I found a great place near the station.

examplePolite.romaji: eki no chikaku de ii mise o mitsukemashita.
examplePolite.ja: 駅の近くでいい店を見つけました。
examplePolite.english: I found a nice place near the station.

items.notes: Mitsukaru is 'be found': kagi ga mitsukatta (I found my keys).

items.use: Losing things you had, like keys or a wallet; also losing confidence or interest.

example.ja: また鍵なくした。
example.english: I've lost my keys again.

examplePolite.romaji: mata kagi o nakushimashita.
examplePolite.ja: また鍵をなくしました。
examplePolite.english: I've lost my keys again.

items.notes: Nakunaru is 'go missing, run out'. Losing a game is makeru, not nakusu.

items.use: Dropping things, or losing something while you were out: saifu o otoshita.

example.ja: 財布落としちゃった。
example.english: I've lost my wallet.

examplePolite.romaji: saifu o otoshite shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 財布を落としてしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I've lost my wallet.

items.notes: Ochiru is 'fall' (by itself). Keshou o otosu = take off make-up.

items.english: pick up (from the ground); find; catch (a taxi)
items.use: Picking things up off the floor or finding something lying around.

example.ja: 道で財布拾った。
example.english: I found a wallet on the street.

examplePolite.romaji: michi de saifu o hiroimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 道で財布を拾いました。
examplePolite.english: I found a wallet on the street.

items.notes: Opposite: suteru (throw away). Takushii o hirou = catch a taxi.

items.use: Hiding things, or keeping the truth or feelings to yourself.

example.ja: 何隠してるの？
example.english: What are you hiding?

examplePolite.romaji: nani o kakushite iru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 何を隠しているんですか？
examplePolite.english: What are you hiding?

items.notes: Kakureru is 'hide yourself, be hidden'.

items.use: Formal as a verb; casually it's a happy 'hakken!' or shinhakken (a new find).

example.ja: これおいしい！新発見だ。
example.english: This is great! What a find.

examplePolite.romaji: kore oishii desu ne! shinhakken desu.
examplePolite.ja: これおいしいですね！新発見です。
examplePolite.english: This is delicious! What a discovery.

items.notes: For the everyday 'find', use mitsukeru.

blocks.label: Push, pull, throw, catch
blocks.rationale: Lets you describe basic hand actions, from doors to balls to taxis.
blocks.interference: Hiku also means catching a cold, but tsukamaeru is catching a person, animal or taxi.

example.romaji: kono botan osu dake da yo.
example.ja: このボタン押すだけだよ。
example.english: You just press this button.

examplePolite.romaji: kono botan o osu dake desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: このボタンを押すだけですよ。
examplePolite.english: You just press this button.

items.notes: Opposite: hiku (pull). Jikan ga oshiteru = we're running behind.

items.english: pull; catch (a cold); look up (a word)
items.use: Doors marked hiku mean PULL; kaze o hiku is the set way to say you caught a cold.

example.ja: 風邪ひいちゃったみたい。
example.english: I think I've caught a cold.

examplePolite.romaji: kaze o hiite shimatta mitai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 風邪をひいてしまったみたいです。
examplePolite.english: I seem to have caught a cold.

items.notes: Slang hiku is 'be put off': chotto hiita (that was a bit much). Same sound as hiku 弾く, play (piano, guitar).

example.ja: ボール、こっちに投げて！
example.english: Throw the ball over here!

examplePolite.romaji: booru o kotchi ni nagete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: ボールをこっちに投げてください。
examplePolite.english: Please throw the ball over here.

items.notes: 'Throw away' is suteru. Nagedasu = give up, throw in the towel.

items.english: catch (a person, animal); grab; flag down (a taxi)
items.use: Catching something that moves: a thief, a bug, a taxi, a busy person.

example.ja: タクシー捕まえてくるね。
example.english: I'll go grab a taxi.

examplePolite.romaji: takushii o tsukamaete kimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: タクシーを捕まえてきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll go and get a taxi.

items.notes: Tsukamaru is 'be caught' or 'hold on'; tsukamu is 'grip, grab'.

blocks.label: Polite do and handle
blocks.rationale: Lets you follow shop and office talk about who will do or handle something.
blocks.interference: itasu lowers your own action and nasaru raises the other person's; swapping them is a real blunder.

items.use: Humble suru for your own actions, almost always as itashimasu in shops and business.

example.ja: こちらで確認いたします。
example.english: We'll check that for you.

items.notes: Set lines: shitsurei itashimasu, yoroshiku onegai itashimasu. Never for what the listener does.

items.use: Respectful suru for what the listener or a superior does.

example.romaji: okyakusama, onomimono wa dou nasaimasu ka?
example.ja: お客様、お飲み物はどうなさいますか？
example.english: And what would you like to drink?

items.notes: The masu form is irregular: nasaimasu. Never about yourself; that's itasu.

items.use: Handling a customer, problem or situation; common at work and in shops.

example.ja: これ、誰が対応する？
example.english: Who's going to handle this?

examplePolite.romaji: kore wa dare ga taiou shimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: これは誰が対応しますか？
examplePolite.english: Who will handle this?

items.notes: taiou ga hayai: quick to respond. Also 'supports': eigo taiou (English available).

blocks.label: How it turned out
blocks.rationale: Lets you say whether something worked, failed, got finished or passed.
blocks.interference: seikou suru sounds big; for everyday things, umaku iku is the natural 'it worked'.

items.use: Plans, work or relationships working out; umaku ikanai means it isn't working.

example.ja: 大丈夫、きっとうまくいくよ。
example.english: Don't worry, it'll work out.

examplePolite.romaji: daijoubu desu, kitto umaku ikimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 大丈夫です、きっとうまくいきますよ。
examplePolite.english: Don't worry, I'm sure it'll work out.

items.notes: Past is umaku itta (it went well).

items.use: Any failure, from a big project to burning dinner.

example.ja: 今日の料理、失敗しちゃった。
example.english: I messed up dinner today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou no ryouri wa shippai shite shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今日の料理は失敗してしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I'm afraid I messed up dinner today.

items.notes: X ni shippai suru: fail at X. Also a noun: shippai da (it's a flop). Opposite: seikou.

items.use: Sounds big for small things; for an everyday 'it worked', umaku iku is more natural.

example.ja: サプライズ、成功したね！
example.english: The surprise worked!

examplePolite.romaji: sapuraizu wa seikou shimashita ne!
examplePolite.ja: サプライズは成功しましたね！
examplePolite.english: The surprise worked!

items.notes: Also a noun: daiseikou (a huge success). Opposite: shippai.

items.use: Something being made is finished: a building, a dish, a project.

example.ja: 模型、やっと完成したよ！
example.english: My model's finally finished!

examplePolite.romaji: mokei ga yatto kansei shimashita!
examplePolite.ja: 模型がやっと完成しました！
examplePolite.english: My model is finally finished!

items.notes: The thing is the subject: ie ga kansei shita (the house is finished).

items.use: Passing an exam, interview or entrance test: shiken ni goukaku suru.

example.ja: 試験、合格したよ！
example.english: I passed the exam!

examplePolite.romaji: shiken ni goukaku shimashita!
examplePolite.ja: 試験に合格しました！
examplePolite.english: I passed the exam!

items.notes: Failing is ochiru: shiken ni ochita. goukaku omedetou! means 'congrats on passing'.

blocks.label: Getting work done
blocks.rationale: Lets you push a job forward, sort out a problem, wrap things up and take on tasks.
blocks.interference: susumeru (go ahead with) sounds the same as susumeru (recommend).

items.use: Pushing a plan, job or talks forward: shigoto o susumeru.

example.ja: じゃあ、このまま進めよう。
example.english: OK, let's carry on as we are.

examplePolite.romaji: dewa, kono mama susumemashou.
examplePolite.ja: では、このまま進めましょう。
examplePolite.english: Well then, let's carry on as we are.

items.notes: Sounds the same as susumeru 'recommend' (勧める). susumu is 'it moves forward'.

items.use: Works both ways: mondai o kaiketsu suru (solve it), mondai ga kaiketsu suru (it gets solved).

example.romaji: mondai wa mou kaiketsu shita yo.
example.ja: 問題はもう解決したよ。
example.english: The problem's already sorted.

examplePolite.romaji: mondai wa mou kaiketsu shimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 問題はもう解決しました。
examplePolite.english: The problem has already been solved.

items.notes: sore ja kaiketsu ni naranai: that doesn't solve anything.

items.use: Gathering things into one: notes, luggage, a group, an idea.

example.ja: 荷物、もう全部まとめた？
example.english: Have you packed up all your things?

examplePolite.romaji: nimotsu wa mou zenbu matomemashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 荷物はもう全部まとめましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you packed up all your things?

items.notes: hanashi o matomeru: wrap up a discussion. Noun: matome (summary).

items.english: take on; accept (a job or request)
items.use: Agreeing to take responsibility for a job or a favour.

example.romaji: ii yo, sono shigoto hikiukeru yo.
example.ja: いいよ、その仕事引き受けるよ。
example.english: Sure, I'll take that job on.

examplePolite.romaji: wakarimashita, sono shigoto o hikiukemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 分かりました、その仕事を引き受けます。
examplePolite.english: Understood, I'll take that job on.

items.notes: Polite set form: ohikiuke shimasu. To turn it down: kotowaru.

blocks.label: Trying and aiming high
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about goals, effort, trying things out and going head to head.
blocks.interference: tamesu tests something and chousen suru takes on something hard; everyday 'try doing' is -te miru.

items.use: Aiming at a goal or a place: X o mezasu (aim to become or reach X).

example.ja: 医者を目指してるんだ。
example.english: I'm working towards becoming a doctor.

examplePolite.romaji: isha o mezashite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 医者を目指しています。
examplePolite.english: I'm working towards becoming a doctor.

items.notes: Also for direction: choujou o mezasu (head for the summit).

items.use: A contest to decide who wins: a game, a bet, a moment of truth.

example.ja: じゃあ、じゃんけんで勝負しよう。
example.english: OK, let's settle it with rock-paper-scissors.

examplePolite.romaji: dewa, janken de shoubu shimashou.
examplePolite.ja: では、じゃんけんで勝負しましょう。
examplePolite.english: Well then, let's settle it with rock-paper-scissors.

items.notes: shoubu suru: go head to head. koko ga shoubu: this is the moment that counts.

items.use: Steady effort over time toward a goal.

example.romaji: kare wa sugoku doryoku shita n da yo.
example.ja: 彼はすごく努力したんだよ。
example.english: He worked really hard for it.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa sugoku doryoku shita n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 彼はすごく努力したんですよ。
examplePolite.english: He worked really hard for it.

items.notes: Also a noun: doryoku ga mukuwareta (the effort paid off). For a quick push, say ganbaru.

items.use: Testing something to see if it works or suits you.

example.ja: 新しいアプリ、試してみた？
example.english: Have you tried the new app?

examplePolite.romaji: atarashii apuri wa tameshite mimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 新しいアプリは試してみましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you tried the new app?

items.notes: For 'try doing', -te miru is more common: tabete miru (try eating it).

items.english: take on (a challenge); have a go at
items.use: Taking on something hard or new: X ni chousen suru.

example.romaji: kotoshi wa marason ni chousen suru n da.
example.ja: 今年はマラソンに挑戦するんだ。
example.english: This year I'm taking on a marathon.

examplePolite.romaji: kotoshi wa marason ni chousen shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今年はマラソンに挑戦します。
examplePolite.english: This year I'm taking on a marathon.

items.notes: English 'challenge' meaning a problem is kadai; chousen is the attempt itself.

blocks.label: Danger and escape
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about running away, getting dragged into trouble and bad experiences.
blocks.interference: me ni au uses 遭う (run into trouble), not 会う (meet someone).

items.use: Getting away from danger or a place, or ducking a hard situation.

example.ja: ここは危ない、早く逃げて！
example.english: It's dangerous here, get out quick!

examplePolite.romaji: koko wa abunai desu, hayaku nigete kudasai!
examplePolite.ja: ここは危ないです、早く逃げてください！
examplePolite.english: It's dangerous here, please get out quickly!

items.notes: nigeru na! (don't run away!) is a stock drama line. Also 'avoid facing': genjitsu kara nigeru (run from reality).

items.use: Mostly heard in crime dramas, and as an angry threat: korosu zo!

example.romaji: kare wa mushi mo korosenai yo.
example.ja: 彼は虫も殺せないよ。
example.english: He wouldn't hurt a fly.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa mushi mo korosenai hito desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 彼は虫も殺せない人ですよ。
examplePolite.english: He's someone who wouldn't hurt a fly.

items.notes: Passive korosareru: be killed. Also 'hold back': koe o korosu (keep your voice down).

items.use: Often passive: X ni makikomareru (get caught up in an accident, a fight, trouble).

example.romaji: gomen, hen na koto ni makikonjatta.
example.ja: ごめん、変なことに巻き込んじゃった。
example.english: Sorry for dragging you into this mess.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, hen na koto ni makikonde shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、変なことに巻き込んでしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry for dragging you into this mess.

items.notes: jiko ni makikomareta: got caught up in an accident.

items.english: go through (something bad); have a bad time
items.use: Always after a describing word: hidoi me ni au (have an awful time), abunai me ni au (have a close call).

example.romaji: kinou hidoi me ni atta yo.
example.ja: 昨日ひどい目に遭ったよ。
example.english: I had an awful time yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou wa hidoi me ni aimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日はひどい目に遭いました。
examplePolite.english: I had an awful time yesterday.

items.notes: au here is 遭う (run into trouble), not 会う (meet someone).

blocks.label: Living your life
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about being alive, how you live and how you spend your time.
blocks.interference: ikiru and kurasu both translate as 'live', but where you live is sumu.

items.use: Being alive or living a certain way; not for where you live.

example.ja: 自分のために生きたい。
example.english: I want to live for myself.

examplePolite.romaji: jibun no tame ni ikitai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 自分のために生きたいです。
examplePolite.english: I want to live for myself.

items.notes: Where you live is sumu: Tokyo ni sunde iru. ikiteru means 'alive'.

items.use: Day-to-day living, who with and how: hitori de kurasu (live alone).

example.ja: 今は一人で暮らしてる。
example.english: I live on my own now.

examplePolite.romaji: ima wa hitori de kurashite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今は一人で暮らしています。
examplePolite.english: I live on my own now.

items.notes: Noun: kurashi (life, lifestyle); hitorigurashi is living alone.

items.use: Spending a stretch of time a certain way: holidays, weekends, time with someone.

example.ja: 週末はどう過ごした？
example.english: How did you spend the weekend?

examplePolite.romaji: shuumatsu wa dou sugoshimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 週末はどう過ごしましたか？
examplePolite.english: How did you spend the weekend?

items.notes: For spending money, use tsukau.

blocks.label: Men, women, people
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about men, women and people in general.
blocks.interference: otoko and onna sound blunt about a specific person; josei or otoko no hito is the polite choice.

items.use: On its own it sounds blunt about a specific man; otoko no hito is the neutral way to say 'a man'.

example.romaji: otoko tte hontou ni baka da yo ne.
example.ja: 男って本当にバカだよね。
example.english: Men are so dumb, aren't they?

examplePolite.romaji: otoko tte hontou ni baka desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 男って本当にバカですよね。
examplePolite.english: Men are so dumb, aren't they?

items.notes: otoko no ko is a boy. Opposite: onna.

items.use: On its own it sounds blunt, even rude, about a specific woman; onna no hito is the neutral way to say 'a woman'.

example.ja: 女って難しいな。
example.english: Women are hard to figure out.

examplePolite.romaji: onna tte muzukashii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 女って難しいですね。
examplePolite.english: Women are hard to figure out, aren't they?

items.notes: onna no ko is a girl. Opposite: otoko.

items.use: Stresses being human or what kind of person someone is; for 'a person' in daily talk, hito is the usual word.

example.romaji: ningen dakara, machigai mo aru yo.
example.ja: 人間だから、間違いもあるよ。
example.english: We're only human. Mistakes happen.

examplePolite.romaji: ningen desu kara, machigai mo arimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 人間ですから、間違いもありますよ。
examplePolite.english: We're only human. Mistakes happen.

items.notes: ningen kankei: relationships with the people around you, at work or school.

items.use: The polite, neutral word for a woman, common in news, shops and whenever you want to sound respectful.

example.romaji: ano josei, dare da ka shitteru?
example.ja: あの女性、誰だか知ってる？
example.english: Do you know who that woman is?

examplePolite.romaji: ano josei, dare da ka shitte imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: あの女性、誰だか知っていますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you know who that woman is?

items.notes: The male counterpart is dansei. Softer than onna.

blocks.label: Who someone is to you
blocks.rationale: Lets you say how you know someone: teacher, senior, or just an acquaintance.
blocks.interference: sensei also means a doctor, and senpai is anyone who started before you, not a mentor.

items.use: Also a title for doctors, lawyers and writers, used alone or after a name: Tanaka-sensei.

example.ja: 先生に聞いてみよう。
example.english: Let's ask the teacher.

examplePolite.romaji: sensei ni kiite mimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 先生に聞いてみましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's ask the teacher.

items.notes: Never used about yourself.

items.use: Anyone who joined your school, club or company before you; used as a name, alone or after a surname.

example.ja: 先輩にご飯おごってもらった。
example.english: My senpai bought me dinner.

examplePolite.romaji: senpai ni gohan o ogotte moraimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 先輩にご飯をおごってもらいました。
examplePolite.english: My senpai bought me dinner.

items.notes: Opposite: kouhai (junior). You usually speak to a senpai in desu/masu.

items.use: Someone you know but aren't close to.

example.ja: あの人、知り合いなの？
example.english: Do you know that person?

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito, shiriai na n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: あの人、知り合いなんですか？
examplePolite.english: Do you know that person?

items.notes: A friend is tomodachi. shiriai ni naru: get to know someone.

items.use: People on the same side: a team, a crew, a close group of friends.

example.romaji: minna daiji na nakama da yo.
example.ja: みんな大事な仲間だよ。
example.english: They're all friends who matter to me.

examplePolite.romaji: minna daiji na nakama desu.
examplePolite.ja: みんな大事な仲間です。
examplePolite.english: They're all friends who matter to me.

items.notes: Warmer and more group-minded than tomodachi.

items.use: Every single member of a set group, like a class, team or family.

example.ja: じゃあ、全員そろったから始めよう。
example.english: OK, everyone's here, so let's start.

examplePolite.romaji: dewa, zen'in soroimashita node hajimemashou.
examplePolite.ja: では、全員そろいましたので始めましょう。
examplePolite.english: Well, everyone's here, so let's begin.

items.notes: minna is the casual 'everyone'; zen'in stresses that nobody is left out.

blocks.label: Customers and crowds
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about customers, a crowd, or the person in question.
blocks.interference: kyaku alone sounds blunt; okyakusan is the everyday form.

items.use: The everyday polite way to say kyaku; used by staff and hosts alike.

example.ja: 今日はお客さん多いね。
example.english: Lots of customers today, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa okyakusan ga ooi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はお客さんが多いですね。
examplePolite.english: There are a lot of customers today.

items.notes: Shop staff say okyakusama to customers' faces.

items.use: The plain form; sounds blunt on its own, so say okyakusan when customers can hear.

example.romaji: ano mise, kyaku zenzen inakatta yo.
example.ja: あの店、客全然いなかったよ。
example.english: That place had no customers at all.

examplePolite.romaji: ano mise wa kyaku ga zenzen imasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: あの店は客が全然いませんでした。
examplePolite.english: That shop had no customers at all.

items.english: the person themselves; the person in question
items.use: Points to the person being talked about, as opposed to others speaking for them.

example.ja: 本人に聞いてよ。
example.english: Just ask them directly.

examplePolite.romaji: gohonnin ni kiite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: ご本人に聞いてください。
examplePolite.english: Please ask the person directly.

items.notes: Add go- (gohonnin) when speaking politely about someone else.

items.use: Only for people, never things; often oozei no hito.

example.ja: 昨日、大勢来て大変だった。
example.english: Tons of people came yesterday, it was crazy.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou wa oozei kite taihen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日は大勢来て大変でした。
examplePolite.english: Lots of people came yesterday, so it was hectic.

items.notes: Mix-up: takusan works for anything; oozei is people only.

blocks.label: Plans and occasions
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about plans, this time, today and the other day.
blocks.interference: honjitsu and senjitsu are formal; in chat use kyou and kono aida.

items.use: The current occasion, compared with past or future ones.

example.romaji: konkai wa watashi ga ogoru yo.
example.ja: 今回は私がおごるよ。
example.english: This time it's my treat.

examplePolite.romaji: konkai wa watashi ga ogorimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今回は私がおごります。
examplePolite.english: This time it's on me.

items.notes: Last time is zenkai. kondo can mean this time but usually means next time.

items.use: yotei ga aru = I have plans; after a verb it means you plan to do it.

example.ja: 週末、何か予定ある？
example.english: Got any plans this weekend?

examplePolite.romaji: shuumatsu wa nanika yotei ga arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 週末は何か予定がありますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you have any plans this weekend?

items.notes: ashita iku yotei = I'm planning to go tomorrow.

items.use: The formal word heard in shops, announcements and business; in chat say kyou.

example.ja: 本日はありがとうございました。
example.english: Thank you for today.

items.use: Polite; in chat people say kono aida.

example.ja: 先日はお世話になりました。
example.english: Thank you for your help the other day.

blocks.label: Life and living
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about your life, its chances, struggles and memories.
blocks.interference: jinsei is life as a whole; seikatsu is daily living.

items.use: Life as a whole story; daily routine is seikatsu.

example.ja: 人生で一番楽しかった。
example.english: That was the most fun I've had in my life.

examplePolite.romaji: jinsei de ichiban tanoshikatta desu.
examplePolite.ja: 人生で一番楽しかったです。
examplePolite.english: It was the most fun I've ever had.

items.notes: Not life as in being alive; that's inochi.

items.use: Your everyday routine and how you get by.

example.ja: こっちの生活、もう慣れた？
example.english: Used to life here yet?

examplePolite.romaji: kochira no seikatsu ni wa mou naremashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: こちらの生活にはもう慣れましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you gotten used to life here?

items.notes: Also seikatsu suru: to live, get by.

items.use: A good opportunity, not a probability.

example.ja: 今がチャンスだよ！
example.english: Now's your chance!

examplePolite.romaji: ima ga chansu desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 今がチャンスですよ。
examplePolite.english: Now is your chance.

items.notes: For likelihood, say kanousei.

items.use: Mostly as kurou suru (to struggle, have a hard time).

example.romaji: heya sagashi, kekkou kurou shita yo.
example.ja: 部屋探し、結構苦労したよ。
example.english: Finding an apartment was a real struggle.

examplePolite.romaji: heya sagashi ni wa kekkou kurou shimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 部屋探しには結構苦労しました。
examplePolite.english: I had quite a hard time finding an apartment.

items.notes: gokurousama = thanks for your hard work, said to staff or juniors.

items.use: A memory you keep, not the ability to remember.

example.ja: いい思い出になったね。
example.english: That turned into a great memory.

examplePolite.romaji: ii omoide ni narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: いい思い出になりました。
examplePolite.english: It became a wonderful memory.

items.notes: The verb is omoidasu (to recall).

blocks.label: Past present and future
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about the past, the present and the future.
blocks.interference: mirai is the big future; your own future is shourai.

items.use: Also for periods of your own life: gakusei jidai (student days).

example.romaji: gakusei jidai wa okane nakatta naa.
example.ja: 学生時代はお金なかったなあ。
example.english: I had no money back in my student days.

examplePolite.romaji: gakusei jidai wa okane ga arimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 学生時代はお金がありませんでした。
examplePolite.english: I didn't have any money in my student days.

items.notes: jidai ga chigau (times have changed) is a common line.

items.use: The big, open-ended future.

example.romaji: mirai no koto nante wakannai yo.
example.ja: 未来のことなんてわかんないよ。
example.english: Nobody knows the future.

examplePolite.romaji: mirai no koto wa wakarimasen yo.
examplePolite.ja: 未来のことはわかりませんよ。
examplePolite.english: No one can know the future.

items.notes: Mix-up: your own future (career, plans) is usually shourai.

items.use: Often someone's history: kako no koto (what happened before).

example.romaji: kako no koto wa mou ii yo.
example.ja: 過去のことはもういいよ。
example.english: Let's forget about the past.

examplePolite.romaji: kako no koto wa mou ii desu.
examplePolite.ja: 過去のことはもういいです。
examplePolite.english: The past doesn't matter anymore.

items.notes: For 'long ago', mukashi is often more natural.

items.use: Sounds formal, as on forms, news and announcements; in chat say ima.

example.romaji: genzai no juusho, koko ni kaite ne.
example.ja: 現在の住所、ここに書いてね。
example.english: Write your current address here.

examplePolite.romaji: genzai no juusho o koko ni kaite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 現在の住所をここに書いてください。
examplePolite.english: Please write your current address here.

items.notes: genzaichi = 'you are here' on maps.

blocks.label: Pointing to a time
blocks.rationale: Lets you place events in time: back when, before, from now, the moment.
blocks.interference: izen and kongo are a bit formal; in chat use mae and kore kara.

items.use: Follows a description: kodomo no koro (when I was a kid).

example.romaji: kodomo no koro, koko de yoku asondeta.
example.ja: 子供の頃、ここでよく遊んでた。
example.english: I used to play here a lot as a kid.

examplePolite.romaji: kodomo no koro, koko de yoku asonde imashita.
examplePolite.ja: 子供の頃、ここでよく遊んでいました。
examplePolite.english: I often played here when I was a child.

items.notes: After a clock time it becomes -goro: sanji goro (around three).

items.use: A bit formal; in chat people mostly say kore kara.

example.ja: 今後気をつけてね。
example.english: Be more careful from now on.

examplePolite.romaji: kongo wa ki o tsukemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今後は気をつけます。
examplePolite.english: I'll be more careful from now on.

items.notes: kongo tomo yoroshiku onegai shimasu is a set business sign-off.

items.use: After a past-form verb: mita shunkan (the moment I saw it).

example.ja: 顔見た瞬間、わかったよ。
example.english: I knew the moment I saw his face.

examplePolite.romaji: kao o mita shunkan, wakarimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 顔を見た瞬間、わかりました。
examplePolite.english: I knew the instant I saw his face.

items.use: A little formal; in chat people usually say mae.

example.romaji: izen koko de hataraiteta n da.
example.ja: 以前ここで働いてたんだ。
example.english: I used to work here.

examplePolite.romaji: izen koko de hataraite imashita.
examplePolite.ja: 以前ここで働いていました。
examplePolite.english: I used to work here.

items.notes: X izen = X or earlier: sanji izen (by three).

blocks.label: The future and chances
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about what's ahead and the chances you get.
blocks.interference: Kikai (an opportunity) vs kanousei (a likelihood); shourai vs mirai for 'future'.

items.use: Your own future, career and life plans: shourai no yume (your dream for the future).

example.ja: 将来、何になりたい?
example.english: What do you want to be when you grow up?

examplePolite.romaji: shourai, nani ni naritai desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 将来、何になりたいですか?
examplePolite.english: What would you like to do in the future?

items.notes: Mirai is the future in general (the world, sci-fi); shourai is a person's own.

example.ja: ちょっとタイミングが悪かったね
example.english: The timing was a bit off, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto taimingu ga warukatta desu ne
examplePolite.ja: ちょっとタイミングが悪かったですね
examplePolite.english: The timing was a bit off, wasn't it?

items.notes: Taimingu ga ii = good timing. Taimingu o miru = wait for the right moment.

items.use: How likely something is (~ kanousei ga aru, it might ~), or someone's potential.

example.romaji: ame ni naru kanousei mo aru yo
example.ja: 雨になる可能性もあるよ
example.english: There's a chance it'll rain, too.

examplePolite.romaji: ame ni naru kanousei mo arimasu yo
examplePolite.ja: 雨になる可能性もありますよ
examplePolite.english: There's a chance it'll rain, too.

items.notes: Kanousei wa zero ja nai = it's not impossible. An opportunity is kikai, not kanousei.

items.use: Both time (from here on) and place (further along this way).

example.romaji: kono saki dou naru ka wakaranai
example.ja: この先どうなるかわからない
example.english: I don't know what'll happen from here.

examplePolite.romaji: kono saki dou naru ka wakarimasen
examplePolite.ja: この先どうなるかわかりません
examplePolite.english: I don't know what'll happen from here.

items.notes: For places: eki wa kono saki desu (the station is just up ahead). For time, kore kara is the plainer word.

items.use: A chance to do something: ~ kikai ga aru / nai. Mata no kikai ni = some other time.

example.romaji: nakanaka au kikai ga nai ne
example.ja: なかなか会う機会がないね
example.english: We hardly ever get a chance to meet, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: nakanaka au kikai ga arimasen ne
examplePolite.ja: なかなか会う機会がありませんね
examplePolite.english: We hardly ever get a chance to meet, do we?

items.notes: Sounds the same as kikai (machine). Chansu is the casual, big-break 'chance'.

blocks.label: Happiness and thanks
blocks.rationale: Lets you say you're happy, grateful, smiling or still hopeful.
blocks.interference: Shiawase is deep happiness; for 'glad about this one thing' learners should still reach for ureshii.

items.use: For a warm, settled happiness about your life or a moment.

example.romaji: oishii mono tabeteru toki ga ichiban shiawase
example.ja: おいしいもの食べてる時が一番幸せ
example.english: I'm happiest when I'm eating something good.

examplePolite.romaji: oishii mono o tabete iru toki ga ichiban shiawase desu
examplePolite.ja: おいしいものを食べている時が一番幸せです
examplePolite.english: I'm happiest when I'm eating something good.

items.notes: Glad about one specific thing (good news, a gift) is ureshii, not shiawase.

items.use: Heavier than arigatou: deep thanks, often to family or for long-term help.

example.romaji: oya ni wa hontou ni kansha shiteru
example.ja: 親には本当に感謝してる
example.english: I'm really grateful to my parents.

examplePolite.romaji: ryoushin ni wa hontou ni kansha shite imasu
examplePolite.ja: 両親には本当に感謝しています
examplePolite.english: I'm truly grateful to my parents.

items.notes: Grateful to someone: [person] ni kansha suru. Kansha shika nai = I can't thank you enough.

items.use: The smile as a thing someone has; the verb 'to smile' is warau.

example.romaji: ano ko, egao ga kawaii yo ne
example.ja: あの子、笑顔がかわいいよね
example.english: She's got a cute smile, hasn't she?

examplePolite.romaji: ano kata wa egao ga suteki desu ne
examplePolite.ja: あの方は笑顔がすてきですね
examplePolite.english: She has a lovely smile, doesn't she?

items.notes: Egao de = with a smile. Egao ni naru = break into a smile.

items.use: Big-picture hope (there's still hope), and in bookings or shops, what you'd prefer.

example.ja: まだ希望はあるよ
example.english: There's still hope.

examplePolite.romaji: mada kibou wa arimasu yo
examplePolite.ja: まだ希望はありますよ
examplePolite.english: There's still hope.

items.notes: Kibou no jikan = the time you'd like (for a delivery or booking). For personal dreams, people often say yume.

blocks.label: Relief and worry
blocks.rationale: Lets you say a worry has lifted or is still there, and whether you're satisfied.
blocks.interference: Two pairs that sound alike: anshin / fuan and manzoku / fuman.

items.use: Said when a worry lifts; anshin shite (don't worry) reassures someone.

example.romaji: buji de yokatta, anshin shita yo
example.ja: 無事でよかった、安心したよ
example.english: I'm so glad you're safe. What a relief.

examplePolite.romaji: buji de yokatta desu, anshin shimashita
examplePolite.ja: 無事でよかったです、安心しました
examplePolite.english: I'm so glad you're safe. What a relief.

items.notes: Opposite: fuan (anxious). Hotto suru is a softer 'feel relieved'.

items.use: A nagging worry about what's coming, not sudden fear.

example.ja: 明日の面接、ちょっと不安
example.english: I'm a bit nervous about tomorrow's interview.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita no mensetsu ga chotto fuan desu
examplePolite.ja: 明日の面接がちょっと不安です
examplePolite.english: I'm a bit nervous about tomorrow's interview.

items.notes: Fuan ni naru = start to worry. Shinpai is worry about a specific thing or person; fuan is a general uneasy feeling.

items.use: Being content with a result or situation; also a jab: kore de manzoku? (Happy now?).

example.romaji: kono kekka ni wa manzoku shiteru
example.ja: この結果には満足してる
example.english: I'm happy with how this turned out.

examplePolite.romaji: kono kekka ni wa manzoku shite imasu
examplePolite.ja: この結果には満足しています
examplePolite.english: I'm happy with how this turned out.

items.notes: Opposite: fuman. Also a na-adjective: manzoku na kekka (a satisfying result).

items.use: A grievance you hold; most often fuman ga aru (have a complaint).

example.ja: なんか不満でもあるの?
example.english: Got a problem with that?

examplePolite.romaji: nanika fuman demo arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 何か不満でもありますか?
examplePolite.english: Is there something you're unhappy with?

items.notes: Opposite: manzoku. Fumansou na kao = a disgruntled look.

blocks.label: Relationships and boundaries
