blocks.rationale: Lets you ask how people are connected and say what's your own business.
blocks.interference: Jiyuu means free to choose, not free of charge.

items.use: Links between people or things: futari no kankei (their relationship), ~ to kankei ga aru (be connected to ~).

example.ja: あの二人、どういう関係?
example.english: What's the deal with those two?

examplePolite.romaji: ano futari wa dou iu kankei desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: あの二人はどういう関係ですか?
examplePolite.english: How do those two know each other?

items.notes: Ningen kankei = relationships with people (at work, school). The negative kankei nai is very common.

items.english: has nothing to do with; doesn't matter
items.use: A curt shutdown in arguments, and 'doesn't matter': toshi wa kankei nai (age doesn't matter).

example.romaji: sore, ima no hanashi to kankei nai yo
example.ja: それ、今の話と関係ないよ
example.english: That's got nothing to do with what we're talking about.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa ima no hanashi to kankei arimasen yo
examplePolite.ja: それは今の話と関係ありませんよ
examplePolite.english: That has nothing to do with what we're talking about.

items.notes: Anata ni wa kankei nai = it's none of your business; it sounds cold.

items.use: Free to do as you like, not free of charge (that's tada or muryou).

example.romaji: kyou wa jiyuu ni shite ii yo
example.ja: 今日は自由にしていいよ
example.english: You can do whatever you like today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa jiyuu ni shite ii desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 今日は自由にしていいですよ
examplePolite.english: Feel free to do whatever you like today.

items.notes: Jiyuu ni = freely, as you like. Jiyuu jikan = free time.

items.use: Your life outside work: puraibeeto na koto (personal stuff), puraibeeto de (in your own time).

example.ja: 仕事とプライベートは分けたい
example.english: I want to keep work and my private life separate.

examplePolite.romaji: shigoto to puraibeeto wa waketai desu
examplePolite.ja: 仕事とプライベートは分けたいです
examplePolite.english: I'd like to keep work and my private life separate.

items.notes: Puraibeeto de au = meet socially, not for work.

blocks.label: Situations and ways
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about what's going on, how things stand, and what to do if.
blocks.interference: Joukyou (situation) and joutai (condition) sound alike.

items.use: After a verb or noun to mean 'in case of' or 'if': okureru baai wa (if you'll be late).

example.romaji: okureru baai wa renraku shite ne
example.ja: 遅れる場合は連絡してね
example.english: If you're going to be late, let me know.

examplePolite.romaji: okureru baai wa renraku shite kudasai
examplePolite.ja: 遅れる場合は連絡してください
examplePolite.english: If you're going to be late, please let us know.

items.notes: Sonna koto itteru baai ja nai = this is no time to be saying that.

items.use: The overall situation or what's going on: ima no joukyou (the current situation).

example.romaji: ima dou iu joukyou na no?
example.ja: 今どういう状況なの?
example.english: So what's going on right now?

examplePolite.romaji: ima dou iu joukyou desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今どういう状況ですか?
examplePolite.english: What's the situation right now?

items.notes: Joutai is the condition of one person or thing; joukyou is the wider picture.

items.use: A way to get something done: ~ houhou ga nai (there's no way to ~), ii houhou (a good way).

example.romaji: hoka ni houhou wa nai no?
example.ja: 他に方法はないの?
example.english: Isn't there any other way?

examplePolite.romaji: hoka ni houhou wa arimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 他に方法はありませんか?
examplePolite.english: Is there no other way?

items.notes: Yarikata is the casual 'way of doing it'. Shikata ga nai = it can't be helped.

items.use: How a person or thing is doing: kanja no joutai (the patient's condition), kuruma no joutai.

example.romaji: konna joutai de shigoto nante muri da yo
example.ja: こんな状態で仕事なんて無理だよ
example.english: There's no way I can work in this state.

examplePolite.romaji: konna joutai de shigoto wa muri desu
examplePolite.ja: こんな状態で仕事は無理です
examplePolite.english: I can't work in this condition.

items.notes: Sounds close to joukyou (situation); joutai is about how one thing is doing.

blocks.label: Reasons and facts
blocks.rationale: Lets you give the why, the facts, the backstory and who's to blame.
blocks.interference: Jijitsu (fact) vs jitsu wa (actually) vs jijou (circumstances).

items.use: Asking or giving the why: riyuu wa? (why?), riyuu ga aru (there's a reason).

example.romaji: betsu ni riyuu wa nai kedo
example.ja: 別に理由はないけど
example.english: No particular reason, though.

examplePolite.romaji: betsu ni riyuu wa arimasen kedo
examplePolite.ja: 別に理由はありませんけど
examplePolite.english: There's no particular reason, though.

items.notes: To just ask why, people say naze or doushite. An excuse is iiwake.

items.use: Taking or placing blame: ~ no sekinin (someone's fault).

example.romaji: zenbu watashi no sekinin da yo
example.ja: 全部私の責任だよ
example.english: It's all my fault.

examplePolite.romaji: subete watashi no sekinin desu
examplePolite.ja: すべて私の責任です
examplePolite.english: It's entirely my responsibility.

items.notes: Sekinin o toru = take responsibility. Sekininkan = a sense of responsibility.

items.use: What actually happened, as opposed to rumor or opinion.

example.romaji: uwasa ja nakute jijitsu da yo
example.ja: 噂じゃなくて事実だよ
example.english: It's not a rumor, it's a fact.

examplePolite.romaji: uwasa de wa naku jijitsu desu
examplePolite.ja: 噂ではなく事実です
examplePolite.english: It's not a rumor, it's a fact.

items.notes: Don't mix it up with jitsu wa (actually, to be honest). The everyday 'true' is hontou.

items.use: The background behind something, often private: jijou ga aru (there are reasons I'd rather not explain).

example.romaji: ironna jijou ga atte, ikenaku natta
example.ja: いろんな事情があって、行けなくなった
example.english: Some things came up, so now I can't go.

examplePolite.romaji: iroiro na jijou ga atte, ikenaku narimashita
examplePolite.ja: いろいろな事情があって、行けなくなりました
examplePolite.english: Due to various circumstances, I'm no longer able to go.

items.notes: A polite, vague way to avoid explaining. Joukyou is the situation as it stands now.

blocks.label: Right, wrong, opposite
blocks.rationale: Lets you call something a mistake, the right call, or the other way round.
blocks.interference: Gyaku is just the reverse; hantai also means being against something.

example.ja: これ、なんか間違いじゃない？
example.english: Isn't this some kind of mistake?

examplePolite.romaji: kore wa nanika no machigai ja nai desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: これは何かの間違いじゃないですか？
examplePolite.english: Isn't this some kind of mistake?

items.notes: Machigai nai = definitely, no doubt; the verb is machigaeru (get wrong).

items.english: the opposite; the other way round, reverse
items.use: Often 'gyaku ni' (actually, on the contrary) to flip what was just said.

example.romaji: gyaku da yo, migi ja nakute hidari.
example.ja: 逆だよ、右じゃなくて左。
example.english: Other way round, it's left, not right.

examplePolite.romaji: gyaku desu yo, migi ja nakute hidari desu.
examplePolite.ja: 逆ですよ、右じゃなくて左です。
examplePolite.english: It's the other way round: left, not right.

items.use: Two uses: being against something (hantai suru), and the opposite side or direction.

example.ja: 結婚、親に反対された。
example.english: My parents were against the marriage.

examplePolite.romaji: kekkon o oya ni hantai saremashita.
examplePolite.ja: 結婚を親に反対されました。
examplePolite.english: My parents were against the marriage.

items.notes: Hantai gawa = the other side; for 'the reverse', gyaku is more natural.

items.use: Often said of a decision that turned out well: X shite seikai datta.

example.ja: 傘持ってきて正解だった。
example.english: Good thing I brought an umbrella.

examplePolite.romaji: kasa o motte kite seikai deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 傘を持ってきて正解でした。
examplePolite.english: Good thing I brought an umbrella.

items.notes: Called out in quizzes: Seikai! (Correct!).

blocks.label: Information and secrets
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about things you find out, read, keep track of or keep quiet.
blocks.interference: Kiroku (record) and kiji (article) sound alike.

example.romaji: kore, minna ni wa himitsu ne.
example.ja: これ、みんなには秘密ね。
example.english: Keep this a secret from everyone, okay?

examplePolite.romaji: kore wa minna ni wa himitsu ni shite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: これはみんなには秘密にしてください。
examplePolite.english: Please keep this a secret from everyone.

items.notes: Himitsu ni suru = keep something secret.

items.use: Facts you find out or are told; often in thanks for a useful tip.

example.ja: 情報ありがとう、本当に助かった。
example.english: Thanks for the info, that really helped.

examplePolite.romaji: jouhou arigatou gozaimasu, hontou ni tasukarimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 情報ありがとうございます、本当に助かりました。
examplePolite.english: Thanks for the information, it really helped.

items.use: Kiroku suru = write down, log; also a record in sport (shin kiroku = a new record).

example.ja: 毎日体重を記録してる。
example.english: I log my weight every day.

examplePolite.romaji: mainichi taijuu o kiroku shite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 毎日体重を記録しています。
examplePolite.english: I log my weight every day.

items.notes: For recording sound or video, say rokuon or rokuga.

example.ja: 昨日面白い記事読んだよ。
example.english: I read an interesting article yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou omoshiroi kiji o yomimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日面白い記事を読みました。
examplePolite.english: I read an interesting article yesterday.

items.notes: Same sound as kiji 'fabric' or 'dough' (生地); context makes it clear.

blocks.label: From place to world
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about where things are, from one spot to the whole world.
blocks.interference: Sekai is the world; sekaijuu means all over it.

items.use: A specific spot where something is or happens, including a spot to sit or park.

example.ja: いい場所知ってるよ。
example.english: I know a good place.

examplePolite.romaji: ii basho o shitte imasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: いい場所を知っていますよ。
examplePolite.english: I know a good place.

items.notes: Tokoro is the vaguer, softer 'place'; in questions, 'where' is doko.

items.english: town; part of town, the streets
items.use: Can mean a small town or the busy streets of a city, as in going into town.

example.ja: この町、静かで好き。
example.english: I like this town, it's quiet.

examplePolite.romaji: kono machi wa shizuka de suki desu.
examplePolite.ja: この町は静かで好きです。
examplePolite.english: I like this town; it's quiet.

items.notes: Also written 街 for a busy city area; same sound.

items.use: Also a field or scene, like the world of music or fashion.

example.romaji: sekai de ichiban suki na tabemono wa raamen.
example.ja: 世界で一番好きな食べ物はラーメン。
example.english: Ramen is my favourite food in the whole world.

examplePolite.romaji: sekai de ichiban suki na tabemono wa raamen desu.
examplePolite.ja: 世界で一番好きな食べ物はラーメンです。
examplePolite.english: Ramen is my favourite food in the whole world.

items.notes: Sekai ichi = the best in the world, often said playfully about food or a person.

items.english: all over the world; the whole world
items.use: -juu means throughout, as in ichinichijuu (all day long).

example.romaji: sekaijuu de ninki aru n da yo.
example.ja: 世界中で人気あるんだよ。
example.english: It's popular all over the world.

examplePolite.romaji: sekaijuu de ninki ga aru n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 世界中で人気があるんですよ。
examplePolite.english: It's popular all over the world.

blocks.label: Jobs and days off
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about your job, your pay and your time off.
blocks.interference: Yasumi is the day off itself; the verb to rest or take off is yasumu.

example.romaji: ashita yasumi da kara asobi ni ikou yo
example.ja: 明日休みだから遊びに行こうよ
example.english: I'm off tomorrow, let's go out.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa yasumi na node asobi ni ikimashou
examplePolite.ja: 明日は休みなので遊びに行きましょう
examplePolite.english: I'm off tomorrow, so let's go out.

items.notes: Natsuyasumi is the summer holiday, hiruyasumi the lunch break. The verb is yasumu.

items.use: Short for arubaito; the usual word for students' jobs and side jobs.

example.ja: 今日バイトあるから無理
example.english: I can't today, I've got work.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa baito ga aru node muri desu
examplePolite.ja: 今日はバイトがあるので無理です
examplePolite.english: I can't today because I have my part-time job.

items.notes: Baito suru means work part-time.

example.romaji: kongetsu, kyuuryou chotto sukunakatta n da
example.ja: 今月、給料ちょっと少なかったんだ
example.english: My pay was a bit low this month.

examplePolite.romaji: kongetsu wa kyuuryou ga chotto sukunakatta n desu
examplePolite.ja: 今月は給料がちょっと少なかったんです
examplePolite.english: My pay was a little low this month.

items.notes: Kyuuryoubi is payday. Kyuuryou ga agaru means get a raise.

blocks.label: Injuries and emergencies
blocks.rationale: Handle an accident: who got hurt and who to call.
blocks.interference: Kega is the injury, kizu the visible cut or mark.

items.english: to get hurt; to be injured
items.use: Any physical injury, from a scraped knee to a bad accident.

example.ja: 大丈夫？どこもケガしなかった？
example.english: You okay? You didn't hurt yourself anywhere?

examplePolite.romaji: daijoubu desu ka? doko mo kega shimasen deshita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 大丈夫ですか？どこもケガしませんでしたか？
examplePolite.english: Are you all right? You weren't hurt anywhere?

items.notes: The noun kega = an injury: kega wa nai? = anyone hurt? Kizu is the cut or wound itself.

items.use: The police as an organisation; a single officer is keisatsukan, or omawarisan.

example.ja: すぐ警察に電話して！
example.english: Call the police right now!

examplePolite.romaji: sugu keisatsu ni denwa shite kudasai!
examplePolite.ja: すぐ警察に電話してください！
examplePolite.english: Please call the police right away!

items.notes: Keisatsu o yobu = call the police (110 in Japan). A kouban is the local police box.

items.use: An unplanned accident, most often a traffic accident.

example.romaji: eki no mae de jiko ga atta n datte.
example.ja: 駅の前で事故があったんだって。
example.english: I heard there was an accident in front of the station.

examplePolite.romaji: eki no mae de jiko ga atta sou desu.
examplePolite.ja: 駅の前で事故があったそうです。
examplePolite.english: I heard there was an accident in front of the station.

items.notes: Jiko ni au = be in an accident. Jiken is an incident, often a crime.

items.use: A cut or scar on skin, a scratch on an object, or hurt feelings.

example.ja: この傷、どうしたの？
example.english: How did you get this cut?

examplePolite.romaji: sono kizu wa dou shita n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: その傷はどうしたんですか？
examplePolite.english: How did you get that cut?

items.notes: Kega is the injury itself; kizu is the cut or mark you can see. Kizutsuku = to get hurt, often feelings.

example.ja: 誰か、早く救急車呼んで！
example.english: Someone, quick, call an ambulance!

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, kyuukyuusha o yonde kudasai!
examplePolite.ja: すみません、救急車を呼んでください！
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, please call an ambulance!

items.notes: Kyuukyuusha o yobu = call an ambulance. In Japan the number is 119.

blocks.label: Over, within, except
blocks.rationale: Put limits on amounts and times, and leave things out.
blocks.interference: Igai (except) sounds like igai (surprising); ijou and inai include the number.

items.use: After a number it includes the number: juunin ijou = ten or more people.

example.ja: 一時間以上待ったよ。
example.english: I waited over an hour.

examplePolite.romaji: ichijikan ijou machimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 一時間以上待ちました。
examplePolite.english: I waited more than an hour.

items.notes: Ending a talk or an order, ijou desu = 'that's all'.

example.romaji: niku igai nara nan demo ii yo.
example.ja: 肉以外ならなんでもいいよ。
example.english: Anything's fine except meat.

examplePolite.romaji: niku igai nara nan demo ii desu.
examplePolite.ja: 肉以外ならなんでもいいです。
examplePolite.english: Anything but meat is fine.

items.notes: Sounds the same as igai (surprising); context tells them apart.

example.ja: 十分以内に着くよ。
example.english: I'll be there within ten minutes.

examplePolite.romaji: juppun inai ni tsukimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 十分以内に着きます。
examplePolite.english: I'll arrive within ten minutes.

items.notes: Includes the number: mikka inai = in three days or less. Sounds like inai (isn't here).

items.use: After an amount it means 'about': sanjuppun teido = about thirty minutes.

example.ja: ある程度はわかるよ。
example.english: I understand it to some extent.

examplePolite.romaji: aru teido wa wakarimasu.
examplePolite.ja: ある程度はわかります。
examplePolite.english: I understand it up to a point.

items.notes: Aru teido = to some extent. Gurai is the casual 'about'.

blocks.label: Looks and what's inside
blocks.rationale: Describe how something looks versus what it really is.
blocks.interference: Mitame (looks) and nakami (what's inside) are opposites.

example.romaji: mitame wa warui kedo, oishii yo.
example.ja: 見た目は悪いけど、おいしいよ。
example.english: It doesn't look great, but it tastes good.

examplePolite.romaji: mitame wa warui desu kedo, oishii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 見た目は悪いですけど、おいしいですよ。
examplePolite.english: It doesn't look like much, but it's delicious.

items.notes: Often set against nakami (what's inside, someone's character).

example.romaji: kono kumo, hen na katachi da ne.
example.ja: この雲、変な形だね。
example.english: This cloud's a weird shape.

examplePolite.romaji: kono kumo, hen na katachi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この雲、変な形ですね。
examplePolite.english: This cloud has a strange shape.

items.notes: Also 'form' as opposed to substance: katachi dake = just for show.

example.ja: 箱の中身なんだろう。
example.english: I wonder what's in the box.

examplePolite.romaji: hako no nakami wa nan deshou ka.
examplePolite.ja: 箱の中身は何でしょうか。
examplePolite.english: I wonder what's inside the box.

items.notes: Also a person's inner self, as opposed to mitame (looks).

items.use: Real as opposed to fake, or someone truly skilled: kare wa honmono da.

example.ja: これって本物のダイヤ？
example.english: Is this a real diamond?

examplePolite.romaji: kore wa honmono no daiya desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: これは本物のダイヤですか？
examplePolite.english: Is this a real diamond?

items.notes: Opposite: nisemono (a fake).

blocks.label: Sad and missing
blocks.rationale: Lets you say you're sad, lonely or nostalgic, or feel sorry for someone.
blocks.interference: Kanashii (sad) vs sabishii (lonely); kawaisou sounds like kawaii but means pity.

items.english: lonely; sad to be apart; (a place) empty
items.use: Also how you say you'll miss someone: 'sabishiku naru ne' = I'll miss you.

example.ja: みんな帰っちゃうと寂しいな。
example.english: It's lonely when everyone goes home.

examplePolite.romaji: minna ga kaeru to sabishii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: みんなが帰ると寂しいですね。
examplePolite.english: It's lonely when everyone goes home.

items.notes: Also pronounced samishii.

example.ja: その映画、悲しすぎて泣いた。
example.english: That movie was so sad I cried.

examplePolite.romaji: sono eiga wa kanashisugite nakimashita.
examplePolite.ja: その映画は悲しすぎて泣きました。
examplePolite.english: That movie was so sad I cried.

items.notes: Sabishii is lonely or missing someone; kanashii is sad about something that happened.

items.english: poor thing; pitiful; that's sad (for them)
items.use: Feeling sorry for a person or animal: 'kawaisou!' = oh, poor thing!

example.romaji: kono neko, ame de nurete kawaisou.
example.ja: この猫、雨で濡れてかわいそう。
example.english: This poor cat is soaked from the rain.

examplePolite.romaji: kono neko, ame de nurete kawaisou desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この猫、雨で濡れてかわいそうですね。
examplePolite.english: This poor cat is soaked from the rain.

items.notes: Sounds like kawaii + sou, but it only means pity, never 'looks cute'.

items.use: Said the moment something from the past comes back: an old song, a photo, an old friend.

example.ja: うわ、この写真懐かしい！
example.english: Wow, this photo takes me back!

examplePolite.romaji: kono shashin, natsukashii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この写真、懐かしいですね。
examplePolite.english: This photo really takes me back.

items.notes: A warm, happy feeling, not a sad one.

blocks.label: Fine, grateful, awkward
blocks.rationale: Lets you say something doesn't bother you, helps you, or feels awkward.
blocks.interference: Heiki vs daijoubu; arigatai describes the help while arigatou is the thanks.

items.use: Says something doesn't bother or hurt you: 'heiki, heiki' = I'm fine, no problem.

example.ja: これぐらい平気だよ。
example.english: This much is nothing.

examplePolite.romaji: kore gurai heiki desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: これぐらい平気ですよ。
examplePolite.english: This much is no problem.

items.notes: Close to daijoubu, but more 'it doesn't get to me'. Heiki de uso o tsuku = lie without a second thought.

items.english: much appreciated; a big help; grateful
items.use: Says something helps you: 'sore wa arigatai' = that would really help.

example.ja: 手伝ってくれるの？ありがたい！
example.english: You'll help me? That's a huge help!

examplePolite.romaji: tetsudatte itadakeru n desu ka. arigatai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 手伝っていただけるんですか。ありがたいです。
examplePolite.english: You'll help me? I really appreciate it.

items.notes: Arigatou comes from it: arigatai describes the help, arigatou is the thanks you say.

items.use: Social awkwardness: silence after a fight, running into an ex.

example.romaji: kenka shita bakari dakara, kimazui na.
example.ja: けんかしたばかりだから、気まずいな。
example.english: We just had a fight, so it's awkward.

examplePolite.romaji: kenka shita bakari na node, kimazui desu.
examplePolite.ja: けんかしたばかりなので、気まずいです。
examplePolite.english: We just had a fight, so it's awkward.

items.notes: Kimazui fun'iki = an awkward atmosphere.

blocks.label: Skill and praise
blocks.rationale: Lets you say what you're good or bad at and praise someone.
blocks.interference: Tokui pairs with nigate, heta with jouzu; erai praises effort, yuushuu ability.

items.use: X ga tokui = I'm good at X; fine to say about yourself without sounding like bragging.

example.ja: 料理は得意だよ。
example.english: I'm good at cooking.

examplePolite.romaji: ryouri wa tokui desu.
examplePolite.ja: 料理は得意です。
examplePolite.english: I'm good at cooking.

items.notes: Opposite is nigate (weak at, not my thing). Jouzu is praise for others; tokui works for yourself.

items.use: X ga heta = bad at X; fine about yourself, blunt about others.

example.romaji: uta, heta dakara karaoke wa iya.
example.ja: 歌、下手だからカラオケは嫌。
example.english: I'm bad at singing, so no karaoke.

examplePolite.romaji: uta ga heta na node, karaoke wa chotto.
examplePolite.ja: 歌が下手なので、カラオケはちょっと。
examplePolite.english: I'm bad at singing, so karaoke isn't really for me.

items.notes: Opposite is jouzu. Nigate is 'not my thing'; heta is about lack of skill.

items.use: Praise for effort, even small: 'erai!' = well done!; 'erai hito' = a big shot.

example.romaji: mainichi benkyou shiteru no? erai ne!
example.ja: 毎日勉強してるの？偉いね！
example.english: You study every day? Good for you!

examplePolite.romaji: mainichi benkyou shite iru n desu ka. erai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 毎日勉強しているんですか。偉いですね。
examplePolite.english: You study every day? That's impressive.

items.notes: Praising a superior with erai sounds condescending; use it for peers, juniors and kids.

items.use: Praise for someone who has grown up or done well, and for grand things like a big house.

example.romaji: ano ko, rippa na otona ni natta ne.
example.ja: あの子、立派な大人になったね。
example.english: That kid grew up into a fine adult.

examplePolite.romaji: ano ko wa rippa na otona ni narimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの子は立派な大人になりましたね。
examplePolite.english: That child has grown into a fine adult.

items.notes: Rippa na ie = an impressive house. Sounds a little grown-up or formal from a young speaker.

items.use: Praise for ability at school or work; a bit formal.

example.romaji: kanojo, sugoku yuushuu nan da yo.
example.ja: 彼女、すごく優秀なんだよ。
example.english: She's really sharp.

examplePolite.romaji: kanojo wa totemo yuushuu desu.
examplePolite.ja: 彼女はとても優秀です。
examplePolite.english: She's very capable.

items.notes: About ability, not character; for character use rippa or erai.

blocks.label: Strange and surprising
blocks.rationale: React when something seems off, odd or unexpected.
blocks.interference: Okashii is 'something's wrong', ayashii is 'suspicious', fushigi is 'mysterious' with no blame.

items.use: Mostly 'something's off': 'nanka okashii' means something's wrong.

example.ja: この機械、なんかおかしいよ。
example.english: Something's wrong with this machine.

examplePolite.romaji: kono kikai, nanika okashii desu.
examplePolite.ja: この機械、何かおかしいです。
examplePolite.english: Something seems wrong with this machine.

items.notes: Before a noun you also hear 'okashina': 'okashina hanashi' (a strange story). 'Okashi' is sweets.

items.use: Mostly 'igai to' (surprisingly): 'igai to oishii'.

example.ja: 意外とおいしいね、これ。
example.english: This is surprisingly good.

examplePolite.romaji: igai to oishii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 意外とおいしいですね。
examplePolite.english: It's surprisingly good.

items.notes: Sounds the same as 'igai' (except, other than); context tells them apart.

items.use: For things you can't explain, said with wonder rather than suspicion.

example.ja: 不思議だね、全然疲れない。
example.english: Weird, I'm not tired at all.

examplePolite.romaji: fushigi desu ne, zenzen tsukaremasen.
examplePolite.ja: 不思議ですね、全然疲れません。
examplePolite.english: It's strange, I'm not tired at all.

items.notes: 'Fushigi ja nai' means 'no wonder, that's not surprising'.

example.ja: あの人、なんか怪しいね。
example.english: That guy seems kind of shady.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito, nanka ayashii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの人、なんか怪しいですね。
examplePolite.english: That person seems a bit suspicious.

items.notes: Also 'doubtful, iffy': 'Ashita wa chotto ayashii' means tomorrow might not work.

blocks.label: Special and wonderful
blocks.rationale: Praise something or say it stands out.
blocks.interference: Suteki and subarashii overlap; in casual talk both often become 'sugoi'.

example.romaji: kyou wa tokubetsu na hi da kara ne.
example.ja: 今日は特別な日だからね。
example.english: Today's a special day, you know.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa tokubetsu na hi desu kara.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は特別な日ですから。
examplePolite.english: Today is a special day, after all.

items.notes: 'Tokubetsu ni' means 'as an exception, just this once'.

items.use: 'Famous for X' is 'X de yuumei'.

example.romaji: kono mise, raamen de yuumei na n da yo.
example.ja: この店、ラーメンで有名なんだよ。
example.english: This place is famous for its ramen.

examplePolite.romaji: kono mise wa raamen de yuumei desu.
examplePolite.ja: この店はラーメンで有名です。
examplePolite.english: This restaurant is famous for its ramen.

items.use: A warm compliment for clothes, places and people.

example.ja: その服、すてきだね。
example.english: That outfit's lovely.

examplePolite.romaji: sono fuku, suteki desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: その服、すてきですね。
examplePolite.english: Your outfit is lovely.

items.notes: Leans polite and a little feminine; 'ii ne' is the everyday version.

items.use: 'Kanpeki!' alone means 'Perfect!'

example.ja: 準備は完璧だよ。
example.english: We're all set.

examplePolite.romaji: junbi wa kanpeki desu.
examplePolite.ja: 準備は完璧です。
examplePolite.english: Everything is ready.

items.notes: 'Kanpeki ni' means perfectly: 'kanpeki ni oboeta' (I've got it memorised).

items.use: Sounds a bit formal or emphatic; friends usually say 'sugoi'.

example.ja: この景色、すばらしいね。
example.english: This view is amazing.

examplePolite.romaji: subarashii keshiki desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: すばらしい景色ですね。
examplePolite.english: What a wonderful view.

blocks.label: Heavy, light, old, cold
blocks.rationale: Describe things you carry, touch or drink.
blocks.interference: Tsumetai is cold to the touch; cold weather is 'samui'.

example.ja: この荷物、すごい重い。
example.english: This bag is super heavy.

examplePolite.romaji: kono nimotsu, sugoku omoi desu.
examplePolite.ja: この荷物、すごく重いです。
examplePolite.english: This luggage is very heavy.

items.notes: Also heavy-going: 'omoi hanashi' is a heavy topic, and a clingy partner is 'omoi'.

example.ja: この傘、すごい軽いね。
example.english: This umbrella's really light.

examplePolite.romaji: kono kasa, totemo karui desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この傘、とても軽いですね。
examplePolite.english: This umbrella is very light.

items.notes: Not light as in bright; that's 'akarui'. A 'karui hito' is a frivolous person.

example.ja: このパソコン、もう古いよ。
example.english: This computer's old now.

examplePolite.romaji: kono pasokon wa mou furui desu.
examplePolite.ja: このパソコンはもう古いです。
examplePolite.english: This computer is old now.

items.notes: Not for a person's age; said of someone it means old-fashioned. Opposite: 'atarashii'.

items.use: For things you touch or drink; cold weather is 'samui'.

example.ja: 冷たい飲み物が欲しいな。
example.english: I want something cold to drink.

examplePolite.romaji: tsumetai nomimono ga hoshii desu.
examplePolite.ja: 冷たい飲み物が欲しいです。
examplePolite.english: I'd like something cold to drink.

items.notes: About a person it means cold-hearted: 'Tsumetai ne' is 'That's cold.'

blocks.label: Important and precious
blocks.rationale: Say what matters, and brush off what doesn't.
blocks.interference: Taisetsu is personal and warm; juuyou is businesslike.

items.use: For things and people that matter to you personally.

example.romaji: kore, sugoku taisetsu na mono na n da.
example.ja: これ、すごく大切なものなんだ。
example.english: This is really precious to me.

examplePolite.romaji: kore wa totemo taisetsu na mono na n desu.
examplePolite.ja: これはとても大切なものなんです。
examplePolite.english: This is very precious to me.

items.notes: 'Taisetsu ni suru' means to take good care of. 'Juuyou' is the colder, businesslike 'important'.

items.english: much, serious, great (mostly with a negative)
items.use: Mostly in 'taishita koto nai': it's nothing, no big deal.

example.romaji: taishita koto nai yo, ki ni shinaide.
example.ja: 大したことないよ、気にしないで。
example.english: It's no big deal, don't worry about it.

examplePolite.romaji: taishita koto ja arimasen yo.
examplePolite.ja: 大したことじゃありませんよ。
examplePolite.english: It's nothing serious.

items.notes: Only goes before a noun. Positive use: 'Taishita mon da' means 'That's impressive.'

items.use: Sounds businesslike; for personal things 'taisetsu' or 'daiji' is warmer.

example.romaji: kore, kekkou juuyou na hanashi da yo.
example.ja: これ、けっこう重要な話だよ。
example.english: This is actually important.

examplePolite.romaji: kore wa juuyou na hanashi desu.
examplePolite.ja: これは重要な話です。
examplePolite.english: This is an important matter.

items.use: For scarce things: time, chances, experiences, belongings.

example.romaji: sore, kichou na keiken da ne.
example.ja: それ、貴重な経験だね。
example.english: That's a valuable experience.

examplePolite.romaji: kichou na keiken deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 貴重な経験でした。
examplePolite.english: It was a valuable experience.

items.notes: 'Kichouhin' means valuables.

blocks.label: Distance and space
blocks.rationale: Say how far a place is and how roomy or huge something is.
blocks.interference: Hiroi and semai are for space; 'ookii' and 'chiisai' are for an object's size.

items.use: 'Close to X' is 'X kara chikai' or 'X ni chikai'.

example.ja: うち、駅から近いよ。
example.english: My place is close to the station.

examplePolite.romaji: uchi wa eki kara chikai desu.
examplePolite.ja: うちは駅から近いです。
examplePolite.english: My home is close to the station.

items.notes: 'The nearby X' is usually 'chikaku no X': 'chikaku no konbini'.

items.use: 'Far from X' is 'X kara tooi'.

example.ja: 駅までちょっと遠いよ。
example.english: It's a bit far to the station.

examplePolite.romaji: eki made chotto tooi desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 駅までちょっと遠いですよ。
examplePolite.english: It's a little far to the station.

items.notes: 'Tooku' means far away: 'tooku ni sunde iru' (lives far away).

items.use: For rooms and areas, where English often says 'big'.

example.ja: 新しい部屋、けっこう広いよ。
example.english: My new room is pretty big.

examplePolite.romaji: atarashii heya wa kekkou hiroi desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 新しい部屋はけっこう広いですよ。
examplePolite.english: The new room is quite spacious.

items.notes: A big room is 'hiroi', not 'ookii'; 'ookii' is the size of an object.

items.use: For rooms and spaces, where English says 'small'.

example.ja: うち、狭いけどどうぞ。
example.english: My place is small, but come on in.

examplePolite.romaji: semai desu kedo, douzo.
examplePolite.ja: 狭いですけど、どうぞ。
examplePolite.english: It's a bit cramped, but please come in.

items.notes: A small room is 'semai', not 'chiisai'. 'Sekai wa semai' means it's a small world.

items.use: A punchier 'ookii'; often stretched to 'dekkai'.

example.ja: うわ、このハンバーガーでかい！
example.english: Whoa, this burger is huge!

items.notes: In polite speech, say 'ookii'.

blocks.label: Definitely, no matter what
blocks.rationale: Lets you promise, insist and invite with conviction.
blocks.interference: Zehi is for wishes and invitations, kanarazu for promises and facts.

items.use: Stresses that something will definitely happen or always does; common in promises.

example.ja: 明日、必ず来るよ。
example.english: I'll definitely come tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita kanarazu kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 明日必ず来ます。
examplePolite.english: I will definitely come tomorrow.

items.notes: Not for guesses about others; for 'he'll surely come' use kitto.

items.english: no matter what; really; just can't
items.use: With a positive verb you're set on it; with a negative, you just can't however hard you try.

example.ja: どうしても行きたいんだ。
example.english: I really want to go, no matter what.

examplePolite.romaji: doushitemo ikitai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: どうしても行きたいんです。
examplePolite.english: I really do want to go.

items.notes: Doushitemo omoidasenai: 'I just can't remember it.'

items.english: no doubt about it; definitely; a sure bet
items.use: Confirms something is certain, or praises something you can't go wrong with.

example.romaji: kono mise wa machigai nai yo.
example.ja: この店は間違いないよ。
example.english: This place is a sure bet.

examplePolite.romaji: kono mise wa machigai arimasen yo.
examplePolite.ja: この店は間違いありませんよ。
examplePolite.english: You can't go wrong with this place.

items.notes: Also after a noun: kare ni machigai nai, 'it's definitely him'.

items.english: by all means; definitely; I'd love to
items.use: Adds warmth to invitations, requests and wishes; zehi! alone is 'I'd love to!'.

example.romaji: kondo zehi asobi ni kite yo.
example.ja: 今度ぜひ遊びに来てよ。
example.english: You should definitely come over sometime.

examplePolite.romaji: kondo zehi asobi ni kite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 今度ぜひ遊びに来てください。
examplePolite.english: Please do come and visit sometime.

items.notes: Only for things you want or ask for, not predictions; for 'it'll definitely rain' use kitto.

blocks.label: How you do or say it
blocks.rationale: Lets you say something is done properly, clearly or directly.
blocks.interference: Shikkari and kichinto both mean properly; shikkari adds effort, kichinto neatness.

items.use: Doing something thoroughly and seriously, or holding on tight.

example.ja: 今日はしっかり休んでね。
example.english: Get some proper rest today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa shikkari yasunde kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はしっかり休んでください。
examplePolite.english: Please get some proper rest today.

items.notes: Shikkari shite! means 'pull yourself together!'; shikkari shita hito is a dependable person.

items.use: Doing something without a go-between: to someone's face, yourself, from the source.

example.ja: 直接言ってよ。
example.english: Just tell me to my face.

examplePolite.romaji: chokusetsu itte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 直接言ってください。
examplePolite.english: Please tell me directly.

items.notes: Chokusetsu au means meeting in person rather than by message or phone.

items.use: Saying things straight out, or something being clearly seen, heard or known.

example.ja: はっきり言うと、ちょっと嫌。
example.english: To be honest, I don't really like it.

examplePolite.romaji: hakkiri iu to, chotto iya desu.
examplePolite.ja: はっきり言うと、ちょっと嫌です。
examplePolite.english: To put it plainly, I'd rather not.

items.notes: Hakkiri shinai means vague or undecided: hakkiri shinai hito, a wishy-washy person.

items.use: Doing things the right, tidy way, by the rules; a bit more formal than chanto.

example.ja: きちんと片付けてね。
example.english: Tidy it up properly, OK?

examplePolite.romaji: kichinto katazukete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: きちんと片付けてください。
examplePolite.english: Please tidy up properly.

items.notes: Chanto is the everyday word; shikkari adds effort and firmness.

items.use: Points to a way of doing or saying something just mentioned.

example.ja: そんなふうに言わないでよ。
example.english: Don't say it like that.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna fuu ni iwanaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: そんなふうに言わないでください。
examplePolite.english: Please don't put it that way.

items.notes: Konna fuu ni is 'like this'; dou iu fuu ni asks 'in what way?'.

blocks.label: As expected or not
blocks.rationale: Lets you compare things with what you'd expect.
blocks.interference: Masa ni (exactly) sounds like masaka (no way!), and sasuga ni differs from sasuga (well done!).

items.english: just like; as if; (not) at all
items.use: Sets up a comparison that ends in mitai or you na.

example.ja: まるで夢みたい。
example.english: It's like a dream.

examplePolite.romaji: marude yume no you desu.
examplePolite.ja: まるで夢のようです。
examplePolite.english: It's just like a dream.

items.notes: With a negative it means 'not at all': marude wakaranai, 'I don't get it at all'.

items.english: understandably; even so; as you'd expect
items.use: Says something has gone past a reasonable limit, so the reaction is natural.

example.romaji: sasuga ni sore wa muri da yo.
example.ja: さすがにそれは無理だよ。
example.english: Come on, that's really asking too much.

examplePolite.romaji: sasuga ni sore wa muri desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: さすがにそれは無理ですよ。
examplePolite.english: That really is too much to ask.

items.notes: Sasuga alone is praise, 'just what I'd expect of you!'.

items.use: Stresses a perfect match: this is precisely it.

example.romaji: masa ni sore ga iitakatta n da yo.
example.ja: まさにそれが言いたかったんだよ。
example.english: That's exactly what I wanted to say.

examplePolite.romaji: masa ni sore ga iitakatta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: まさにそれが言いたかったんです。
examplePolite.english: That's exactly what I meant to say.

items.notes: Don't mix with masaka, 'no way!'.

items.use: When something turns out different from what you assumed, usually better or easier.

example.ja: 案外おいしいね、これ。
example.english: This is surprisingly good.

examplePolite.romaji: kore, angai oishii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: これ、案外おいしいですね。
examplePolite.english: This is surprisingly tasty.

items.notes: Igai to means the same and is a bit more common in speech.

blocks.label: Not at all, never
blocks.rationale: Lets you say 'not at all' and 'never' with force.
blocks.interference: All need a negative verb; kesshite is the solemn 'never'.

items.use: With a negative it means 'not at all'; on its own it's an exasperated sigh.

example.ja: 彼の話、まったくわからなかった。
example.english: I didn't understand a word he said.

examplePolite.romaji: kare no hanashi wa mattaku wakarimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 彼の話はまったくわかりませんでした。
examplePolite.english: I didn't understand his talk at all.

items.notes: Mattaku mou! = honestly! (annoyed). Mattaku onaji = exactly the same.

items.use: Mostly sappari wakaranai (no idea at all); sappari shita describes light food or a fresh, clean feeling.

example.ja: この問題、さっぱりわからない。
example.english: I have no clue how to do this problem.

examplePolite.romaji: kono mondai wa sappari wakarimasen.
examplePolite.ja: この問題はさっぱりわかりません。
examplePolite.english: I don't understand this problem at all.

items.notes: Sappari shita aji = a light, refreshing taste.

items.use: A firm, total 'none': issai kankei nai (nothing whatsoever to do with it).

example.romaji: sono ken ni wa issai kankei nai yo.
example.ja: その件には一切関係ないよ。
example.english: I have absolutely nothing to do with that.

examplePolite.romaji: sono ken ni wa issai kankei arimasen.
examplePolite.ja: その件には一切関係ありません。
examplePolite.english: I have nothing whatsoever to do with that matter.

items.notes: Stiffer than zenzen; common in rules and notices.

items.use: A serious 'never' for promises and warnings.

example.romaji: kono koto wa kesshite dare ni mo iwanai.
example.ja: このことは決して誰にも言わない。
example.english: I'll never tell anyone about this.

examplePolite.romaji: kono koto wa kesshite dare ni mo iimasen.
examplePolite.ja: このことは決して誰にも言いません。
examplePolite.english: I will never tell anyone about this.

items.notes: Zettai ...nai is the everyday 'never'; kesshite sounds more solemn.

blocks.label: Quite a lot
blocks.rationale: Lets you say something has changed a lot or is seriously so.
blocks.interference: Sukkari (completely) sounds like sukkiri (refreshed).

items.use: Usually about change or progress: daibu yoku natta, daibu nareta.

example.ja: 風邪、だいぶよくなったよ。
example.english: My cold's a lot better.

examplePolite.romaji: kaze wa daibu yoku narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 風邪はだいぶよくなりました。
examplePolite.english: My cold is much better.

items.notes: For a plain 'very' with an adjective, use totemo.

items.use: A state that has fully changed: sukkari wasureta, sukkari kawatta.

example.ja: ごめん、すっかり忘れてた。
example.english: Sorry, I totally forgot.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, sukkari wasurete imashita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、すっかり忘れていました。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry, it completely slipped my mind.

items.notes: Don't mix with sukkiri (refreshed).

items.use: Stresses a high degree, often of something bad or impressive.

example.ja: 彼、相当怒ってたよ。
example.english: He was seriously mad.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa soutou okotte imashita yo.
examplePolite.ja: 彼は相当怒っていましたよ。
examplePolite.english: He was quite angry.

items.notes: After an amount it means 'worth': ichiman'en soutou (worth 10,000 yen).

items.use: Guesses at a high degree from what you see: yoppodo tsukareteru n da ne (you must be really tired).

example.romaji: yoppodo onaka suiteta n da ne.
example.ja: よっぽどお腹すいてたんだね。
example.english: You must have been really hungry.

examplePolite.romaji: yoppodo onaka ga suite ita n desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: よっぽどお腹がすいていたんですね。
examplePolite.english: You must have been very hungry.

items.notes: In comparisons, 'way more': kotchi no hou ga yoppodo ii (this one's way better). Casual form of yohodo.

blocks.label: Very and really
blocks.rationale: Lets you say 'really', 'super' and 'dead tired' at the right strength.
blocks.interference: Zuibun is about a surprising amount or change, not a plain 'very'.

items.use: A warmer, more emphatic totemo, common in friendly or gushing speech.

example.ja: このケーキ、とってもおいしい！
example.english: This cake is so good!

examplePolite.romaji: kono keeki, tottemo oishii desu.
examplePolite.ja: このケーキ、とってもおいしいです。
examplePolite.english: This cake is really delicious.

items.notes: Plain totemo is the neutral form.

items.use: Informal intensifier before adjectives and verbs; on its own it means a mess or ruined.

example.ja: 昨日の試合、めちゃくちゃ面白かった。
example.english: Yesterday's game was super fun.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou no shiai wa mechakucha omoshirokatta desu.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日の試合はめちゃくちゃ面白かったです。
examplePolite.english: Yesterday's game was really fun.

items.notes: Often shortened to mecha (mecha oishii). Heya ga mechakucha da = the room is a total mess.

items.use: Comments on a surprising amount or change: zuibun hayai ne, zuibun kawatta.

example.ja: 随分大きくなったね！
example.english: You've grown so much!

examplePolite.romaji: zuibun ookiku narimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: 随分大きくなりましたね。
examplePolite.english: He's grown so much.

items.notes: Can sound critical: zuibun na iikata da ne (that's a harsh thing to say).

items.use: Casual exaggeration with feelings and states: shinu hodo tsukareta, shinu hodo waratta.

example.ja: 今日は死ぬほど疲れた。
example.english: I'm dead tired today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa shinu hodo tsukaremashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は死ぬほど疲れました。
examplePolite.english: I'm exhausted today.

items.notes: Hodo after a verb means 'to the point of': naku hodo ureshii (so happy I could cry).

blocks.label: And then
blocks.rationale: Lets you tell what happened next in a story.
blocks.interference: Soshite sounds tidy; in chat sore kara is more natural, and soshitara often signals a surprise.

items.english: and then; after that; since then
items.use: Links the next step in a sequence, or adds one more item to a list.

example.romaji: gohan tabete, sore kara eiga mita.
example.ja: ご飯食べて、それから映画見た。
example.english: We ate, and then watched a movie.

examplePolite.romaji: gohan o tabete, sore kara eiga o mimashita.
examplePolite.ja: ご飯を食べて、それから映画を見ました。
examplePolite.english: We ate, and then watched a movie.

items.notes: After a past event it can mean 'since then': sore kara zutto (ever since).

items.use: Sounds tidy, like storytelling or a speech.

example.romaji: kare ga kite, soshite nani mo iwazu ni kaetta.
example.ja: 彼が来て、そして何も言わずに帰った。
example.english: He came, and then left without a word.

examplePolite.romaji: kare ga kite, soshite nani mo iwazu ni kaerimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 彼が来て、そして何も言わずに帰りました。
examplePolite.english: He came, and then left without a word.

items.notes: In casual chat, sore de and sore kara are more common.

items.english: and then (it turned out); in that case
items.use: Tells what happened next, often a surprise, or suggests a next step after hearing a plan.

example.romaji: doa aketa no. soshitara neko ga ita.
example.ja: ドア開けたの。そしたら猫がいた。
example.english: I opened the door, and there was a cat.

examplePolite.romaji: doa o akemashita. soshitara neko ga imashita.
examplePolite.ja: ドアを開けました。そしたら猫がいました。
examplePolite.english: I opened the door, and there was a cat.

items.notes: Short for sou shitara. For 'in that case' you also hear ja or dattara.

items.use: Points to a later time, often with a gap; sore kara is more 'the next step'.

example.ja: その後どこ行ったの?
example.english: Where did you go after that?

examplePolite.romaji: sono ato doko ni ikimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: その後どこに行きましたか?
examplePolite.english: Where did you go after that?

items.notes: The same kanji read sono go is the formal version heard in news and reports.

blocks.label: Even so and but
blocks.rationale: Lets you push back, add a caveat or set a condition.
blocks.interference: Sore demo (even so) vs sore de (so); dakara tte (just because) vs dakara (so).

items.english: but, only thing is; just, only
items.use: At the start of a sentence it adds a caveat after agreeing.

example.romaji: ii to omou yo. tada, chotto takai kana.
example.ja: いいと思うよ。ただ、ちょっと高いかな。
example.english: I think it's good. Only thing is, it's a bit pricey.

examplePolite.romaji: ii to omoimasu. tada, chotto takai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: いいと思います。ただ、ちょっと高いですね。
examplePolite.english: I think it's good. Only thing is, it's a bit pricey.

items.notes: Tada no tomodachi = just a friend; tada de = for free (casual for muryou).

items.use: Says something still holds despite what was just said.

example.romaji: takai yo. sore demo kau no?
example.ja: 高いよ。それでも買うの?
example.english: It's expensive. You're still buying it?

examplePolite.romaji: takai desu yo. sore demo kaimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 高いですよ。それでも買いますか?
examplePolite.english: It's expensive. Are you still buying it?

items.notes: Don't confuse with sore de (so, and then); the mo turns it into 'even so'.

items.english: just because (that doesn't mean); even so
items.use: Pushes back: the reason given doesn't justify the conclusion.

example.romaji: dakara tte, sonna ni okoranakute mo ii jan.
example.ja: だからって、そんなに怒らなくてもいいじゃん。
example.english: Even so, you don't need to get that angry.

items.notes: The polite form is dakara to itte. Pattern: dakara tte ... wake ja nai (just because ... doesn't mean).

items.use: Accepts what was said, then comes back to how striking something is.

example.romaji: sore ni shite mo, kyou atsui ne.
example.ja: それにしても、今日暑いね。
example.english: Still, it's really hot today, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: sore ni shite mo, kyou wa atsui desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: それにしても、今日は暑いですね。
examplePolite.english: Still, it's really hot today.

items.notes: Often an exclamation that breaks into the conversation, like 'man, ...'; for a plain 'even so' use sore demo.

items.use: Sets a condition or trade-off right after agreeing to something.

example.romaji: ii yo. sono kawari, ranchi ogotte ne.
example.ja: いいよ。その代わり、ランチおごってね。
example.english: Sure. But in exchange, you buy me lunch.

examplePolite.romaji: ii desu yo. sono kawari, ranchi o ogotte kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: いいですよ。その代わり、ランチをおごってくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Sure. But in exchange, you buy me lunch.

items.notes: Also for a trade-off in facts: yasui. sono kawari, tooi (it's cheap, but then it's far). X no kawari ni = instead of X.

blocks.label: Changing the subject
blocks.rationale: Lets you switch topics or slip in a side fact.
blocks.interference: Tokoro de opens a new topic; chinami ni adds a side fact on the same one.

items.use: Switches to a new topic, often the one you really wanted to bring up.

example.romaji: tokoro de, ashita no yoru hima?
example.ja: ところで、明日の夜暇?
example.english: By the way, are you free tomorrow night?

examplePolite.romaji: tokoro de, ashita no yoru wa ohima desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ところで、明日の夜はお暇ですか?
examplePolite.english: By the way, are you free tomorrow night?

items.notes: Chinami ni adds a side fact on the same topic; tokoro de changes the topic.

items.use: Brushes the current topic aside for something more pressing.

example.romaji: sore yori, hayaku ikanai to okureru yo.
example.ja: それより、早く行かないと遅れるよ。
example.english: Never mind that, we'll be late if we don't hurry.

examplePolite.romaji: sore yori, hayaku ikanai to okuremasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: それより、早く行かないと遅れますよ。
examplePolite.english: Never mind that, we'll be late if we don't hurry.

items.notes: Sore yori mo means the same, a bit more emphatic. Literally 'than that', so it also compares: sore yori kore ga ii (this is better).

items.english: by the way; just so you know
items.use: Adds a related side fact to what was just said.

example.romaji: chinami ni, kono kutsu ichiman en datta.
example.ja: ちなみに、この靴一万円だった。
example.english: Just so you know, these shoes were 10,000 yen.

examplePolite.romaji: chinami ni, kono kutsu wa ichiman en deshita.
examplePolite.ja: ちなみに、この靴は一万円でした。
examplePolite.english: Just so you know, these shoes were 10,000 yen.

items.notes: Also opens a curious question: chinami ni, nan sai? (Out of curiosity, how old are you?)

items.use: Said to yourself or a group when moving on to the next thing.

example.ja: さて、そろそろ帰ろうか。
example.english: Well then, shall we head home?

examplePolite.romaji: sate, sorosoro kaerimashou ka.
examplePolite.ja: さて、そろそろ帰りましょうか。
examplePolite.english: Well then, shall we head home?

items.notes: Sounds a little deliberate, like getting up to start a task; common in presentations: sate, tsugi wa...

blocks.label: Rephrasing and hedging
blocks.rationale: Lets you correct yourself, flip an expectation or hedge.
blocks.interference: Mushiro picks the better of two options; gyaku ni flips an expectation.

items.use: Corrects or reframes what was just said, or abruptly changes the topic.

example.romaji: tte iu ka, sore mou owatta yo.
example.ja: っていうか、それもう終わったよ。
example.english: Actually, that's already done.

items.notes: The polite form is to iu ka. Mid-sentence it means 'more like': tsukareta tte iu ka nemui (not tired, more like sleepy). Slangier: tteka.

items.english: on the contrary; if anything; actually
items.use: Flags that the truth is the opposite of what you'd expect.

example.romaji: yasumi da to, gyaku ni tsukareru n da yo ne.
example.ja: 休みだと、逆に疲れるんだよね。
example.english: On days off, I actually get more tired.

examplePolite.romaji: yasumi da to, gyaku ni tsukareru n desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 休みだと、逆に疲れるんですよね。
examplePolite.english: On days off, I actually get more tired.

items.notes: Literally 'in reverse': gyaku da yo (it's the other way round).

items.english: in a sense; in a way
items.use: Softens a claim that's only true from one angle, often an ironic one.

example.ja: ある意味、すごいよね。
example.english: In a way, it's kind of amazing.

examplePolite.romaji: aru imi, sugoi desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: ある意味、すごいですよね。
examplePolite.english: In a way, it's kind of amazing.

items.notes: Often backhanded: aru imi tensai (a genius, in a sense) is rarely a compliment.

items.use: Says the second option fits better than the first: not A, but rather B.

example.romaji: samui no wa heiki. mushiro suki.
example.ja: 寒いのは平気。むしろ好き。
example.english: The cold doesn't bother me. If anything, I like it.

examplePolite.romaji: samui no wa heiki desu. mushiro suki desu.
examplePolite.ja: 寒いのは平気です。むしろ好きです。
examplePolite.english: The cold doesn't bother me. If anything, I like it.

items.notes: Close to gyaku ni; mushiro picks the better of two options, gyaku ni flips an expectation.

items.use: Comes before a noun to label something with a familiar term.

example.romaji: kare wa iwayuru otaku da ne.
example.ja: 彼はいわゆるオタクだね。
example.english: He's what you'd call an otaku.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa iwayuru otaku desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼はいわゆるオタクですね。
examplePolite.english: He's what you'd call an otaku.

items.notes: Unlike English 'so-called', it isn't sarcastic; it just means 'as people call it'.

blocks.label: Reasons and conclusions
blocks.rationale: Lets you get to the root of things and draw conclusions.
blocks.interference: Dakara koso (exactly why) vs dakara tte (just because ... doesn't mean).

items.english: in the first place; to begin with
items.use: Goes back to the root of a problem, often to question or blame.

example.romaji: somosomo, nande koko ni iru no?
example.ja: そもそも、なんでここにいるの?
example.english: Why are you even here in the first place?

examplePolite.romaji: somosomo, doushite koko ni iru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: そもそも、どうしてここにいるんですか?
examplePolite.english: Why are you here in the first place?

items.notes: Often sounds like a challenge; in calm talk it just means 'originally' (somosomo no genin, the root cause).

items.use: Draws a conclusion from what the other person just said, often to check it.

example.romaji: tte koto wa, kare mo kuru n da.
example.ja: ってことは、彼も来るんだ。
example.english: So that means he's coming too.

items.notes: The polite form is to iu koto wa. Ending a sentence with ... tte koto? checks: 'You mean ...?'

items.use: Turns a reason around: the very thing mentioned is the reason, often against expectation.

example.romaji: muzukashii yo. dakara koso yaritai n da.
example.ja: 難しいよ。だからこそやりたいんだ。
example.english: It's hard. That's exactly why I want to do it.

examplePolite.romaji: muzukashii desu. dakara koso yaritai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 難しいです。だからこそやりたいんです。
examplePolite.english: It's hard. That's exactly why I want to do it.

items.notes: Koso stresses 'that very one': kochira koso (no, I should be thanking you).

items.use: Points back hard at what was said: that would truly be X.

example.romaji: ima yametara, sore koso muda ni naru yo.
example.ja: 今やめたら、それこそ無駄になるよ。
example.english: If you quit now, then it really would be a waste.

examplePolite.romaji: ima yametara, sore koso muda ni narimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 今やめたら、それこそ無駄になりますよ。
examplePolite.english: If you quit now, then it really would be a waste.

items.notes: Also an intensifier before an example: sore koso mainichi (literally every day).

blocks.label: Adding and choosing
blocks.rationale: Lets you add another point or offer a choice.
blocks.interference: Sore to (and also) and sore to mo (or) differ by one syllable.

items.english: and what's more; on top of that
items.use: Adds a second point that makes the first stronger, good or bad.

example.romaji: ano mise yasui shi, shikamo oishii yo.
example.ja: あの店安いし、しかもおいしいよ。
example.english: That place is cheap, and what's more it's good.

examplePolite.romaji: ano mise wa yasukute, shikamo oishii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの店は安くて、しかもおいしいですよ。
examplePolite.english: That place is cheap, and what's more it's good.

items.notes: Often used to pile on bad news with a tone of disbelief.

items.use: Offers a second option in a question: A? sore to mo B?

example.romaji: koohii ni suru? sore to mo ocha?
example.ja: コーヒーにする?それともお茶?
example.english: Do you want coffee? Or tea?

examplePolite.romaji: koohii ni shimasu ka? sore to mo ocha ni shimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: コーヒーにしますか?それともお茶にしますか?
examplePolite.english: Would you like coffee, or tea?

items.notes: Only for choices in questions; inside one phrase use ka (koohii ka ocha). Don't confuse with sore to, 'and also'.

items.use: Adds another reason or point, often when explaining why.

example.romaji: kyou wa ii ya. tsukareta shi, sore ni ame da shi.
example.ja: 今日はいいや。疲れたし、それに雨だし。
example.english: I'll pass today. I'm tired, and besides, it's raining.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa yamete okimasu. tsukarete imasu shi, sore ni ame desu shi.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はやめておきます。疲れていますし、それに雨ですし。
examplePolite.english: I'll pass today. I'm tired, and besides, it's raining.

items.notes: Close to shikamo; sore ni lists reasons side by side, shikamo stresses that the extra point is even more.

items.use: Adds one more thing to a list or request, often as an afterthought.

example.romaji: gyuunyuu katte kite. a, sore to pan mo.
example.ja: 牛乳買ってきて。あ、それとパンも。
example.english: Get some milk. Oh, and bread too.

examplePolite.romaji: gyuunyuu o onegai shimasu. a, sore to pan mo.
examplePolite.ja: 牛乳をお願いします。あ、それとパンも。
examplePolite.english: Milk, please. Oh, and some bread too.

items.notes: With mo added, sore to mo means 'or' in a question.

blocks.label: Driving and stopping
blocks.rationale: Drive, give turns and say when something stops or won't move.
blocks.interference: tomaru and ugoku happen by themselves; doing it to something is tomeru and ugokasu.

items.use: Something stops by itself; stopping something yourself is tomeru.

example.ja: 電車、また途中で止まっちゃった。
example.english: The train's stopped partway again.

examplePolite.romaji: densha ga mata tochuu de tomatte shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 電車がまた途中で止まってしまいました。
examplePolite.english: The train has stopped partway again.

items.notes: Same sound as 泊まる tomaru, stay the night: hoteru ni tomaru.

items.use: For something moving by itself; moving something yourself is ugokasu.

example.ja: 動かないで！写真撮るから。
example.english: Don't move! I'm taking a photo.

examplePolite.romaji: ugokanaide kudasai. shashin o torimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 動かないでください。写真を撮ります。
examplePolite.english: Please don't move. I'm taking a photo.

items.notes: Also for machines: pasokon ga ugokanai (my computer won't work).

items.use: The corner takes o, the direction ni: kado o migi ni magaru.

example.romaji: tsugi no kado, migi ni magatte.
example.ja: 次の角、右に曲がって。
example.english: Turn right at the next corner.

examplePolite.romaji: tsugi no kado o migi ni magatte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 次の角を右に曲がってください。
examplePolite.english: Please turn right at the next corner.

items.notes: Also for things bent or crooked: nekutai magatteru yo (your tie's crooked).

example.romaji: kaeri wa watashi ga unten suru yo.
example.ja: 帰りは私が運転するよ。
example.english: I'll drive on the way back.

examplePolite.romaji: kaeri wa watashi ga unten shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 帰りは私が運転します。
examplePolite.english: I'll drive on the way back.

items.notes: unten menkyo = driver's licence; unten miawase = trains not running.

blocks.label: Following and chasing
blocks.rationale: Follow, tag along, approach, chase or spot someone.
blocks.interference: tsuite kuru (follow me) and tsuite iku (I'll go with you) flip on direction, like kuru and iku.

items.use: Movement toward the speaker; you going along with someone is tsuite iku.

example.ja: 道分かるから、ついてきて。
example.english: I know the way, follow me.

examplePolite.romaji: michi ga wakarimasu kara, tsuite kite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 道が分かりますから、ついてきてください。
examplePolite.english: I know the way, so please follow me.

items.notes: Also 'comes with' for extras: omake ga tsuite kuru (it comes with a freebie).

items.english: go along with, follow; keep up
items.use: Movement away from the speaker: you go with someone.

example.ja: 私もついていっていい？
example.english: Can I come along too?

examplePolite.romaji: watashi mo tsuite itte mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 私もついていってもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: May I come along too?

items.notes: tsuite ikenai = can't keep up (with a class or the pace).

items.use: The thing approached takes ni.

example.romaji: ano inu ni chikazukanai hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: あの犬に近づかない方がいいよ。
example.english: Better not go near that dog.

examplePolite.romaji: ano inu ni wa chikazukanai hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの犬には近づかない方がいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You'd better not go near that dog.

items.notes: Also for time drawing near: shiken ga chikazuite kita (the exam is coming up).

example.romaji: kinou, inu ni oikakerareta n da yo!
example.ja: 昨日、犬に追いかけられたんだよ！
example.english: A dog chased me yesterday!

examplePolite.romaji: kinou, inu ni oikakeraremashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日、犬に追いかけられました。
examplePolite.english: I was chased by a dog yesterday.

items.notes: Also chasing a dream: yume o oikakeru.

items.english: happen to see, spot, come across

example.romaji: kinou, eki de tanaka-san mikaketa yo.
example.ja: 昨日、駅で田中さん見かけたよ。
example.english: I saw Tanaka at the station yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou, eki de tanaka-san o mikakemashita yo.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日、駅で田中さんを見かけましたよ。
examplePolite.english: I happened to see Mr Tanaka at the station yesterday.

items.notes: Also for things you see around: saikin yoku mikakeru ne (you see those a lot lately).

blocks.label: Laugh, sing, dance, kiss
blocks.rationale: Describe a fun night out or an affectionate moment.
blocks.interference: nameru also means 'look down on' (namenna yo!), unrelated to licking.

items.use: Laughing at someone takes o: hito o warau.

example.romaji: chotto, warawanaide yo! shinken nan dakara.
example.ja: ちょっと、笑わないでよ！真剣なんだから。
example.english: Hey, don't laugh! I'm serious.

examplePolite.romaji: warawanaide kudasai. shinken nan desu.
examplePolite.ja: 笑わないでください。真剣なんです。
examplePolite.english: Please don't laugh. I'm serious.

items.notes: Covers smiling too: waratte! = smile! (for photos).

example.ja: カラオケで何歌う？
example.english: What are you going to sing at karaoke?

examplePolite.romaji: karaoke de nani o utaimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: カラオケで何を歌いますか？
examplePolite.english: What will you sing at karaoke?

example.ja: 一緒に踊ろうよ！
example.english: Come dance with me!

examplePolite.romaji: issho ni odorimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 一緒に踊りませんか？
examplePolite.english: Would you like to dance?

items.notes: dansu suru is also common, especially for modern dance.

example.ja: え、二人キスしたの？
example.english: Wait, you two kissed?

examplePolite.romaji: e, futari wa kisu shita n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: え、二人はキスしたんですか？
examplePolite.english: Wait, the two of you kissed?

items.notes: Casual and cute: chuu (suru).

items.use: The 'look down on' sense is common in arguments: namenna yo! (don't mess with me).

example.romaji: aite o namenai hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: 相手をなめない方がいいよ。
example.english: Better not underestimate them.

examplePolite.romaji: aite o namenai hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 相手をなめない方がいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You shouldn't underestimate them.

items.notes: The lick sense is everyday too: aisu o nameru (lick an ice cream), ame o nameru (suck a candy).

blocks.label: Praise and telling off
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about being praised, warned, lectured, or someone showing off.
blocks.interference: Chuui is a short warning; sekkyou is a long lecture.

example.ja: 今日、部長に褒められた!
example.english: My manager praised me today!

examplePolite.romaji: kyou, buchou ni homeraremashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今日、部長に褒められました。
examplePolite.english: My manager praised me today.

items.notes: Often heard in the passive: homerareta = I got praised.

items.use: Chuui sareta = I got told off; signs and announcements use chuui for 'caution'.

example.ja: また先生に注意された。
example.english: I got told off by the teacher again.

examplePolite.romaji: mata sensei ni chuui saremashita.
examplePolite.ja: また先生に注意されました。
examplePolite.english: I was told off by the teacher again.

items.notes: For 'be careful' in speech, ki o tsukete is more usual; chuui shite sounds like a warning.

items.use: A long telling-off, usually from a parent or boss; also a sermon.

example.ja: また親に説教された。
example.english: My parents lectured me again.

examplePolite.romaji: mata oya ni sekkyou saremashita.
examplePolite.ja: また親に説教されました。
examplePolite.english: My parents lectured me again.

items.notes: Mostly heard in the passive: sekkyou sareta. Chuui is the short version.

items.english: boast, show off; be proud of

example.ja: また彼女の自慢してる。
example.english: He's bragging about his girlfriend again.

examplePolite.romaji: mata kanojo no jiman o shite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: また彼女の自慢をしています。
examplePolite.english: He's bragging about his girlfriend again.

items.notes: Jiman no musuko = a son someone is proud of. Jiman ja nai kedo = not to brag, but.

blocks.label: Discussing plans
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk a plan through, suggest something, back it, or raise a new idea.
blocks.interference: Teian puts an idea forward; sansei backs someone else's.

items.use: Two or more people talking something through to settle it.

example.romaji: ichido futari de chanto hanashiaou yo.
example.ja: 一度二人でちゃんと話し合おうよ。
example.english: Let's sit down and talk it over properly.

examplePolite.romaji: ichido futari de chanto hanashiaimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 一度二人でちゃんと話し合いましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's sit down and talk it over properly.

items.notes: Hanashiai = a discussion. Soudan suru is asking someone's advice.

items.use: Teian suru = suggest; mostly a work and planning word.

example.romaji: hitotsu teian ga aru n da kedo.
example.ja: 一つ提案があるんだけど。
example.english: I've got a suggestion.

examplePolite.romaji: hitotsu teian ga aru n desu ga.
examplePolite.ja: 一つ提案があるんですが。
examplePolite.english: I have a suggestion.

items.use: Agreeing with a plan or proposal; sansei! alone = 'I'm in!'

example.romaji: minna sansei shiteru kara, sore de ikou.
example.ja: みんな賛成してるから、それで行こう。
example.english: Everyone's for it, so let's go with that.

examplePolite.romaji: minna sansei shite iru node, sore de ikimashou.
examplePolite.ja: みんな賛成しているので、それで行きましょう。
examplePolite.english: Everyone's in favour, so let's go with that.

items.notes: Opposite: hantai (against). To agree with what someone just said, people usually say sou da ne.

items.english: bring up; start saying; be the first to suggest
items.use: Often something sudden or awkward: kyuu ni ... tte iidasu.

example.romaji: kare, kyuu ni kaisha yameru tte iidashita n da.
example.ja: 彼、急に会社辞めるって言い出したんだ。
example.english: He suddenly announced he's quitting his job.

examplePolite.romaji: kare ga kyuu ni kaisha o yameru to iidashita n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 彼が急に会社を辞めると言い出したんです。
examplePolite.english: He suddenly announced he's quitting his job.

items.notes: Iidashippe = whoever suggested it (and so has to do it).

blocks.label: Excited and moved
blocks.rationale: Lets you describe a lively mood, being moved and getting worked up.
blocks.interference: Moriagaru is a lively group mood; koufun suru is one person worked up.

items.english: liven up, get lively; get excited (as a group)
items.use: For parties, chats or crowds getting fun.

example.romaji: kinou no nomikai, sugoku moriagatta ne.
example.ja: 昨日の飲み会、すごく盛り上がったね。
example.english: Last night's drinks were really lively, weren't they?

examplePolite.romaji: kinou no nomikai wa sugoku moriagarimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日の飲み会はすごく盛り上がりましたね。
examplePolite.english: Last night's drinks were really lively, weren't they?

items.notes: Moriageru is making it lively: 'ba o moriageru' (liven up the room).

items.use: For films, music, kindness or a view that stirs you: 'Kandou shita!'.

example.romaji: ano eiga, hontou ni kandou shita.
example.ja: あの映画、本当に感動した。
example.english: That movie really moved me.

examplePolite.romaji: ano eiga ni wa hontou ni kandou shimashita.
examplePolite.ja: あの映画には本当に感動しました。
examplePolite.english: That movie really moved me.

items.notes: Wider than English 'moved': also for being blown away by great food or skill.

items.use: For one person's excitement or agitation.

example.ja: 興奮して全然寝れなかった。
example.english: I was too excited to sleep at all.

examplePolite.romaji: koufun shite zenzen nemuremasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 興奮して全然眠れませんでした。
examplePolite.english: I was too excited to sleep at all.

items.notes: It can also mean agitated or angry, so wakuwaku suru is safer for happy anticipation.

blocks.label: Sticking with things
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about keeping at something, getting bored, being picky and learning from mistakes.
blocks.interference: Akiru is boredom, not tiredness (tsukareru).

items.use: After a verb stem it means 'keep on': 'tabetsuzukeru' (keep eating).

example.romaji: mainichi tsuzukeru no ga taihen da yo.
example.ja: 毎日続けるのが大変だよ。
example.english: The hard part is keeping it up every day.

examplePolite.romaji: mainichi tsuzukeru no ga taihen desu.
examplePolite.ja: 毎日続けるのが大変です。
examplePolite.english: The hard part is keeping it up every day.

items.notes: Tsuzuku is the version with no object: 'Ame ga tsuzuku' (The rain keeps going).

items.english: get tired of, get bored of
items.use: Usually in the past: 'Kono geemu, mou akita' (I'm bored of this game now). The thing takes ni.

example.romaji: mainichi onaji gohan de, mou akita yo.
example.ja: 毎日同じご飯で、もう飽きたよ。
example.english: It's the same food every day, I'm sick of it.

examplePolite.romaji: mainichi onaji gohan de, mou akimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 毎日同じご飯で、もう飽きました。
examplePolite.english: It's the same food every day, I'm tired of it.

items.notes: Not physically tired; that's tsukareru. Akippoi describes someone who gets bored quickly.

items.use: Usually pride in details; the thing takes ni.

example.romaji: kare, koohii ni wa sugoku kodawaru n da yo.
example.ja: 彼、コーヒーにはすごくこだわるんだよ。
example.english: He's really particular about his coffee.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa koohii ni sugoku kodawaru n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 彼はコーヒーにすごくこだわるんですよ。
examplePolite.english: He's really particular about his coffee.

items.notes: The noun kodawari is a personal standard. It can also mean being hung up on something: 'Sonna koto ni kodawaranaide'.

items.english: reflect on one's mistakes, be sorry
items.use: For owning a mistake and resolving not to repeat it.

example.romaji: kinou no koto, chanto hansei shiteru yo.
example.ja: 昨日のこと、ちゃんと反省してるよ。
example.english: I really am sorry about yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou no koto wa, hontou ni hansei shite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日のことは、本当に反省しています。
examplePolite.english: I truly regret what happened yesterday.

items.notes: Stronger than a quick sorry. A hanseikai is a meeting to review what went wrong.

blocks.label: Hurt, down or angry
blocks.rationale: Lets you say you're feeling low, hurt or annoyed.
blocks.interference: Mukatsuku is cruder than haradatsu; kizutsuku is hurt feelings, ochikomu is a low mood.

items.use: Usually in -te iru: 'Ochikonderu' (She's feeling down). 'Ochikomanaide' means 'Don't let it get you down'.

example.romaji: shiken ni ochite, ochikonderu n da.
example.ja: 試験に落ちて、落ち込んでるんだ。
example.english: I failed the exam, so I'm feeling down.

examplePolite.romaji: shiken ni ochite, ochikonde iru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 試験に落ちて、落ち込んでいるんです。
examplePolite.english: I failed the exam, so I'm feeling down.

items.notes: Also sales or numbers dropping.

items.use: Mostly emotional hurt from words or actions.

example.romaji: sonna koto iwareru to kizutsuku yo.
example.ja: そんなこと言われると傷つくよ。
example.english: It hurts when you say things like that.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna koto o iwareru to kizutsukimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: そんなことを言われると傷つきますよ。
examplePolite.english: It hurts when you say things like that.

items.notes: Kizutsukeru is the other side: to hurt someone.

items.use: Said about the person or thing: 'Aitsu mukatsuku' (That guy pisses me off).

example.romaji: ano hito no taido, maji mukatsuku.
example.ja: あの人の態度、マジムカつく。
example.english: That guy's attitude really pisses me off.

items.notes: Its original sense is feeling sick to the stomach. Softer: haradatsu or iraira suru.

items.use: Said about what makes you mad: 'Are, hontou ni haradatsu' (That really makes me mad).

example.ja: 今思い出しても腹立つ。
example.english: It still makes me mad just thinking about it.

examplePolite.romaji: ima omoidashite mo hara ga tachimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今思い出しても腹が立ちます。
examplePolite.english: It still makes me angry just thinking about it.

items.notes: Full form hara ga tatsu. Less crude than mukatsuku.

blocks.label: Courtesy and forgiveness
blocks.rationale: Covers everyday courtesies: forgiving, sorry-to-keep-you-waiting, don't be shy, giving way, it's fine.
blocks.interference: Enryo shinaide invites someone in, but enryo shimasu politely says no.

items.use: 'Yurushite' (forgive me) and 'Zettai yurusanai' (I'll never forgive you) are the everyday uses.

example.ja: もう怒ってないよ、許してあげる。
example.english: I'm not mad anymore. I forgive you.

examplePolite.romaji: mou okotte imasen. yurushimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: もう怒っていません。許しますよ。
examplePolite.english: I'm not angry anymore. I forgive you.

items.notes: The 'allow' sense is mostly formal, as in 'jikan ga yuruseba' (if time allows).

items.use: Mostly in apologies on arrival: 'Omatase!' or 'Matasete gomen'.

example.ja: ごめんね、長いこと待たせちゃって。
example.english: Sorry for keeping you waiting so long.

examplePolite.romaji: nagai koto omatase shite, sumimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 長いことお待たせして、すみませんでした。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry for keeping you waiting so long.

items.notes: The causative of matsu (wait). Staff say 'Omatase shimashita' when they bring your order.

items.english: hold back (out of politeness); politely decline
items.use: 'Enryo shinaide' means 'Don't be shy, help yourself'; 'Enryo shimasu' politely turns something down.

example.ja: 遠慮しないで、たくさん食べてね。
example.english: Don't be shy, eat as much as you like.

examplePolite.romaji: enryo shinaide, takusan tabete kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 遠慮しないで、たくさん食べてくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Don't be shy, please eat as much as you like.

items.notes: 'Goenryo kudasai' on signs means 'please refrain', as with smoking or photos.

items.english: give up (a seat, a turn); hand over
items.use: The classic use is giving up your seat on a train: 'seki o yuzuru'.

example.romaji: obaachan ni seki o yuzutta yo.
example.ja: おばあちゃんに席を譲ったよ。
example.english: I gave my seat to an old lady.

examplePolite.romaji: obaasan ni seki o yuzurimashita.
examplePolite.ja: おばあさんに席を譲りました。
examplePolite.english: I gave my seat to an old lady.

items.notes: Also letting someone go first, or passing something on to them.

items.use: Often after -te mo: 'Tsukatte mo kamawanai yo' (You're welcome to use it).

example.ja: 明日でも構わないよ。
example.english: Tomorrow's fine with me too.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita demo kamaimasen yo.
examplePolite.ja: 明日でも構いませんよ。
examplePolite.english: Tomorrow is fine too.

items.notes: In casual talk, 'ii yo' is more common; kamawanai sounds a little firmer.

blocks.label: Keeping people close or away
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about getting involved, being disliked or avoided, and wanting attention or to be left alone.
blocks.interference: Kamawanaide and hottoite both mean 'leave me alone'; kirau is rare next to kirai da.

items.english: get involved with; have to do with
items.use: Often a warning: 'Aitsu to wa kakawaranai hou ga ii' (Better not get mixed up with him).

example.romaji: ano hito to wa amari kakawaranai hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: あの人とはあまり関わらない方がいいよ。
example.english: Better not get too involved with that person.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito to wa amari kakawaranai hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの人とはあまり関わらない方がいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: It's better not to get too involved with that person.

items.notes: Also 'be a matter of': 'inochi ni kakawaru' (life-threatening).

items.use: Mostly heard as kirawareru (be disliked): 'Kirawareta kamo' (Maybe they hate me now).

example.ja: 彼に嫌われたかもしれない。
example.english: He might hate me now.

examplePolite.romaji: kare ni kirawareta kamo shiremasen.
examplePolite.ja: 彼に嫌われたかもしれません。
examplePolite.english: He might dislike me now.

items.notes: To say you dislike something yourself, kirai da is far more common than kirau.

items.use: For avoiding people, topics or crowds; sakerareru means 'be avoided'.

example.romaji: saikin, nanka sakerareteru ki ga suru.
example.ja: 最近、なんか避けられてる気がする。
example.english: Lately I feel like I'm being avoided.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin, sakerarete iru ki ga shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 最近、避けられている気がします。
examplePolite.english: Lately I feel like I'm being avoided.

items.notes: Also physically dodging something, like a ball or a puddle.

items.english: pay attention to, fuss over; mind
items.use: 'Kamatte' asks for attention; 'Kamawanaide' means 'Leave me alone'.

example.ja: 猫が構ってほしいみたい。
example.english: The cat seems to want some attention.

examplePolite.romaji: neko ga kamatte hoshii mitai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 猫が構ってほしいみたいです。
examplePolite.english: The cat seems to want some attention.

items.notes: The 'mind' sense lives in the negative: kamawanai, kamaimasen (I don't mind).

items.use: Casually shortened to hottoku: 'Hottoite!' (Leave me alone!).

example.ja: もういいから、ほっといて。
example.english: Just forget it and leave me alone.

examplePolite.romaji: mou kekkou desu kara, houtte oite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: もう結構ですから、放っておいてください。
examplePolite.english: That's enough, please just leave me alone.

items.notes: Also leaving a problem untouched: 'Houtte oku to waruku naru' (It'll get worse if you leave it).

blocks.label: Dating and breaking up
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about asking someone out, dating, being popular and splitting up.
blocks.interference: Wakareta (broke up) sounds like wakatta (got it).

items.english: go out with, date; keep someone company
items.use: 'Tsukiatte kudasai' is the classic ask to be someone's partner; 'tsukiatteru' means they're dating.

example.ja: あの二人、付き合ってるらしいよ。
example.english: Apparently those two are going out.

examplePolite.romaji: ano futari wa tsukiatte iru rashii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの二人は付き合っているらしいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Apparently those two are going out.

items.notes: Second sense: come along with someone, as in 'Kaimono ni tsukiatte' (come shopping with me).

items.use: The person you split from takes to: 'Kare to wakareta' (I broke up with him).

example.ja: 彼女と別れたんだ。
example.english: I broke up with my girlfriend.

examplePolite.romaji: kanojo to wakareta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 彼女と別れたんです。
examplePolite.english: I broke up with my girlfriend.

items.notes: Wakareta (broke up) sounds close to wakatta (got it).

items.english: confess one's feelings, ask someone out
items.use: The big moment of telling someone you like them and asking to date.

example.romaji: kinou, yuki ni kokuhaku shita n da.
example.ja: 昨日、ユキに告白したんだ。
example.english: I told Yuki how I feel yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou, yuki-san ni kokuhaku shita n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日、ユキさんに告白したんです。
examplePolite.english: I told Yuki how I feel yesterday.

items.notes: Slang kokuru is short for kokuhaku suru. It can also mean confessing a secret, but the romance sense dominates.

items.english: be popular romantically, get a lot of attention
items.use: Often as motesou (looks like they'd be popular) or motenai (gets no attention).

example.ja: 彼、絶対モテるよね。
example.english: I bet he's really popular with girls.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa zettai motemasu yo ne.
