items.notes: Majime ni kotaete = answer me seriously. Majime is a personality; shinken is the attitude in the moment.

items.use: In speech it mostly means careless or whatever-works: 'tekitou ni yatta' = I just winged it.

example.romaji: kare no henji, itsumo tekitou da yo ne.
example.ja: 彼の返事、いつも適当だよね。
example.english: His answers are always half-hearted.

examplePolite.romaji: kare no henji wa itsumo tekitou desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼の返事はいつも適当ですね。
examplePolite.english: His answers are always half-hearted.

items.notes: The written sense 'suitable' survives in tekitou ni suwatte = sit wherever you like.

items.use: Fully serious about something right now: 'shinken ni kangaete' = think about it seriously.

example.romaji: shinken ni hanashiteru n da kedo.
example.ja: 真剣に話してるんだけど。
example.english: I'm being serious here.

examplePolite.romaji: shinken ni hanashite iru n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: 真剣に話しているんですけど。
examplePolite.english: I'm being serious here.

items.notes: Shinken na kao = a serious face.

items.english: sloppy; irresponsible; (iikagen ni shite) enough already
items.use: Iikagen na hito = someone you can't rely on; 'iikagen ni shite!' = knock it off!

example.ja: もう、いいかげんにしてよ！
example.english: Come on, knock it off already!

examplePolite.romaji: mou, iikagen ni shite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: もう、いいかげんにしてください。
examplePolite.english: Please, that's enough.

items.notes: Close to tekitou, but more blaming. Iikagen na shigoto = sloppy work.

blocks.label: Odd, open, quiet
blocks.rationale: Lets you sum up someone's personality in a word.
blocks.interference: Sunao (open, accepting) vs shoujiki (not lying); otonashii is behaviour, shizuka is noise.

items.use: For a person or thing that isn't like the rest; often fond, sometimes a soft way to say weird.

example.ja: 彼、ちょっと変わってるよね。
example.english: He's a bit odd, isn't he?

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa chotto kawatte imasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼はちょっと変わっていますね。
examplePolite.english: He's a bit unusual, isn't he?

items.notes: From kawaru (change); kawatta hito = an odd person. Softer than hen (weird).

items.use: Takes things as they are without pride or stubbornness: accepts advice, says what they feel.

example.romaji: sunao ni ayamatta hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: 素直に謝ったほうがいいよ。
example.english: You should just own up and apologize.

examplePolite.romaji: sunao ni ayamatta hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 素直に謝ったほうがいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You should just own up and apologize.

items.notes: Sunao ni ureshii = I'm honestly happy. Shoujiki is honest as in not lying.

items.use: For people and animals that are calm and make no fuss: a shy kid, a gentle dog.

example.ja: 今日はずいぶんおとなしいね。
example.english: You're awfully quiet today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa zuibun otonashii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はずいぶんおとなしいですね。
examplePolite.english: You're very quiet today.

items.notes: Otonashiku shite! = settle down! (to kids). Shizuka is quiet as in no noise.

blocks.label: Pushy and cocky
blocks.rationale: Lets you complain about people who nag, act superior, overreact or force things.
blocks.interference: Erasou (acts superior) vs namaiki (cheeky junior); shitsukoi (keeps at it) vs gouin (forces it).

items.english: annoyingly persistent; won't let it go; (food) too rich
items.use: For someone who keeps asking, calling or nagging.

example.romaji: ano hito, nankai mo denwa shite kite shitsukoi.
example.ja: あの人、何回も電話してきてしつこい。
example.english: That guy keeps calling. He won't give up.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito wa nankai mo denwa shite kite, shitsukoi desu.
examplePolite.ja: あの人は何回も電話してきて、しつこいです。
examplePolite.english: That person keeps calling. He won't give up.

items.notes: Shitsukoi na! = give it a rest! Shitsukoi aji = a heavy, lingering taste.

items.english: bossy; full of yourself; acting superior
items.use: Criticism of someone who acts important: 'erasou ni iu' = talk down to people.

example.romaji: ano senpai, itsumo erasou da yo ne.
example.ja: あの先輩、いつも偉そうだよね。
example.english: That senior always acts so superior.

examplePolite.romaji: ano senpai wa itsumo erasou desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの先輩はいつも偉そうですね。
examplePolite.english: That senior always acts so superior.

items.notes: Erai + -sou, but it means 'acts superior', not 'looks admirable'.

items.use: Usually a reply to someone making a fuss: 'oogesa da na' = you're overreacting.

example.romaji: oogesa da yo, sonna ni itakunai desho.
example.ja: 大げさだよ、そんなに痛くないでしょ。
example.english: You're overreacting, it can't hurt that much.

examplePolite.romaji: oogesa desu yo. sonna ni itakunai deshou.
examplePolite.ja: 大げさですよ。そんなに痛くないでしょう。
examplePolite.english: You're overreacting. It can't hurt that much.

items.notes: Oogesa ni iu = exaggerate when telling something.

items.use: Said of someone younger or junior acting above their place.

example.romaji: kono ko, chiisai noni namaiki da na.
example.ja: この子、小さいのに生意気だな。
example.english: This kid is so cheeky for someone so little.

examplePolite.romaji: kono ko wa chiisai noni namaiki desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この子は小さいのに生意気ですね。
examplePolite.english: This child is quite cheeky for someone so small.

items.notes: You call kids and juniors namaiki, never your boss; for anyone acting superior, use erasou.

items.use: Pushing things through without asking others: 'gouin ni kimeta' = forced the decision.

example.romaji: kare, chotto gouin na tokoro aru yo ne.
example.ja: 彼、ちょっと強引なところあるよね。
example.english: He can be a bit pushy, right?

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa chotto gouin na tokoro ga arimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼はちょっと強引なところがありますね。
examplePolite.english: He can be a bit forceful.

items.notes: Shitsukoi is pushy by repeating; gouin is pushy by force. In romance it can be a compliment (assertive).

blocks.label: Safe or in danger
blocks.rationale: Ask if people are okay and things are going well.
blocks.interference: Buji is coming through unharmed; anzen is a safe condition.

items.use: Usually 'buji ni' (safely) or 'buji de yokatta' (glad you're okay).

example.ja: 無事に着いた？よかった。
example.english: You got there okay? Good.

examplePolite.romaji: buji ni tsukimashita ka? yokatta desu.
examplePolite.ja: 無事に着きましたか？よかったです。
examplePolite.english: Did you arrive safely? I'm glad.

items.notes: 'Anzen' is safe as a condition; 'buji' is coming through something unharmed.

items.use: Sounds serious, like a warning; in chat 'abunai' is more common.

example.romaji: asoko wa yoru, kiken da yo.
example.ja: あそこは夜、危険だよ。
example.english: That area's dangerous at night.

examplePolite.romaji: asoko wa yoru wa kiken desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あそこは夜は危険ですよ。
examplePolite.english: That area is dangerous at night.

example.romaji: nihon tte, yoru mo anzen da yo ne.
example.ja: 日本って、夜も安全だよね。
example.english: Japan's safe even at night, right?

examplePolite.romaji: nihon wa yoru mo anzen desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 日本は夜も安全ですね。
examplePolite.english: Japan is safe even at night.

items.notes: Opposite: 'kiken', or the everyday 'abunai'.

items.use: A common answer to 'How's it going?': 'Junchou da yo.'

example.ja: 新しい仕事、順調にいってる？
example.english: Is the new job going well?

examplePolite.romaji: atarashii oshigoto wa junchou desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 新しいお仕事は順調ですか。
examplePolite.english: Is your new job going well?

blocks.label: Easy, handy, in the way
blocks.rationale: Say whether something makes life easier or gets in the way.
blocks.interference: Raku is 'no effort', not 'easy to understand' ('kantan').

items.use: Said of things blocking you and people interrupting you.

example.romaji: sono hako, jama da kara dokete.
example.ja: その箱、邪魔だからどけて。
example.english: That box is in the way, move it.

examplePolite.romaji: sono hako, jama na node dokete moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: その箱、邪魔なのでどけてもらえますか。
examplePolite.english: That box is in the way. Could you move it?

items.notes: Also a verb: 'jama shinaide' means 'don't bother me'. 'Ojama shimasu' is what you say entering someone's home.

items.use: 'Raku ni shite' means 'make yourself comfortable'.

example.ja: この仕事、楽だよ。
example.english: This job's easy.

examplePolite.romaji: kono shigoto wa raku desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: この仕事は楽ですよ。
examplePolite.english: This job is easy.

items.notes: Easy as in 'no strain'; an easy test or question is 'kantan'.

items.use: For size, temperature, amount or timing.

example.ja: このサイズ、ちょうどいい。
example.english: This size is just right.

examplePolite.romaji: kono saizu ga choudo ii desu.
examplePolite.ja: このサイズがちょうどいいです。
examplePolite.english: This size is just right.

items.notes: Changes like 'ii': 'choudo yokatta' (that worked out perfectly).

example.romaji: kono apuri, sugoi benri da yo.
example.ja: このアプリ、すごい便利だよ。
example.english: This app is really handy.

examplePolite.romaji: kono apuri wa totemo benri desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: このアプリはとても便利ですよ。
examplePolite.english: This app is very convenient.

items.notes: Opposite: 'fuben' (inconvenient).

blocks.label: Describing a room
blocks.rationale: Comment on a room or place: noise, light, mess and smell.
blocks.interference: Urusai is also 'annoying' and 'Shut up!', not just loud.

example.ja: 隣の部屋、うるさいね。
example.english: The room next door is noisy, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: tonari no heya ga urusai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 隣の部屋がうるさいですね。
examplePolite.english: The room next door is noisy, isn't it.

items.notes: Said alone, 'Urusai!' means 'Shut up!' and is rude. 'Aji ni urusai' means picky about taste.

items.use: 'Shizuka ni!' or 'Shizuka ni shite' means 'Be quiet!'

example.romaji: kono kafe, shizuka de ii ne.
example.ja: このカフェ、静かでいいね。
example.english: This cafe is nice and quiet.

examplePolite.romaji: kono kafe wa shizuka de ii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: このカフェは静かでいいですね。
examplePolite.english: This cafe is nice and quiet.

items.notes: Opposite: 'urusai' (noisy).

items.use: Common for personalities: an 'akarui hito' is an upbeat person.

example.ja: この部屋、明るくていいね。
example.english: This room's nice and bright.

examplePolite.romaji: kono heya wa akarukute ii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この部屋は明るくていいですね。
examplePolite.english: This room is nice and bright.

items.notes: Opposite: 'kurai' (dark; gloomy).

items.use: Also for cheating: 'Kitanai!' means 'That's dirty!'

example.ja: ごめん、部屋汚いけど。
example.english: Sorry, my room's a mess.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, heya ga kitanai desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、部屋が汚いですけど。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, the room is a mess.

items.notes: Opposite: 'kirei' (clean). Messy handwriting is also 'kitanai'.

items.use: 'X kusai' means smells of X: 'tabako kusai'.

example.ja: なんかこの部屋、臭くない？
example.english: Doesn't this room smell?

examplePolite.romaji: kono heya, chotto kusai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この部屋、ちょっと臭いですね。
examplePolite.english: This room smells a bit.

items.notes: As an ending it also means '-ish, seems like': 'mendokusai' (a pain), 'uso kusai' (sounds like a lie).

blocks.label: Right and obvious
blocks.rationale: Say something is right, obvious, certain or sensible.
blocks.interference: Atarimae is 'of course'; akiraka is 'plain to see'.

items.use: 'Atarimae!' or 'Atarimae jan' answers a question with 'Of course!'

example.ja: 当たり前じゃん、友達だもん。
example.english: Of course, we're friends.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa atarimae desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: それは当たり前ですよ。
examplePolite.english: That's only natural.

items.notes: Said flatly, it can sound like 'Duh.'

items.use: For answers, facts and morally right choices.

example.ja: やっぱり、こっちが正しいよ。
example.english: Yeah, this one's right.

examplePolite.romaji: yappari, kochira ga tadashii desu.
examplePolite.ja: やっぱり、こちらが正しいです。
examplePolite.english: Yes, this one is correct.

items.notes: To confirm an answer in casual talk, 'atteru' (that's right) is more common.

items.use: 'Kakujitsu ni' means for sure, without fail.

example.romaji: kono hou ga kakujitsu da yo.
example.ja: この方が確実だよ。
example.english: This way's the safer bet.

examplePolite.romaji: kono hou ga kakujitsu desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: この方が確実ですよ。
examplePolite.english: This way is more reliable.

items.notes: 'Tashika' is the everyday 'sure'; 'kakujitsu' stresses it will definitely happen or work.

items.use: Mostly in complaints: 'matomo na shigoto' (a proper job), 'matomo ja nai' (not normal).

example.romaji: kinou kara matomo na mono tabete nai.
example.ja: 昨日からまともなもの食べてない。
example.english: I haven't had a proper meal since yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou kara matomo na mono o tabete imasen.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日からまともなものを食べていません。
examplePolite.english: I haven't eaten a proper meal since yesterday.

items.notes: 'Matomo ni' means properly: 'matomo ni hanasenai' (can't even talk properly).

items.use: Mostly 'akiraka ni' (clearly, obviously).

example.romaji: sore, akiraka ni uso da yo.
example.ja: それ、明らかに嘘だよ。
example.english: That's obviously a lie.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa akiraka ni uso desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: それは明らかに嘘ですよ。
examplePolite.english: That's clearly a lie.

items.notes: 'Atarimae' is 'of course, naturally'; 'akiraka' is 'plain to see'.

blocks.label: Waste and no point
blocks.rationale: Say something is pointless, wasteful or beyond help.
blocks.interference: Muda is useless effort; mottainai is regret over wasting something good.

items.use: 'Muda da' means it's no use; 'jikan no muda' is a waste of time.

example.ja: 言っても無駄だよ。
example.english: It's no use telling him.

examplePolite.romaji: itte mo muda desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 言っても無駄ですよ。
examplePolite.english: There's no point telling him.

items.notes: 'Mudazukai' is wasting money.

items.english: what a waste; too good to waste
items.use: Said when something useful is thrown away or left unused.

example.ja: まだ食べられるのに、もったいないよ。
example.english: It's still good to eat, what a waste.

examplePolite.romaji: mada taberareru noni, mottainai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: まだ食べられるのに、もったいないですよ。
examplePolite.english: It's still edible. That's such a waste.

items.notes: 'Muda' is useless effort; 'mottainai' is regret over wasting something good.

items.use: Often after a te-form: 'itte mo imi nai' (no point saying it).

example.romaji: imasara isoide mo imi nai yo.
example.ja: 今さら急いでも意味ないよ。
example.english: No point hurrying now.

examplePolite.romaji: imasara isoide mo imi ga arimasen yo.
examplePolite.ja: 今さら急いでも意味がありませんよ。
examplePolite.english: There's no point hurrying now.

items.notes: Different from 'imi wakannai' (makes no sense).

items.english: hopeless, nothing can be done; useless (person)
items.use: About a situation: nothing can be done; about a person: hopeless.
items.politeJa: どうしようもありません

example.romaji: ame da kara, dou shiyou mo nai ne.
example.ja: 雨だから、どうしようもないね。
example.english: It's raining, nothing we can do.

examplePolite.romaji: ame na node, dou shiyou mo arimasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: 雨なので、どうしようもありませんね。
examplePolite.english: It's raining, so there's nothing we can do.

items.notes: 'Shou ga nai' is the everyday 'oh well'; 'dou shiyou mo nai' is stronger: truly hopeless.

blocks.label: Still, already, originally
blocks.rationale: Lets you compare now with how things were before.
blocks.interference: Imada ni (still) and tokku ni (long ago) point in opposite directions.

items.english: as always; same as ever; still
items.use: Often a friendly remark that someone hasn't changed; can also tease.

example.ja: 相変わらず元気だね。
example.english: You're as lively as ever.

examplePolite.romaji: aikawarazu ogenki desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 相変わらずお元気ですね。
examplePolite.english: You're as well as ever.

items.notes: Aikawarazu da ne on its own means 'same old you'.

items.english: originally; to begin with; by nature
items.use: Points back to how things were before, or how someone has always been.

example.romaji: motomoto amai mono wa suki ja nai n da.
example.ja: もともと甘いものは好きじゃないんだ。
example.english: I've never liked sweets to begin with.

examplePolite.romaji: motomoto amai mono wa suki ja nai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: もともと甘いものは好きじゃないんです。
examplePolite.english: I've never really liked sweet things.

items.notes: Motomoto wa often contrasts with now: motomoto wa kissaten datta, 'it used to be a café'.

items.use: Stresses something happened way earlier than the other person thinks.

example.romaji: sonna no tokku ni shitteru yo.
example.ja: そんなのとっくに知ってるよ。
example.english: I've known that for ages.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa tokku ni shitte imasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: それはとっくに知っていますよ。
examplePolite.english: I've known that for a long time.

items.notes: Stronger than mou, 'already', often with a hint of 'obviously'.

items.use: Stresses something has dragged on longer than it should, often with surprise or annoyance.

example.ja: いまだに信じられないよ。
example.english: I still can't believe it.

examplePolite.romaji: imada ni shinjiraremasen.
examplePolite.ja: いまだに信じられません。
examplePolite.english: I still can't believe it.

items.notes: Stronger than mada, 'still'.

blocks.label: Again, for now, never again
blocks.rationale: Lets you say when something pauses, carries on or happens again.
blocks.interference: Nido to needs a negative verb, unlike mata 'again'.

items.use: Always followed by a negative verb; strong and emotional.

example.romaji: nido to konai yo, konna mise.
example.ja: 二度と来ないよ、こんな店。
example.english: I'm never coming back to this place.

examplePolite.romaji: kono mise ni wa nido to kimasen.
examplePolite.ja: この店には二度と来ません。
examplePolite.english: I'll never come to this shop again.

items.notes: Nido to shinai is a firm promise: 'I'll never do it again.'

items.english: for the first time in ages; after a long time

example.ja: 久しぶりに映画見た。
example.english: I saw a movie for the first time in ages.

examplePolite.romaji: hisashiburi ni eiga o mimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 久しぶりに映画を見ました。
examplePolite.english: I watched a movie for the first time in a long while.

items.notes: Hisashiburi! on its own is the greeting 'long time no see'.

items.english: again (another time); anew; once more, properly
items.use: Doing something over at a better time or more formally, or seeing it with fresh eyes.

example.romaji: jaa, mata aratamete renraku suru ne.
example.ja: じゃあ、また改めて連絡するね。
example.english: OK, I'll get back to you another time.

examplePolite.romaji: mata aratamete renraku shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: また改めて連絡します。
examplePolite.english: I'll contact you again later.

items.notes: Aratamete omou to... means 'now that I think about it again...', for a fresh realization.

items.english: for now; for a moment; once
items.use: Pauses or switches something temporarily before carrying on: stop for now, go home first.

example.ja: いったん家に帰るね。
example.english: I'll head home for now.

examplePolite.romaji: ittan ie ni kaerimasu.
examplePolite.ja: いったん家に帰ります。
examplePolite.english: I'll go home first.

items.notes: Ittan kyuukei shiyou, 'let's take a break for now', is common in meetings and practice.

items.use: Says something carries on unchanged; very common at work and in meetings.

example.ja: 午後も引き続き頑張ろう。
example.english: Let's keep at it this afternoon too.

examplePolite.romaji: gogo mo hikitsuzuki ganbarimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 午後も引き続き頑張りましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's keep it up this afternoon as well.

items.notes: Hikitsuzuki yoroshiku onegai shimasu is a stock sign-off at work.

blocks.label: Of course, actually, apparently
blocks.rationale: Lets you frame a fact as obvious, real, inferred or unfortunate.
blocks.interference: Douyara is a guess from evidence; jissai states what is really so.

items.english: natural; only to be expected; of course
items.use: Says something is obvious or deserved; touzen desho is 'obviously!'.

example.ja: 怒って当然だよ。
example.english: You've every right to be angry.

examplePolite.romaji: okotte touzen desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 怒って当然ですよ。
examplePolite.english: You have every right to be angry.

items.notes: Also an adverb: touzen shitteru, 'of course I know'. Touzen desho! can sound smug.

items.use: Contrasts reality with expectations or claims; also opens a sentence, 'honestly...'.

example.romaji: jissai yatte miru to, muzukashii yo.
example.ja: 実際やってみると、難しいよ。
example.english: Once you actually try it, it's hard.

examplePolite.romaji: jissai yatte miru to, muzukashii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 実際やってみると、難しいですよ。
examplePolite.english: When you actually try it, it's difficult.

items.notes: Jissai ni means the same.

items.use: Draws a conclusion from what you've seen or heard; usually ends with mitai or rashii.

example.ja: どうやら道を間違えたみたい。
example.english: Looks like we took a wrong turn.

examplePolite.romaji: douyara michi o machigaeta you desu.
examplePolite.ja: どうやら道を間違えたようです。
examplePolite.english: It seems we've taken the wrong road.

items.use: Softens bad news at the start of a sentence; a little formal.

example.ja: 残念ながら、売り切れだって。
example.english: Unfortunately, they say it's sold out.

examplePolite.romaji: zannen nagara, urikire da sou desu.
examplePolite.ja: 残念ながら、売り切れだそうです。
examplePolite.english: Unfortunately, it seems they're sold out.

items.notes: In casual chat people often just say zannen! 'what a shame'.

blocks.label: Suddenly and all at once
blocks.rationale: Lets you describe abrupt changes and ones you didn't notice.
blocks.interference: Totsuzen and ikinari overlap; ikinari is more casual and often a complaint.

items.use: For unexpected events and changes; more neutral and news-like than ikinari.

example.ja: 突然雨が降ってきた。
example.english: It suddenly started raining.

examplePolite.romaji: totsuzen ame ga futte kimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 突然雨が降ってきました。
examplePolite.english: It suddenly started to rain.

items.notes: Totsuzen desu ga... ('sorry this is sudden, but...') opens an unexpected request.

items.english: suddenly; out of the blue; right off
items.use: Casual; often a complaint that someone acted abruptly, without warning or build-up.

example.ja: いきなり怒り出したんだよ。
example.english: He suddenly got angry out of nowhere.

examplePolite.romaji: ikinari okoridashita n desu.
examplePolite.ja: いきなり怒り出したんです。
examplePolite.english: He suddenly got angry.

items.notes: Also 'straight away, skipping the warm-up', as in ikinari honban, going live with no rehearsal.

items.english: before I knew it; without noticing
items.use: For changes that slipped by unnoticed, like time passing or something going missing.

example.romaji: itsu no ma ni ka nechatta.
example.ja: いつの間にか寝ちゃった。
example.english: I fell asleep before I knew it.

examplePolite.romaji: itsu no ma ni ka nete shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: いつの間にか寝てしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I dozed off without realizing.

items.notes: Totsuzen is a sudden event; itsu no ma ni ka is a gradual change you missed.

items.english: all at once; in one go
items.use: For doing something without stopping, or for a sudden big change.

example.ja: 一気に飲んじゃった。
example.english: I drank it all in one go.

examplePolite.romaji: ikki ni nonde shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 一気に飲んでしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I drank it all at once.

items.notes: Ikki! alone is the drinking chant 'chug!'; ikki ni yonda is 'read it in one sitting'.

blocks.label: Why and somehow
blocks.rationale: Lets you ask why and admit you don't know why.
blocks.interference: Nandaka, nazeka and nantonaku all mean 'somehow' and blur together.

items.use: A firmer, more serious why than nande or doushite; common in speeches, news and heated questions.

example.ja: なぜ黙ってたの?
example.english: Why did you keep quiet about it?

examplePolite.romaji: naze damatte ita n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: なぜ黙っていたんですか?
examplePolite.english: Why didn't you say anything?

items.notes: In everyday chat, nande is the usual casual why and doushite the softer one.

items.use: Strengthens a question to show surprise, frustration or alarm.

example.ja: 一体何があったの?
example.english: What on earth happened?

examplePolite.romaji: ittai nani ga atta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 一体何があったんですか?
examplePolite.english: What on earth happened?

items.notes: Always paired with a question word like nani, doko, dare or doushite.

items.english: somehow; kind of; for some reason
items.use: Hedges a feeling you can't pin down; nandaka hen is 'something feels off'.

example.ja: なんだか眠くなってきた。
example.english: I'm kind of getting sleepy.

examplePolite.romaji: nandaka nemuku natte kimashita.
examplePolite.ja: なんだか眠くなってきました。
examplePolite.english: I'm somehow getting sleepy.

items.notes: Close to nantonaku, which leans more toward 'for no particular reason'.

items.use: Says something happens and you can't explain why; common when telling stories.

example.ja: なぜか今日は眠れない。
example.english: For some reason I can't sleep tonight.

examplePolite.romaji: nazeka kyou wa nemuremasen.
examplePolite.ja: なぜか今日は眠れません。
examplePolite.english: For some reason, I can't sleep tonight.

items.notes: Nazeka is about an unexplained fact; nandaka is about a vague feeling.

items.english: somehow; for no particular reason; vaguely
items.use: For choices and feelings you can't explain; on its own it's a full answer to 'why?'.

example.romaji: nantonaku, kyou wa soto ni detakunai.
example.ja: なんとなく、今日は外に出たくない。
example.english: I just don't feel like going out today.

examplePolite.romaji: nantonaku, kyou wa soto ni detakunai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: なんとなく、今日は外に出たくないんです。
examplePolite.english: For some reason, I don't feel like going out today.

items.notes: Nantonaku wakaru, 'I sort of get it', is a common half-yes.

blocks.label: Sooner or later
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about a vague future and how long things last.
blocks.interference: Sono uchi 'sometime soon' and ima no uchi 'while you still can' sound alike.

items.english: one of these days; sooner or later; soon
items.use: A vague future, from 'soon' to 'eventually'; also a soft way to put things off.

example.romaji: sono uchi nomi ni ikou yo.
example.ja: そのうち飲みに行こうよ。
example.english: Let's go for a drink one of these days.

examplePolite.romaji: sono uchi nomi ni ikimashou.
examplePolite.ja: そのうち飲みに行きましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's go for a drink sometime.

items.notes: Sono uchi naoru yo, 'it'll get better soon', is a common reassurance.

items.english: forever; for as long as; endlessly
items.use: Warm when wishing ('always'), impatient when complaining ('how long are you going to...').

example.ja: いつまでもくよくよしないで。
example.english: Don't keep brooding over it forever.

examplePolite.romaji: itsu made mo kuyokuyo shinaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: いつまでもくよくよしないでください。
examplePolite.english: Please don't keep dwelling on it.

items.notes: Itsu made? alone asks 'until when?'.

items.use: A firm, slightly formal 'eventually' for things bound to happen.

example.ja: いずれバレるよ。
example.english: It'll come out sooner or later.

examplePolite.romaji: izure baremasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: いずれバレますよ。
examplePolite.english: It'll come out eventually.

items.notes: Sono uchi is vaguer and more casual.

items.english: while you can; now, before it's too late
items.use: Urges doing something now while there's still the chance; usually ima no uchi ni.

example.romaji: ima no uchi ni tabete okou.
example.ja: 今のうちに食べておこう。
example.english: Let's eat now while we can.

examplePolite.romaji: ima no uchi ni tabete okimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 今のうちに食べておきましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's eat while we have the chance.

items.notes: Often pairs with -te oku, doing something in advance.

blocks.label: On purpose or forced
blocks.rationale: Lets you say whether something was intended, forced or a kind effort.
blocks.interference: Wazawaza (kindly went out of your way) and wazato (did it on purpose) are easy to swap.

items.english: going out of your way; all the way; specially
items.use: Thanks someone for trouble they took, or grumbles that the effort wasn't needed.

example.ja: わざわざ来てくれてありがとう。
example.english: Thanks for coming all this way.

examplePolite.romaji: wazawaza kite kudasatte arigatou gozaimasu.
examplePolite.ja: わざわざ来てくださってありがとうございます。
examplePolite.english: Thank you so much for taking the trouble to come.

items.notes: Don't mix with wazato, which means on purpose, usually something bad.

items.use: Usually about something mean or wrong done intentionally; common in accusations and denials.

example.ja: わざとじゃないよ!
example.english: I didn't do it on purpose!

examplePolite.romaji: wazato ja nai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: わざとじゃないんです。
examplePolite.english: I didn't mean to.

items.notes: Wazawaza is 'going out of your way', often kind; wazato is deliberate, often bad.

items.use: Making someone do something, or pushing something through, despite resistance.

example.ja: 無理やり連れてこられた。
example.english: I got dragged along against my will.

examplePolite.romaji: muriyari tsurete koraremashita.
examplePolite.ja: 無理やり連れてこられました。
examplePolite.english: I was dragged here against my will.

items.notes: Also for forcing things, like cramming a bag shut or eating when you're full.

items.use: Choosing to do something unusual or harder on purpose, knowing the easy option.

example.ja: あえて何も言わなかった。
example.english: I deliberately didn't say anything.

examplePolite.romaji: aete nani mo iimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: あえて何も言いませんでした。
examplePolite.english: I chose not to say anything.

items.notes: Unlike wazato, aete is a considered choice, not mischief.

blocks.label: Right away, on the spot
blocks.rationale: Lets you say something happens immediately or at the same moment.
blocks.interference: Sassato is an impatient 'hurry up', sassoku an eager 'right away'.

items.use: Pushy: urges someone to get on with it and stop dawdling.

example.ja: さっさと支度して!
example.english: Hurry up and get ready!

examplePolite.romaji: sassato sumasete shimaimashou.
examplePolite.ja: さっさと済ませてしまいましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's just get it done and over with.

items.notes: Sounds impatient when aimed at others; about your own task it just means 'quickly, and be done with it'.

items.use: Doing something promptly and eagerly, like trying a gift or getting started.

example.ja: じゃあ、早速始めよう。
example.english: OK, let's get started right away.

examplePolite.romaji: dewa, sassoku hajimemashou.
examplePolite.ja: では、早速始めましょう。
examplePolite.english: Well then, let's get started.

items.notes: Positive and eager; sassato is the impatient 'hurry up'.

items.use: Almost always heard as douji ni, 'at the same time'.

example.ja: 同時に着いたね。
example.english: We got here at the same time.

examplePolite.romaji: douji ni tsukimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: 同時に着きましたね。
examplePolite.english: We arrived at the same time.

items.notes: Douji ni also links two facts: 'and at the same time...'.

items.use: Usually sono ba de, 'on the spot', for deciding, paying or reacting right there.

example.ja: その場で決めちゃった。
example.english: I decided right there on the spot.

examplePolite.romaji: sono ba de kimete shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: その場で決めてしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I made the decision on the spot.

items.notes: Sono ba ni ita means 'I was there', present when it happened.

blocks.label: By chance
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about luck, coincidence and unlikely possibilities.
blocks.interference: Tamatama sounds like tama ni, 'occasionally'.

items.use: Works as 'by chance' and as the noun 'a coincidence': guuzen da ne! is 'what a coincidence!'.

example.romaji: eki de guuzen sensei ni atta.
example.ja: 駅で偶然先生に会った。
example.english: I ran into my teacher at the station by chance.

examplePolite.romaji: eki de guuzen sensei ni aimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 駅で偶然先生に会いました。
examplePolite.english: I happened to run into my teacher at the station.

items.notes: Tamatama means much the same and is softer and more casual.

items.use: Casual way to say something came about by luck, often to play it down.

example.ja: たまたま近くにいたから。
example.english: I just happened to be nearby.

examplePolite.romaji: tamatama chikaku ni ita n desu.
examplePolite.ja: たまたま近くにいたんです。
examplePolite.english: I just happened to be in the area.

items.notes: Don't confuse with tama ni, 'occasionally'.

items.english: if by some chance; in the unlikely event
items.use: For a rare worst case you're preparing for, usually with -tara or no toki.

example.ja: 万が一遅れたら、連絡して。
example.english: If by some chance you're late, let me know.

examplePolite.romaji: mangaichi okuretara, renraku shite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 万が一遅れたら、連絡してください。
examplePolite.english: Should you be late, please let me know.

items.notes: Literally 'one in ten thousand'; mangaichi no toki means 'in an emergency'.

items.use: Opens a hesitant guess or question, often when you suspect something.

example.ja: ひょっとして、怒ってる?
example.english: Are you angry, by any chance?

examplePolite.romaji: hyotto shite, okotte imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ひょっとして、怒っていますか?
examplePolite.english: Are you upset, by any chance?

items.notes: Moshikashite means the same and is more common.

blocks.label: Enough and complete
blocks.rationale: Lets you say something is enough, plenty, nearly done or totally done.
blocks.interference: Juubun (enough) and juppun (ten minutes) share the same kanji.

items.use: Mou juubun politely turns down more food or help.

example.ja: もう十分だよ、ありがとう。
example.english: That's plenty, thanks.

examplePolite.romaji: mou juubun desu, arigatou gozaimasu.
examplePolite.ja: もう十分です、ありがとうございます。
examplePolite.english: I've had plenty, thank you.

items.notes: The same kanji read juppun means ten minutes.

items.use: Very nearly all or complete: hobo owatta, hobo mainichi.

example.ja: 宿題、ほぼ終わった。
example.english: My homework's almost done.

examplePolite.romaji: shukudai wa hobo owarimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 宿題はほぼ終わりました。
examplePolite.english: I've nearly finished my homework.

items.notes: Close to hotondo (almost all); hobo mainichi = nearly every day.

items.use: Mostly kanzen ni before a verb or adjective: totally, 100%.

example.ja: 完全に道に迷った。
example.english: We're completely lost.

examplePolite.romaji: kanzen ni michi ni mayoimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 完全に道に迷いました。
examplePolite.english: I've got completely lost.

items.notes: Sukkari is softer and about change; kanzen ni is blunt and absolute.

items.use: A generous, full amount, often of food, time or sleep.

example.ja: 昨日はたっぷり寝た。
example.english: I got plenty of sleep last night.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou wa tappuri nemashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日はたっぷり寝ました。
examplePolite.english: I slept plenty last night.

items.notes: Jikan wa tappuri aru = there's plenty of time.

blocks.label: At least, no more
blocks.rationale: Lets you set a minimum, a limit, or say what matters most.
blocks.interference: Semete is a wish; sukunakutomo is a factual minimum.

items.use: The minimum you hope for or ask for.

example.romaji: okureru nara, semete renraku shite yo.
example.ja: 遅れるなら、せめて連絡してよ。
example.english: If you're going to be late, at least let me know.

examplePolite.romaji: okureru nara, semete renraku shite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 遅れるなら、せめて連絡してください。
examplePolite.english: If you'll be late, please at least get in touch.

items.notes: Sukunakutomo is a factual 'at least'; semete is a wish or request.

items.use: A minimum estimate or fact.

example.ja: 少なくとも一時間はかかるよ。
example.english: It'll take at least an hour.

examplePolite.romaji: sukunakutomo ichijikan wa kakarimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 少なくとも一時間はかかります。
examplePolite.english: It will take at least an hour.

items.notes: Also 'at least' for one case: sukunakutomo watashi wa shiranakatta (I, at least, didn't know).

items.use: Usually with a negative to draw a line: kore ijou muri (I can't take any more).

example.ja: もうこれ以上食べられない。
example.english: I can't eat any more.

examplePolite.romaji: mou kore ijou taberaremasen.
examplePolite.ja: もうこれ以上食べられません。
examplePolite.english: I couldn't eat another bite.

items.notes: After a number, ijou means 'or more': juunin ijou (ten or more people).

items.use: Picks out the most important point.

example.romaji: nani yori, minna buji de yokatta.
example.ja: 何より、みんな無事でよかった。
example.english: Most of all, I'm glad everyone's safe.

examplePolite.romaji: nani yori, minasan buji de yokatta desu.
examplePolite.ja: 何より、皆さん無事でよかったです。
examplePolite.english: Above all, I'm glad everyone is safe.

items.notes: Ogenki de nani yori desu = I'm so glad you're well (polite set phrase).

blocks.label: More and more
blocks.rationale: Lets you describe change: fast, gradual or still growing.
blocks.interference: Dondon is about speed; masumasu is about degree.

items.english: more and more; quickly; one after another
items.use: Fast, steady progress or increase; dondon tabete urges someone to dig in.

example.romaji: nihongo, dondon jouzu ni natteru ne.
example.ja: 日本語、どんどん上手になってるね。
example.english: Your Japanese is getting better and better.

examplePolite.romaji: nihongo ga dondon jouzu ni natte imasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 日本語がどんどん上手になっていますね。
examplePolite.english: Your Japanese is improving quickly.

items.notes: Also a banging or drumming sound.

items.english: little by little; a bit at a time
items.use: Gradual progress, or doing something in small portions.

example.ja: 少しずつ慣れてきたよ。
example.english: I'm getting used to it little by little.

examplePolite.romaji: sukoshi zutsu narete kimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 少しずつ慣れてきました。
examplePolite.english: I'm gradually getting used to it.

items.notes: -zutsu means 'each' or 'at a time': hitotsu zutsu (one each).

items.use: Something already true keeps growing: masumasu samuku naru.

example.ja: 説明聞いたら、ますますわからなくなった。
example.english: After the explanation I was even more confused.

examplePolite.romaji: setsumei o kiitara, masumasu wakaranaku narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 説明を聞いたら、ますますわからなくなりました。
examplePolite.english: The explanation left me even more confused.

items.notes: Dondon stresses speed; masumasu stresses growing degree.

items.english: even more; further; on top of that
items.use: Raises the degree of something already said; a bit more formal than motto.

example.romaji: ame ga sara ni tsuyoku natta.
example.ja: 雨がさらに強くなった。
example.english: The rain got even heavier.

examplePolite.romaji: ame ga sara ni tsuyoku narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 雨がさらに強くなりました。
examplePolite.english: The rain has become even heavier.

items.notes: At the start of a sentence it means 'moreover', common in news and ads.

blocks.label: Trips and moves
blocks.rationale: Talk about travel plans and moving: set off, move on, arrive, move house.
blocks.interference: idou suru is getting from place to place; hikkosu is moving house.

example.ja: 来月引っ越すんだ。
example.english: I'm moving next month.

examplePolite.romaji: raigetsu hikkoshimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 来月引っ越します。
examplePolite.english: I'm moving next month.

items.notes: hikkoshi = a move (noun): hikkoshi no junbi (packing for a move).

items.use: Heard in announcements and travel plans; in conversation 'arrive' is usually tsuku.

example.ja: 飛行機の到着、遅れるって。
example.english: They say the plane's going to be late.

examplePolite.romaji: hikouki no touchaku ga okureru sou desu.
examplePolite.ja: 飛行機の到着が遅れるそうです。
examplePolite.english: I hear the plane's arrival is delayed.

items.notes: As a verb, touchaku suru sounds formal: mamonaku touchaku shimasu (we'll arrive shortly).

items.english: move (from one place to another), get from A to B
items.use: Going somewhere else, on foot or by transport; not moving house (hikkosu) or budging (ugoku).

example.ja: そろそろ移動しようか。
example.english: Shall we move on?

examplePolite.romaji: sorosoro idou shimashou ka.
examplePolite.ja: そろそろ移動しましょうか。
examplePolite.english: Shall we head over soon?

items.notes: idouchuu = on the way, in transit (common in texts).

example.ja: 何時に出発する？
example.english: What time are we leaving?

examplePolite.romaji: nanji ni shuppatsu shimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 何時に出発しますか？
examplePolite.english: What time do we leave?

items.notes: shuppatsu! on its own = off we go! In casual talk, deru often does the same job.

blocks.label: Sick days
blocks.rationale: Call in sick, say you've caught a cold and talk about getting better.
blocks.interference: naoru is the illness getting better; naosu is you curing it.

items.english: rest, take a break; take time off (school, work)
items.use: Skipping school or work takes o: gakkou o yasumu.

example.romaji: netsu aru kara, kyou gakkou yasumu.
example.ja: 熱あるから、今日学校休む。
example.english: I've got a fever, so I'm skipping school today.

examplePolite.romaji: netsu ga aru node, kyou wa yasumimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 熱があるので、今日は休みます。
examplePolite.english: I have a fever, so I'll take today off.

items.notes: oyasumi = good night; chotto yasumou = let's take a break.

items.use: The illness or injury is the subject: kaze ga naoru.

example.ja: 風邪、もう治った？大丈夫？
example.english: Is your cold better? You okay?

examplePolite.romaji: kaze wa mou naorimashita ka? daijoubu desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 風邪はもう治りましたか？大丈夫ですか？
examplePolite.english: Has your cold cleared up? Are you all right?

items.notes: 直る naoru, same sound, is things getting fixed. Curing it yourself is naosu.

items.use: Usually past: kaze hiita (I've got a cold).

example.ja: 喉痛い。風邪ひいたみたい。
example.english: My throat hurts. I think I've caught a cold.

examplePolite.romaji: nodo ga itai desu. kaze o hiita mitai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 喉が痛いです。風邪をひいたみたいです。
examplePolite.english: My throat hurts. I think I've caught a cold.

items.notes: Full form is kaze o hiku; don't swap in toru or motsu.

items.use: You or a doctor does it: kaze o naosu.

example.ja: 早く風邪治してね。
example.english: Get over that cold soon.

examplePolite.romaji: hayaku kaze o naoshite kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 早く風邪を治してくださいね。
examplePolite.english: I hope you get over your cold soon.

items.notes: 直す naosu, same sound, means fix or correct things.

blocks.label: Falls and bumps
blocks.rationale: Describe small mishaps: getting soaked, collapsing, tripping, banging into things.
blocks.interference: korobu is tripping over; taoreru is collapsing or toppling.

example.ja: 雨でびしょびしょに濡れた。
example.english: I got soaked in the rain.

examplePolite.romaji: ame de bishobisho ni nuremashita.
examplePolite.ja: 雨でびしょびしょに濡れました。
examplePolite.english: I got soaked in the rain.

items.notes: Making something wet is nurasu.

items.use: For people collapsing, often from illness, and things toppling over.

example.ja: お父さんが倒れたって！
example.english: Dad's collapsed!

examplePolite.romaji: chichi ga taoreta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 父が倒れたんです。
examplePolite.english: My father has collapsed.

items.notes: Tripping while walking is korobu; taoreru is more serious.

example.ja: 昨日、階段で転んじゃった。
example.english: I tripped on the stairs yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou, kaidan de koronde shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日、階段で転んでしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I fell on the stairs yesterday.

items.notes: Collapsing or toppling over is taoreru.

items.use: You bump a thing into something: atama o butsukeru (bang your head).

example.ja: 痛い！棚に頭ぶつけた。
example.english: Ow! I banged my head on the shelf.

examplePolite.romaji: tana ni atama o butsukete shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 棚に頭をぶつけてしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I banged my head on the shelf.

items.notes: butsukaru = to bump into (by itself): hito ni butsukaru.

blocks.label: Hungry, thirsty, sleepy, drunk
blocks.rationale: Say how your body is doing right now.
blocks.interference: onaka suita and nodo kawaita are past forms but mean 'I'm hungry' and 'I'm thirsty' now.

items.english: get hungry (stomach); empty out, get less crowded
items.use: Mostly onaka ga suita (I'm hungry) and suite iru (not crowded).

example.ja: ああ、お腹すいた！なんか食べよう。
example.english: Ugh, I'm starving! Let's eat something.

examplePolite.romaji: onaka ga sukimashita ne. nanika tabemashou.
examplePolite.ja: お腹がすきましたね。何か食べましょう。
examplePolite.english: I'm getting hungry. Let's eat something.

items.notes: The same kanji read aku means 'become free': seki ga aita (a seat opened up).

items.english: dry, get dry; get thirsty (nodo ga kawaku)

example.ja: 喉乾いた。なんか飲もう。
example.english: I'm thirsty. Let's get a drink.

examplePolite.romaji: nodo ga kawakimashita. nanika nomimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 喉が乾きました。何か飲みましょう。
examplePolite.english: I'm thirsty. Let's have something to drink.

items.notes: For thirst the strict kanji is 渇く. Laundry: sentakumono ga kawaita (the washing's dry).

items.use: Actually being asleep; going to bed is neru.

example.ja: 夕べは暑くて全然眠れなかった。
example.english: It was so hot I couldn't sleep at all last night.

examplePolite.romaji: yuube wa atsukute zenzen nemuremasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 夕べは暑くて全然眠れませんでした。
examplePolite.english: It was so hot I couldn't sleep at all last night.

items.notes: nemui = sleepy. nemurenai (can't sleep) is the form you'll hear most.

items.use: yopparatteru = is drunk; yopparai = a drunk.

example.ja: 彼、もう酔っ払ってるよ。
example.english: He's already drunk.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa mou yopparatte imasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 彼はもう酔っ払っていますよ。
examplePolite.english: He's already drunk.

items.notes: A softer 'I'm a bit tipsy' is yotchatta.

blocks.label: Clothes and weight
blocks.rationale: Talk about what you wear, how it looks on you, and gaining or losing weight.
blocks.interference: futotta and yaseta are past forms used for how someone is now.

items.use: Upper-body or whole-body clothes; trousers and shoes are haku, hats kaburu.

example.ja: 明日のパーティー、何着る？
example.english: What are you wearing to the party tomorrow?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita no paatii ni wa nani o kimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日のパーティーには何を着ますか？
examplePolite.english: What will you wear to the party tomorrow?

items.notes: kite iru = is wearing. Sounds like kiru 'cut', but goes kimasu, kite.

items.use: Mostly a compliment on clothes, hair or glasses, often as niatteru.

example.ja: その服、すごく似合うね。
example.english: That outfit really suits you.

examplePolite.romaji: sono fuku, totemo niaimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: その服、とても似合いますね。
examplePolite.english: That outfit looks great on you.

items.notes: oniai desu is the polite version shop staff use.

items.use: futotta = I've put on weight; futotte iru = is fat.

example.ja: 最近ちょっと太っちゃったかも。
example.english: I might've put on a bit of weight lately.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin sukoshi futotte shimatta kamo shiremasen.
examplePolite.ja: 最近少し太ってしまったかもしれません。
examplePolite.english: I may have put on a little weight lately.

items.notes: Opposite: yaseru. Telling someone else futotta is rude.

items.use: yaseta? (have you lost weight?) is a common compliment.

example.romaji: yaseta? nanka kirei ni natta ne.
example.ja: 痩せた？なんか綺麗になったね。
example.english: Have you lost weight? You look great.

examplePolite.romaji: yasemashita ka? kirei ni narimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: 痩せましたか？綺麗になりましたね。
examplePolite.english: Have you lost weight? You look lovely.

items.notes: yasete iru = is thin. Opposite: futoru.

blocks.label: Tidying up
blocks.rationale: Lets you ask someone to tidy, put things away, sort things out or put them on display.
blocks.interference: Katazukeru tidies a whole mess; shimau puts one thing in its place.

items.english: tidy up; put away; clear (the table)
items.use: The everyday word for cleaning up a mess — a room, toys, dishes.

example.ja: お客さん来るから、部屋片付けて。
example.english: Guests are coming, so tidy your room.

examplePolite.romaji: okyakusan ga kuru node, heya o katazukete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: お客さんが来るので、部屋を片付けてください。
examplePolite.english: Guests are coming, so please tidy your room.

items.notes: Also for finishing off work: shigoto o katazukeru. Shimau is putting one thing in its place.

items.use: Putting something into its proper place — a drawer, a cupboard, a bag.

example.ja: おもちゃ、ちゃんとしまってね。
example.english: Put your toys away properly, okay?

examplePolite.romaji: omocha o chanto shimatte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: おもちゃをちゃんとしまってください。
examplePolite.english: Please put your toys away properly.

items.notes: Also the ending -te shimau (-chau), 'end up doing': tabechatta = I ate it all.

items.use: Putting papers, files, data or thoughts in order; for a messy room, katazukeru is more everyday.

example.romaji: ato de shorui seiri suru yo.
example.ja: 後で書類整理するよ。
example.english: I'll sort out the papers later.

examplePolite.romaji: ato de shorui o seiri shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 後で書類を整理します。
examplePolite.english: I'll sort out the papers later.

items.notes: Kimochi o seiri suru = sort out your feelings. Same sound as seiri, a period (menstruation).

items.english: decorate; put on display, put up
items.use: For pictures, flowers or decorations set out to be seen.

example.romaji: kono shashin, heya ni kazarou ka.
example.ja: この写真、部屋に飾ろうか。
example.english: Shall we put this photo up in the room?

examplePolite.romaji: kono shashin o heya ni kazarimashou ka.
examplePolite.ja: この写真を部屋に飾りましょうか。
examplePolite.english: Shall we put this photo up in the room?

items.notes: Kazaranai hito = a down-to-earth, unpretentious person.

blocks.label: Panic and nerves
blocks.rationale: Covers feeling rushed, panicking, getting scared and getting careless.
blocks.interference: Aseru is pressure you feel, awateru is flustered action.

items.use: 'Aseranaide' means 'No need to rush'.

example.romaji: aseranakute ii yo. mada jikan aru kara.
example.ja: 焦らなくていいよ。まだ時間あるから。
example.english: No need to rush. There's still time.

examplePolite.romaji: aseranakute ii desu yo. mada jikan ga arimasu kara.
examplePolite.ja: 焦らなくていいですよ。まだ時間がありますから。
examplePolite.english: No need to rush. There's still time.

items.notes: It conjugates like kaeru (go home): aseranai, aserimasu, not asenai.

items.use: Awatete (in a rush) is the most common form; 'Awatenaide' means 'Don't panic'.

example.romaji: nebou shite, awatete ie o deta.
example.ja: 寝坊して、慌てて家を出た。
example.english: I overslept and rushed out of the house.

examplePolite.romaji: nebou shite, awatete ie o demashita.
examplePolite.ja: 寝坊して、慌てて家を出ました。
examplePolite.english: I overslept and rushed out of the house.

items.notes: Aseru is the pressure you feel inside; awateru is flustered, hurried action.

items.english: get scared, be startled; chicken out
items.use: 'Bibitta!' means 'That scared me!'.

example.romaji: kyuu ni inu ga dete kite, bibitta yo.
example.ja: 急に犬が出てきて、ビビったよ。
example.english: A dog suddenly jumped out and scared me.

examplePolite.romaji: kyuu ni inu ga dete kite, bibirimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 急に犬が出てきて、ビビりました。
examplePolite.english: A dog suddenly jumped out and gave me a fright.

items.notes: Bibiri is a scaredy-cat. Neutral words: odoroku (be surprised), kowai (scary).

items.english: let one's guard down, get careless
items.use: Mostly as a warning: 'Yudan suru na' (Don't let your guard down).

example.romaji: saigo made yudan shicha dame da yo.
example.ja: 最後まで油断しちゃだめだよ。
example.english: Don't let your guard down until the very end.

examplePolite.romaji: saigo made yudan shinaide kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 最後まで油断しないでくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please don't let your guard down until the very end.

items.notes: 'Yudan dekinai' means you have to stay on your toes around someone or something.

blocks.label: Noticing and guessing
blocks.rationale: Lets you say you noticed, had an idea, expected or wrongly assumed something.
blocks.interference: Omoitsuku (think up) gets mixed with omoidasu (remember); omoikomu is always a mistaken belief.

items.use: The thing noticed takes ni: 'Machigai ni kizuita' (I noticed the mistake).

example.ja: ごめん、全然気付かなかったよ。
example.english: Sorry, I didn't notice at all.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, zenzen kizukimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、全然気付きませんでした。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I didn't notice at all.

items.notes: Also written 気づく; ki ga tsuku means the same.

items.english: think of, come up with (an idea)
items.use: For an idea popping into your head: 'Ii koto omoitsuita!' (I've got a great idea!).

example.ja: 何かいいアイデア思いついた？
example.english: Have you thought of any good ideas?

examplePolite.romaji: nanika ii aidea o omoitsukimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 何かいいアイデアを思いつきましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you thought of any good ideas?

items.notes: Omoidasu (remember) sounds close: omoitsuku is a new thought, omoidasu an old one.

items.use: Common in 'yosou yori' (than expected), 'yosou doori' (as expected) and 'yosou gai' (unexpected).

example.romaji: kore, yosou yori zutto oishii ne.
example.ja: これ、予想よりずっとおいしいね。
example.english: This is way tastier than I expected.

examplePolite.romaji: kore, yosou yori zutto oishii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: これ、予想よりずっとおいしいですね。
examplePolite.english: This is much tastier than I expected.

items.notes: Also yosou suru (predict, guess), as with scores or results.

items.use: Usually about a belief that turns out to be wrong.

example.romaji: kyou wa yasumi da to omoikondeta.
example.ja: 今日は休みだと思い込んでた。
example.english: I was sure today was a day off.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa yasumi da to omoikonde imashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は休みだと思い込んでいました。
examplePolite.english: I was convinced today was a day off.

items.notes: The noun omoikomi means a mistaken belief or preconception.

blocks.label: Caring for people
blocks.rationale: Lets you look after people and things, and thank those who looked after you.
blocks.interference: Daiji ni suru and taisetsu ni suru are near twins; sewa ni naru is receiving the care.

items.use: For things, people and health: 'Karada o daiji ni shite' (Look after yourself).

example.ja: 体、大事にしてね。
example.english: Take care of yourself.

examplePolite.romaji: okarada o daiji ni shite kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: お体を大事にしてくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please take care of yourself.

items.notes: 'Odaiji ni' is the set phrase to someone who is ill: 'Get well soon'.

items.use: For people, gifts and memories you hold dear.

example.romaji: kono purezento, zutto taisetsu ni suru ne.
example.ja: このプレゼント、ずっと大切にするね。
example.english: I'll treasure this present forever.

examplePolite.romaji: kono purezento, zutto taisetsu ni shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: このプレゼント、ずっと大切にします。
examplePolite.english: I'll treasure this present forever.

items.notes: Nearly the same as daiji ni suru; taisetsu sounds a little warmer.

items.english: be looked after (by someone); owe someone
items.use: Mostly as thanks, 'Osewa ni narimashita', when leaving a job, a host or a hospital.

example.romaji: iroiro sewa ni natta ne, arigatou.
example.ja: いろいろ世話になったね、ありがとう。
example.english: Thanks for everything you've done for me.

examplePolite.romaji: iroiro osewa ni narimashita. arigatou gozaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: いろいろお世話になりました。ありがとうございました。
examplePolite.english: Thank you for everything you've done for me.

items.notes: 'Osewa ni natte orimasu' opens work calls and emails, roughly 'Thanks for your continued support'.

blocks.label: Joking around
blocks.rationale: Lets you react to jokes and talk about teasing and messing around.
blocks.interference: Ukeru and waraeru both mean 'that's funny'; 'Fuzakeru na!' is angry, not playful.

items.use: 'Fuzakenaide' means 'Stop messing around'; 'Fuzakeru na!' is an angry 'Don't screw with me!'.

example.ja: ふざけないで、ちゃんと聞いてよ。
example.english: Stop messing around and listen properly.

examplePolite.romaji: fuzakenaide, chanto kiite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: ふざけないで、ちゃんと聞いてください。
examplePolite.english: Please stop messing around and listen properly.

items.notes: Fuzaketa describes something outrageous: 'fuzaketa hanashi' (a ridiculous story).

items.english: be funny, get a laugh; go down well
items.use: 'Ukeru!' alone is a casual 'LOL, that's hilarious'.

example.romaji: kare no joudan, minna ni uketeta ne.
example.ja: 彼の冗談、みんなにウケてたね。
example.english: Everyone loved his joke.

examplePolite.romaji: kare no joudan, minna ni ukete imashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼の冗談、みんなにウケていましたね。
examplePolite.english: Everyone loved his joke.

items.notes: Also a product or idea catching on: 'Wakai hito ni ukete iru'.

items.use: Said of something funny: 'Kore, maji waraeru'. Also 'Ima nara waraeru' (I can laugh about it now).

example.ja: この動画、マジ笑える。
example.english: This video is hilarious.

examplePolite.romaji: kono douga, hontou ni waraemasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: この動画、本当に笑えますよ。
examplePolite.english: This video is really funny.

items.notes: 'Waraenai' means it's no laughing matter.

items.use: Usually playful teasing.

example.ja: もう、そんなにからかわないでよ。
example.english: Come on, stop teasing me like that.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna ni karakawanaide kudasai yo.
examplePolite.ja: そんなにからかわないでくださいよ。
examplePolite.english: Please stop teasing me like that.

items.notes: Lighter than baka ni suru (make fun of, look down on).

blocks.label: Open, close, start, stop
blocks.rationale: Lets you ask when places open and close, and start or stop things.
blocks.interference: Aku and shimaru are what doors and shops do by themselves; you open or close them with akeru and shimeru.

items.use: The door or shop opens by itself or is open; for 'I open it' use akeru.

example.ja: あの店、何時に開く？
example.english: What time does that shop open?

examplePolite.romaji: ano mise wa nanji ni akimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: あの店は何時に開きますか？
examplePolite.english: What time does that shop open?

items.notes: Same sound as aku 空く, be free: kono seki aite imasu ka? (is this seat free?). Read hiraku, the same kanji means open a book or hold an event.

items.use: The door or shop closes by itself or is closed; for 'I close it' use shimeru.

example.ja: 郵便局、もう閉まってるよ。
example.english: The post office is already closed.

examplePolite.romaji: yuubinkyoku wa mou shimatte imasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 郵便局はもう閉まっていますよ。
examplePolite.english: The post office is already closed.

items.notes: Train announcements say 'doa ga shimarimasu' (the doors are closing). Opposite: aku.

items.use: Upbeat word for events, races, projects and new chapters; also the noun 'a start' (ii sutaato).

example.romaji: juuji ni sutaato suru kara, okurenaide ne.
example.ja: 10時にスタートするから、遅れないでね。
example.english: It starts at ten, so don't be late.

examplePolite.romaji: juuji ni sutaato shimasu node, okurenaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 10時にスタートしますので、遅れないでください。
examplePolite.english: It starts at ten, so please don't be late.

items.notes: Hajimaru (it starts) and hajimeru (start it) are the everyday native verbs.

items.use: Called out on its own to make someone stop; sutoppu suru for trains, work or supplies grinding to a halt.

example.romaji: sutoppu, sutoppu! ima no mou ikkai.
example.ja: ストップ、ストップ！今のもう一回。
example.english: Stop, stop! Do that bit again.

examplePolite.romaji: sutoppu shite kudasai. ima no o mou ikkai onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: ストップしてください。今のをもう一回お願いします。
examplePolite.english: Please stop. Could you do that part again?

items.notes: Tomaru (it stops) and tomeru (stop it) are the everyday native verbs.

blocks.label: Grow, change, go back
blocks.rationale: Lets you say things grew, changed or went back to normal.
blocks.interference: Nobiru (it grows) vs nobasu (grow it); henka is change that happens, henkou change you make.

items.english: go back to normal; go back to how it was
items.use: Things, people or relationships returning to how they were before.

example.romaji: daijoubu, sugu moto ni modoru yo.
example.ja: 大丈夫、すぐ元に戻るよ。
example.english: Don't worry, it'll be back to normal soon.

examplePolite.romaji: daijoubu desu, sugu moto ni modorimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 大丈夫です、すぐ元に戻りますよ。
examplePolite.english: Don't worry, it'll be back to normal soon.

items.notes: Moto ni modosu is 'put it back how it was' (you do it).

items.english: grow (hair, nails); stretch; improve; go soggy (noodles)
items.use: Things getting longer by themselves; also skills or sales growing.

example.ja: 髪、伸びたね。
example.english: Your hair's grown.

examplePolite.romaji: kami ga nobimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: 髪が伸びましたね。
examplePolite.english: Your hair has grown.

items.notes: Nobasu is 'grow it, stretch it' (you do it). Raamen ga nobiru = the ramen goes soggy.

items.use: You make something longer: grow your hair, stretch out, extend a stay or a deadline.

example.ja: 髪、伸ばそうかな。
example.english: Maybe I'll grow my hair out.

examplePolite.romaji: kami o nobasou ka to omotte imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 髪を伸ばそうかと思っています。
examplePolite.english: I'm thinking of growing my hair out.

items.notes: Nobiru is 'grow, stretch' by itself. In the 'put off' sense it's written 延ばす.

items.use: Change that happens, not change you make; often with aru / nai.

example.ja: 最近、何か変化あった？
example.english: Anything changed for you lately?

examplePolite.romaji: saikin, nanika henka wa arimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 最近、何か変化はありましたか？
examplePolite.english: Has anything changed for you lately?

items.notes: Henka suru is a bit formal; casual talk uses kawaru. Henkou is a change you make to a plan.

blocks.label: Phones and services
blocks.rationale: Lets you use services, connect devices, swap contacts and post online.
blocks.interference: Riyou suru is the formal 'use'; everyday talk uses tsukau.

items.use: Using trains, gyms, apps or cards; signs and staff say goriyou.

example.romaji: kono kaado, konbini de mo riyou dekiru yo.
example.ja: このカード、コンビニでも利用できるよ。
example.english: You can use this card at convenience stores too.

examplePolite.romaji: kono kaado wa konbini de mo riyou dekimasu.
examplePolite.ja: このカードはコンビニでも利用できます。
examplePolite.english: This card can be used at convenience stores too.

items.notes: Tsukau is the everyday 'use'; riyou sounds like services and signs. Of a person, it means use or exploit them.

items.use: Connecting cables or devices, putting a call through, and te o tsunagu (hold hands).

example.ja: これ、どこにつなぐの？
example.english: Where does this plug in?

examplePolite.romaji: kore wa doko ni tsunagu n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: これはどこにつなぐんですか？
examplePolite.english: Where does this connect?

items.notes: Tsunagaru is 'be connected': waifai ga tsunagaranai (the wifi won't connect).

items.use: Swapping contacts or gifts, or getting a faulty item replaced.

example.ja: ライン交換しようよ。
example.english: Let's swap LINE.

examplePolite.romaji: rain o koukan shimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: ラインを交換しませんか？
examplePolite.english: Shall we exchange LINE?

items.notes: Torikaeru is the native verb for swap or replace.

items.use: Casual; posting photos or videos online, or pay, prices or level going up.

example.romaji: kinou no shashin, insuta ni appu shita yo.
example.ja: 昨日の写真、インスタにアップしたよ。
example.english: I posted yesterday's photos on Insta.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou no shashin o insuta ni appu shimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日の写真をインスタにアップしました。
examplePolite.english: I posted yesterday's photos on Instagram.

items.notes: As a suffix it means a rise: kyuuryou appu (pay rise), reberu appu. Opposite: daun.

blocks.label: Gather, sort, pack
blocks.rationale: Lets you collect things or people, split them up, lay them out and pack them.
blocks.interference: Wakeru (divide) sounds like wakaru (understand); atsumeru (gather them) vs atsumaru (they gather).

items.use: Gathering people or things, or collecting as a hobby.

example.ja: 子供の頃、切手集めてた。
example.english: I used to collect stamps as a kid.

examplePolite.romaji: kodomo no koro, kitte o atsumete imashita.
examplePolite.ja: 子供の頃、切手を集めていました。
examplePolite.english: I collected stamps when I was a child.

items.notes: Atsumaru is 'gather, meet up' (people come together).

items.english: be all there; be complete; match
items.use: Mostly for people or things all being present: zen'in sorotta (everyone's here).

example.ja: 全員そろった？じゃあ、始めよう。
example.english: Everyone here? Okay, let's start.

examplePolite.romaji: zen'in soroimashita ka? dewa, hajimemashou.
examplePolite.ja: 全員そろいましたか？では、始めましょう。
examplePolite.english: Is everyone here? Then let's begin.

items.notes: Soroeru is 'get together, make match' (you do it): saizu o soroeru.

items.use: Splitting food or a bill, sharing things out, or sorting rubbish.

example.ja: これ、半分に分けよう。
example.english: Let's split this in half.

examplePolite.romaji: kore o hanbun ni wakemashou.
examplePolite.ja: これを半分に分けましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's split this in half.

items.notes: Don't mix with wakaru (understand). Wakareru = split up, part.

items.english: line up; lay out; set out
items.use: Putting things in a row or setting them out: plates, goods, chairs.

example.ja: お皿、テーブルに並べて。
example.english: Put the plates out on the table.

examplePolite.romaji: osara o teeburu ni narabete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: お皿をテーブルに並べてください。
examplePolite.english: Please set the plates out on the table.

items.notes: Narabu is 'line up, queue' (people do it): retsu ni narabu.

items.english: pack; stuff; fill; move up (make room)
items.use: Packing a box or bag full; 'tsumete' asks people to squeeze up.

example.ja: ちょっと詰めてもらえる？
example.english: Could you scoot over a bit?

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, sukoshi tsumete itadakemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: すみません、少し詰めていただけますか？
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, could you move over a little?

items.notes: Tsumaru is 'be blocked, be packed': hana ga tsumaru (stuffy nose). Obentou ni tsumeru = pack a lunch box.

blocks.label: Paying the bill
blocks.rationale: Lets you pay, order more and check what a price includes.
blocks.interference: Harau and shiharau both mean pay; shiharau is the formal one you hear from staff.

items.use: Kaado de harau = pay by card; betsubetsu ni harau = pay separately.

example.romaji: koko wa watashi ga harau yo.
example.ja: ここは私が払うよ。
example.english: I'll get this.

examplePolite.romaji: koko wa watashi ga haraimasu.
examplePolite.ja: ここは私が払います。
examplePolite.english: I'll pay for this.

items.notes: Shiharau is the more formal 'pay', used for bills and at checkouts.

items.use: More formal than harau: bills, fees and checkout talk.

example.ja: コンビニで支払えるよ。
example.english: You can pay at a convenience store.

examplePolite.romaji: konbini de shiharaemasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: コンビニで支払えますよ。
examplePolite.english: You can pay at a convenience store.

items.notes: Cashiers ask 'oshiharai wa?' (how will you pay?). In casual talk harau is more common.

items.use: Adding to a list, an order or a group.

example.ja: ビール追加しようか？
example.english: Shall we order more beer?

examplePolite.romaji: biiru o tsuika shimashou ka?
examplePolite.ja: ビールを追加しましょうか？
examplePolite.english: Shall we order more beer?

items.notes: To a waiter: 'X tsuika de onegai shimasu' (another X, please). Tsuika ryoukin = extra charge.

items.use: Mostly as 'X o fukumete', including X.

example.romaji: watashi o fukumete gonin da yo.
example.ja: 私を含めて五人だよ。
example.english: There are five of us, including me.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi o fukumete gonin desu.
examplePolite.ja: 私を含めて五人です。
examplePolite.english: There are five of us, including me.

items.notes: For prices, zeikomi (tax included) is the usual word.

blocks.label: Work and school habits
blocks.rationale: Lets you say where you work, and that you're running late or skipping.
blocks.interference: chikoku suru is late for a start time; okureru is late in general.

items.english: be late (for school, work, a meeting)
items.use: Late for a fixed start time.

example.ja: ごめん、ちょっと遅刻する。
example.english: Sorry, I'll be a bit late.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, sukoshi chikoku shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、少し遅刻します。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry, I'll be a little late.

items.notes: okureru is the general 'be late': densha ga okureta (the train was late).

items.use: Skipping something you should do, or slacking off while you're there.

example.ja: 昨日、仕事サボっちゃったんだ。
example.english: I skipped work yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou wa shigoto o saborimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日は仕事をサボりました。
examplePolite.english: I skipped work yesterday.

items.notes: From 'sabotage'. Past is sabotta.

items.use: Saying where you're employed: X ni tsutomete iru.

example.ja: 兄は銀行に勤めてる。
example.english: My brother works at a bank.

examplePolite.romaji: ani wa ginkou ni tsutomete imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 兄は銀行に勤めています。
examplePolite.english: My brother works at a bank.

items.notes: hataraku is 'work' in general; tsutomeru is being on a company's staff.

blocks.label: Fights and friction
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about fights, rows, bullying and not wanting to do something.
blocks.interference: kenka suru is any fight or argument; momeru is a drawn-out dispute.

items.use: Covers both arguments and physical fights, between friends, couples or kids.

example.romaji: kinou kare to kenka shita n da.
example.ja: 昨日彼とケンカしたんだ。
example.english: I had a fight with my boyfriend yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou kare to kenka shita n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日彼とケンカしたんです。
examplePolite.english: I had a fight with my boyfriend yesterday.

items.notes: Usually X to kenka suru (fight with X). kenka o uru: pick a fight.

items.english: argue; have a row; be in dispute
items.use: A drawn-out dispute inside a group, often over money, plans or who decides.

example.romaji: okane no koto de oya to mometeru n da.
example.ja: お金のことで親ともめてるんだ。
example.english: I'm having a row with my parents about money.

examplePolite.romaji: okane no koto de oya to momete iru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: お金のことで親ともめているんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm in a dispute with my parents about money.

items.notes: Noun: momegoto (trouble, a dispute).

items.use: Picking on someone weaker; between friends it can be playful teasing.

example.ja: あんまりいじめないでよ。
example.english: Stop picking on me so much.

examplePolite.romaji: amari ijimenaide kudasai yo.
examplePolite.ja: あまりいじめないでくださいよ。
examplePolite.english: Please don't pick on me so much.

items.notes: Noun: ijime (bullying), a big social issue in Japan.

items.use: Mostly teikou ga aru: you feel uneasy about doing something.

example.romaji: hitomae de hanasu no wa chotto teikou aru na.
example.ja: 人前で話すのはちょっと抵抗あるな。
example.english: I'm not too keen on speaking in front of people.

examplePolite.romaji: hitomae de hanasu no wa chotto teikou ga arimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 人前で話すのはちょっと抵抗があります。
examplePolite.english: I'm a little uneasy about speaking in front of people.

items.notes: teikou suru: resist, fight back.

blocks.label: Boss and coworkers
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about the people you work with.
blocks.interference: joushi is above you, buka below you, douryou beside you.

items.use: Anyone above you at work; said about them, not to them.

example.ja: 上司にまた怒られた。
example.english: My boss yelled at me again.

examplePolite.romaji: joushi ni mata okoraremashita.
examplePolite.ja: 上司にまた怒られました。
examplePolite.english: I got scolded by my boss again.

items.notes: Opposite: buka (subordinate). To their face, use their title or name plus san.

items.use: A company's own staff; seishain is a full-time regular employee.

example.romaji: ano hito, uchi no shain ja nai yo.
example.ja: あの人、うちの社員じゃないよ。
example.english: That guy doesn't work for us.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito wa uchi no shain ja arimasen.
examplePolite.ja: あの人はうちの社員じゃありません。
examplePolite.english: That person isn't one of our employees.

items.notes: kaishain (office worker) is a common answer to 'what do you do?'

items.use: Said about people who report to you, never to address them.

example.ja: 部下が辞めちゃったんだ。
example.english: One of my team quit.

examplePolite.romaji: buka ga yamete shimatta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 部下が辞めてしまったんです。
examplePolite.english: One of my staff quit.

items.notes: Opposite: joushi (boss).

items.use: People at your level at work.

example.romaji: kinou, douryou to nomi ni itta.
example.ja: 昨日、同僚と飲みに行った。
example.english: I went drinking with coworkers yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou, douryou to nomi ni ikimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日、同僚と飲みに行きました。
examplePolite.english: I went for drinks with coworkers yesterday.

items.notes: In chat people often just say kaisha no hito.

blocks.label: Partners and cheating
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about dating, cheating and being single.
blocks.interference: uwaki is cheating in general; furin involves a married person.

example.ja: 彼氏いるの？
example.english: Do you have a boyfriend?

examplePolite.romaji: kareshi wa imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 彼氏はいますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you have a boyfriend?

items.notes: Girlfriend is kanojo. Use iru, not aru: kareshi ga iru.

items.use: Gender-neutral and a bit more serious than kareshi or kanojo.

example.romaji: koibito to issho ni sunderu n da.
example.ja: 恋人と一緒に住んでるんだ。
example.english: I live with my partner.

examplePolite.romaji: koibito to issho ni sunde imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 恋人と一緒に住んでいます。
examplePolite.english: I live with my partner.

items.use: Mostly as uwaki suru (to cheat) and uwaki sareta (got cheated on).

example.ja: 彼に浮気された。
example.english: My boyfriend cheated on me.

examplePolite.romaji: kare ni uwaki saremashita.
examplePolite.ja: 彼に浮気されました。
examplePolite.english: My boyfriend cheated on me.

items.notes: For an affair involving a married person, furin is more common.

items.use: Used when at least one person is married; often furin suru.

example.romaji: ano futari, furin shiteru rashii yo.
example.ja: あの二人、不倫してるらしいよ。
example.english: Apparently those two are having an affair.

examplePolite.romaji: ano futari wa furin shite iru rashii desu.
examplePolite.ja: あの二人は不倫しているらしいです。
examplePolite.english: I hear those two are having an affair.

items.notes: Mix-up: uwaki is cheating in general, including while dating.

items.use: About marriage, not dating: dokushin means not married.

example.romaji: ani wa mada dokushin da yo.
example.ja: 兄はまだ独身だよ。
example.english: My older brother's still single.

examplePolite.romaji: ani wa mada dokushin desu.
examplePolite.ja: 兄はまだ独身です。
examplePolite.english: My older brother is still single.

blocks.label: Teams and groups
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about groups and the roles in them.
blocks.interference: None.

items.use: Often X no daihyou (representing X), and for national teams: nihon daihyou.

example.romaji: kurasu no daihyou de supiichi suru n da.
example.ja: クラスの代表でスピーチするんだ。
example.english: I'm giving a speech for our class.

examplePolite.romaji: kurasu no daihyou de supiichi o shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: クラスの代表でスピーチをします。
examplePolite.english: I'll give a speech on behalf of the class.

items.notes: Also a title for the head of a company or group.

items.english: member (of a team, band or group)
items.use: Also the lineup of people at an event: kyou no menbaa.

example.ja: 今日のメンバー、誰？
example.english: Who's coming today?

examplePolite.romaji: kyou no menbaa wa dare desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今日のメンバーは誰ですか？
examplePolite.english: Who's in the group today?

items.use: Also a group chat or a pop group.

example.ja: グループに写真送っとくね。
example.english: I'll send the photos to the group.

examplePolite.romaji: guruupu ni shashin o okutte okimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: グループに写真を送っておきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll send the photos to the group.

example.ja: リーダーは誰がやる？
example.english: Who's going to be the leader?

examplePolite.romaji: riidaa wa dare ga yarimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: リーダーは誰がやりますか？
examplePolite.english: Who will be the leader?

items.notes: Usually with yaru or naru: riidaa ni naru.

blocks.label: Students and classmates
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about the people you studied with.
blocks.interference: gakusei is mostly university students; seito is school pupils.

items.use: Mainly university students; school kids are usually seito.

example.ja: まだ学生なの？
example.english: You're still a student?

examplePolite.romaji: mada gakusei desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: まだ学生ですか？
examplePolite.english: Are you still a student?

items.notes: gakusei waribiki = student discount.

items.use: Someone who joined after you; they call you senpai.

example.romaji: kore, kouhai ni moratta n da.
example.ja: これ、後輩にもらったんだ。
example.english: I got this from one of my juniors.

examplePolite.romaji: kore wa kouhai ni moraimashita.
examplePolite.ja: これは後輩にもらいました。
examplePolite.english: One of my juniors gave me this.

items.notes: Opposite: senpai. Who joined first decides it, not age.

items.use: School students, especially junior high and high school; also someone taking lessons.

example.romaji: ano sensei, seito ni ninki aru yo.
example.ja: あの先生、生徒に人気あるよ。
example.english: That teacher is popular with the students.

examplePolite.romaji: ano sensei wa seito ni ninki ga arimasu.
examplePolite.ja: あの先生は生徒に人気があります。
examplePolite.english: That teacher is popular with the students.

items.notes: Mix-up: university students are gakusei.

items.english: classmate; someone in your year at school
items.use: Same year at school, even if not the same class.

example.romaji: kare, koukou no doukyuusei na n da.
example.ja: 彼、高校の同級生なんだ。
example.english: He was in my year in high school.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa koukou no doukyuusei desu.
examplePolite.ja: 彼は高校の同級生です。
examplePolite.english: We were in the same year in high school.

items.notes: kurasumeito means the same class only.

blocks.label: Types of people
blocks.rationale: Lets you call someone good-looking, gifted, rich or a beginner.
blocks.interference: bijin is for women, ikemen for men.

items.use: Used for women; for men say ikemen.

example.romaji: ano hito, sugoi bijin da ne.
example.ja: あの人、すごい美人だね。
example.english: She's gorgeous.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito wa totemo bijin desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの人はとても美人ですね。
examplePolite.english: She's very beautiful.

items.notes: bijinsan is a softer, friendly form.

items.use: Casual; also works like an adjective: ikemen da ne.

example.ja: 彼、結構イケメンじゃない？
example.english: Isn't he pretty good-looking?

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa kekkou ikemen desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼は結構イケメンですね。
examplePolite.english: He's quite good-looking.

items.notes: For women, say bijin or kawaii.

items.use: Used loosely as praise, even for small things.

example.romaji: e, mou dekita no? tensai ja nai?
example.ja: え、もうできたの？天才じゃない？
example.english: Wait, done already? You're a genius!

examplePolite.romaji: mou dekita n desu ka? tensai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: もうできたんですか？天才ですね。
examplePolite.english: Done already? You're a genius.

items.notes: Mix-up: tensai also means natural disaster (天災).

items.use: Someone who isn't a professional or doesn't know the field.

example.romaji: shirouto da kara, yoku wakannai yo.
example.ja: 素人だから、よくわかんないよ。
example.english: I'm no expert, so I don't really get it.

examplePolite.romaji: shirouto na node, yoku wakarimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 素人なので、よくわかりません。
examplePolite.english: I'm not an expert, so I don't really understand.

items.notes: Opposite: puro (pro).

items.use: Also works like an adjective: okanemochi da ne (you're rich).

example.romaji: kare no ie, sugoi okanemochi rashii yo.
example.ja: 彼の家、すごいお金持ちらしいよ。
example.english: Apparently his family's super rich.

examplePolite.romaji: kare no ie wa totemo okanemochi da sou desu.
examplePolite.ja: 彼の家はとてもお金持ちだそうです。
examplePolite.english: I hear his family is very rich.

blocks.label: Men and women by setting
blocks.rationale: Words for men and women in formal, group and rough talk.
blocks.interference: dansei is formal and ossan is rude; joshi and danshi are casual group words.

items.use: The neutral, polite word used on forms, in shops and on the news; in chat people say otoko no hito.

example.romaji: dansei no hou ga ooi ne.
example.ja: 男性の方が多いね。
example.english: There are more men, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: dansei no hou ga ooi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 男性の方が多いですね。
examplePolite.english: There are more men, aren't there?

items.notes: Pairs with josei (woman).

items.use: Used casually for women of any age, and in school and sports for the girls' side.

example.romaji: kyou wa joshi dake de nomu n da.
example.ja: 今日は女子だけで飲むんだ。
example.english: Tonight it's just us girls drinking.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa joshi dake de nomimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は女子だけで飲みます。
