examplePolite.english: You should decide this one carefully.

items.notes: Same sound as shinchou (height). Ki o tsukete is the everyday 'be careful'.

items.use: For courteous manners and careful work: 'teinei na setsumei' = a careful explanation.

example.romaji: ano mise, setsumei ga sugoku teinei datta yo.
example.ja: あの店、説明がすごく丁寧だったよ。
example.english: That shop explained everything really carefully.

examplePolite.romaji: ano mise wa setsumei ga totemo teinei deshita.
examplePolite.ja: あの店は説明がとても丁寧でした。
examplePolite.english: That shop explained everything very carefully.

items.notes: Teinei ni = carefully, gently. Teineigo = polite desu/masu speech.

items.use: Usually nesshin ni + verb: 'nesshin ni benkyou suru' = study hard.

example.romaji: ano ko, honto ni nesshin ni renshuu shiteru ne.
example.ja: あの子、ほんとに熱心に練習してるね。
example.english: That kid really practises hard.

examplePolite.romaji: ano ko wa hontou ni nesshin ni renshuu shite imasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの子は本当に熱心に練習していますね。
examplePolite.english: That child really practises hard.

items.notes: Nesshin na fan = a devoted fan. A little more formal than ganbatteru.

blocks.label: Formal and work words
blocks.rationale: Follow polite staff talk and give views at work.
blocks.interference: Yoroshii is not 'yoroshiku'.

items.use: Staff and hosts ask 'Yoroshii desu ka?' (Is that all right? / May I?).

example.romaji: kochira no seki de yoroshii desu ka?
example.ja: こちらの席でよろしいですか。
example.english: Is this seat all right for you?

items.notes: Not 'yoroshiku' (please treat me well). From a boss or parent, a bare 'Yoroshii' sounds stiff and superior.

items.use: Usually 'seishiki ni' (officially) or 'seishiki na' before a noun.

example.romaji: mada seishiki ni kimatta wake ja nai yo.
example.ja: まだ正式に決まったわけじゃないよ。
example.english: It's not officially decided yet.

examplePolite.romaji: mada seishiki ni wa kimatte imasen.
examplePolite.ja: まだ正式には決まっていません。
examplePolite.english: It hasn't been officially decided yet.

items.use: Sounds formal; everyday talk uses 'dekiru' instead.

example.romaji: sore tte, honto ni kanou na no?
example.ja: それって、ほんとに可能なの？
example.english: Is that even possible?

examplePolite.romaji: kyoujuu ni kanou desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今日中に可能ですか。
examplePolite.english: Is it possible by the end of today?

items.notes: 'Kanousei' means possibility, chance.

items.use: Mostly 'gutaiteki ni' (specifically); 'Gutaiteki ni wa?' asks 'Like what, exactly?'

example.romaji: gutaiteki ni nani ga dame na no?
example.ja: 具体的に何がだめなの？
example.english: What exactly is wrong with it?

examplePolite.romaji: gutaiteki ni nani ga dame na n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 具体的に何がだめなんですか。
examplePolite.english: What specifically is the problem?

items.use: 'Kojinteki ni wa' (personally, for me) softens an opinion.

example.romaji: kojinteki ni wa, kotchi no hou ga suki.
example.ja: 個人的には、こっちの方が好き。
example.english: Personally, I like this one better.

examplePolite.romaji: kojinteki ni wa, kochira no hou ga suki desu.
examplePolite.ja: 個人的には、こちらの方が好きです。
examplePolite.english: Personally, I prefer this one.

blocks.label: Rare, common, alike
blocks.rationale: Say how usual something is and whether things match or go separately.
blocks.interference: None.

items.use: Often a comment on someone acting out of character: 'Mezurashii ne!'

example.ja: 遅刻するなんて、珍しいね。
example.english: You, late? That's not like you.

examplePolite.romaji: chikoku suru nante, mezurashii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 遅刻するなんて、珍しいですね。
examplePolite.english: It's unusual for you to be late.

items.use: Before a noun it means 'typical, common': 'yoku aru hanashi'.

example.romaji: sore, yoku aru machigai da yo.
example.ja: それ、よくある間違いだよ。
example.english: That's a common mistake.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa yoku aru machigai desu.
examplePolite.ja: それはよくある間違いです。
examplePolite.english: That's a common mistake.

items.notes: Opposite: 'mezurashii' (rare).

items.english: just like, the spitting image of
items.use: 'X ni sokkuri' means looks just like X.

example.ja: お母さんにそっくりだね。
example.english: You look just like your mom.

examplePolite.romaji: okaasan ni sokkuri desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: お母さんにそっくりですね。
examplePolite.english: You look just like your mother.

items.notes: As an adverb it means 'all of it': 'sokkuri nokotteru' (it's all still there).

items.use: 'Betsubetsu de' at the till means paying separately.

example.ja: 会計、別々にする？
example.english: Want to pay separately?

examplePolite.romaji: okaikei, betsubetsu de onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: お会計、別々でお願いします。
examplePolite.english: Separate checks, please.

items.notes: 'Betsu' alone means different, other: 'betsu no hi' (another day).

blocks.label: Flashy or plain
blocks.rationale: Describe style and how simple or complicated something is.
blocks.interference: Tanjun can call a person simple-minded; shinpuru is the friendly 'simple'.

items.use: For colours and clothes, and for people or lifestyles that stand out.

example.romaji: sono shatsu, chotto hade ja nai?
example.ja: そのシャツ、ちょっと派手じゃない？
example.english: Isn't that shirt a bit loud?

examplePolite.romaji: sono shatsu, chotto hade ja nai desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: そのシャツ、ちょっと派手じゃないですか。
examplePolite.english: Isn't that shirt a little flashy?

items.notes: Opposite: 'jimi' (plain).

items.use: For clothes, colours, people and work that don't stand out.

example.romaji: kyou no fuku, chotto jimi kana.
example.ja: 今日の服、ちょっと地味かな。
example.english: Is my outfit a bit plain today?

examplePolite.romaji: kyou no fuku wa chotto jimi deshou ka.
examplePolite.ja: 今日の服はちょっと地味でしょうか。
examplePolite.english: Is today's outfit a little plain?

items.notes: Opposite: 'hade' (flashy).

items.use: 'Fukuzatsu na kimochi' means mixed feelings.

example.romaji: kono setsumei, fukuzatsu de wakannai yo.
example.ja: この説明、複雑でわかんないよ。
example.english: This explanation is too complicated, I don't get it.

examplePolite.romaji: kono setsumei wa fukuzatsu de wakarimasen.
examplePolite.ja: この説明は複雑でわかりません。
examplePolite.english: This explanation is too complicated to follow.

items.notes: Opposite: 'tanjun' or 'shinpuru'.

items.use: About a person it means easily led or naive, often teasing.

example.romaji: kare, tanjun da kara sugu shinjiru yo.
example.ja: 彼、単純だからすぐ信じるよ。
example.english: He's gullible, he'll believe it right away.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa tanjun na node, sugu shinjimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 彼は単純なので、すぐ信じますよ。
examplePolite.english: He's quite naive, so he'll believe it right away.

items.notes: For a simple design or plan, 'shinpuru' is the positive word.

items.use: Usually positive: a clean design, an uncomplicated plan.

example.romaji: shinpuru na dezain ga ii na.
example.ja: シンプルなデザインがいいな。
example.english: I like a simple design.

examplePolite.romaji: shinpuru na dezain ga ii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: シンプルなデザインがいいですね。
examplePolite.english: A simple design is nice.

items.notes: 'Tanjun' about a person can be an insult; 'shinpuru' isn't.

blocks.label: Finally and coming soon
blocks.rationale: Lets you mark a long-awaited moment that has arrived or is about to.
blocks.interference: Iyoiyo looks ahead to what's about to happen; tsui ni and toutou look back.

items.use: Marks the end of a long wait or build-up, good or bad.

example.romaji: tsui ni katta yo, atarashii pasokon.
example.ja: ついに買ったよ、新しいパソコン。
example.english: I finally bought a new computer.

examplePolite.romaji: tsui ni atarashii pasokon o kaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: ついに新しいパソコンを買いました。
examplePolite.english: I finally bought a new computer.

items.notes: Yatto stresses relief after effort; tsui ni is more dramatic.

items.english: at last (it's here); finally about to
items.use: Builds anticipation for something that's about to start or arrive.

example.ja: いよいよ明日だね。
example.english: It's finally tomorrow!

examplePolite.romaji: iyoiyo ashita desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: いよいよ明日ですね。
examplePolite.english: It's finally tomorrow, isn't it?

items.notes: Looks ahead to a moment arriving; tsui ni and toutou look back at something that has happened.

items.use: For an outcome after a long time or many events, often one that was dreaded.

example.ja: とうとう壊れちゃった。
example.english: It finally broke.

examplePolite.romaji: toutou kowarete shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: とうとう壊れてしまいました。
examplePolite.english: It finally broke down.

items.notes: With a negative it means 'never did': toutou konakatta, 'in the end he never came'.

items.use: Mostly heard in announcements on trains, at stations and in shops.

example.romaji: mamonaku nibansen ni densha ga mairimasu.
example.ja: まもなく2番線に電車が参ります。
example.english: A train will shortly arrive at platform 2.

items.notes: In conversation, say mou sugu.

blocks.label: Small requests and advice
blocks.rationale: Lets you add favours, precautions and gentle advice to what you ask.
blocks.interference: Nen no tame (just in case) gets mixed with mangaichi (if by some chance).

items.use: From nakayoi, 'close'; nakayoku suru means to get along or be friends.

example.ja: 二人とも、仲良くしてね。
example.english: Play nice, you two.

examplePolite.romaji: futari tomo, nakayoku shite kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 二人とも、仲良くしてくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please get along, you two.

items.notes: Kore kara mo nakayoku shite ne is a friendly 'let's stay friends'.

items.english: while you're at it; on the way; also
items.use: Tacks an extra task onto something already happening; a common way to ask small favours.

example.romaji: konbini iku nara, tsuide ni gyuunyuu katte kite.
example.ja: コンビニ行くなら、ついでに牛乳買ってきて。
example.english: If you're going to the store, grab some milk while you're at it.

examplePolite.romaji: konbini ni iku nara, tsuide ni gyuunyuu o katte kite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: コンビニに行くなら、ついでに牛乳を買ってきてください。
examplePolite.english: If you're going to the convenience store, could you pick up some milk too?

items.notes: Tsuide ni iu to means 'while I'm on the subject', adding a side point.

items.english: just in case; to be safe
items.use: Explains a precaution or a double-check.

example.romaji: nen no tame kasa motte ikou.
example.ja: 念のため傘持っていこう。
example.english: Let's take an umbrella just in case.

examplePolite.romaji: nen no tame kasa o motte ikimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 念のため傘を持っていきましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's bring an umbrella just in case.

items.notes: Nen no tame kakunin shimasu, 'let me just double-check', is common at work.

items.english: as much as possible; if possible
items.use: Softens a request or plan: try to, where you can.

example.ja: なるべく早く帰ってきてね。
example.english: Try to come home as early as you can.

examplePolite.romaji: narubeku hayaku kaette kite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: なるべく早く帰ってきてください。
examplePolite.english: Please come home as early as possible.

items.notes: Dekiru dake means the same; narubeku sounds a little softer.

blocks.label: Just a little
blocks.rationale: Lets you play down an amount or a thing.
blocks.interference: Tatta goes before numbers; hon no and chotto shita go before nouns.

items.use: Stresses how small a number or amount is, often with dake.

example.ja: たった五分で終わったよ。
example.english: It only took five minutes.

examplePolite.romaji: tatta gofun de owarimashita yo.
examplePolite.ja: たった五分で終わりましたよ。
examplePolite.english: It took just five minutes.

items.notes: Goes right before the number, while dake follows it: tatta sen'en dake (just 1,000 yen).

items.english: just a; a mere; only a little
items.use: Comes before a noun to make it small: hon no sukoshi (just a tiny bit).

example.ja: ほんの少しだけちょうだい。
example.english: Just give me a tiny bit.

examplePolite.romaji: hon no sukoshi dake kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: ほんの少しだけください。
examplePolite.english: Just a little, please.

items.notes: Hon no kimochi desu = it's just a small token (said when giving a gift).

items.use: Before a noun: a small, casual thing, like chotto shita omiyage (a little gift).

example.romaji: chotto shita mondai ga atte, okureta.
example.ja: ちょっとした問題があって、遅れた。
example.english: There was a small problem, so I was late.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto shita mondai ga atte, okuremashita.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっとした問題があって、遅れました。
examplePolite.english: There was a minor problem, so I was late.

items.notes: Can flip to 'quite a': chotto shita yuumeijin (quite a celebrity).

items.english: a little; somewhat; more or less
items.use: Often in 'even if a bit...' and in hedges: tashou no okure (some delay).

example.romaji: tashou takakute mo, kore ga ii.
example.ja: 多少高くても、これがいい。
example.english: Even if it's a bit pricey, I want this one.

examplePolite.romaji: tashou takakute mo, kore ga ii desu.
examplePolite.ja: 多少高くても、これがいいです。
examplePolite.english: Even if it costs a little more, I'd like this one.

items.notes: Sounds a bit more formal than sukoshi or chotto.

blocks.label: Taking people along
blocks.rationale: Bring or take a friend, child or pet, or ask to be picked up.
blocks.interference: tsurete kuru is toward the speaker, tsurete iku away; for things use motte kuru and motte iku.

items.english: have someone with you; take or bring someone along
items.use: For people and animals, mostly as tsureteru (has with them) or inside tsurete iku and tsurete kuru.

example.romaji: ano hito, itsumo inu tsureteru ne.
example.ja: あの人、いつも犬連れてるね。
example.english: That guy always has his dog with him.

examplePolite.romaji: ano kata wa itsumo inu o tsurete imasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの方はいつも犬を連れていますね。
examplePolite.english: That person always has a dog with them.

items.notes: Things you carry use motsu instead: motte iku, motte kuru.

items.use: For people; coming to collect a thing is tori ni kuru.

example.romaji: eki made mukae ni kite kureru?
example.ja: 駅まで迎えに来てくれる？
example.english: Can you come pick me up at the station?

examplePolite.romaji: eki made mukae ni kite moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 駅まで迎えに来てもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: Could you come and pick me up at the station?

items.notes: Going to pick someone up is mukae ni iku.

items.use: Toward the speaker or the place being talked about.

example.ja: 今度彼女連れてきてよ。
example.english: Bring your girlfriend next time.

examplePolite.romaji: kondo kanojo-san mo tsurete kite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 今度彼女さんも連れてきてください。
examplePolite.english: Please bring your girlfriend next time too.

items.notes: Bringing a thing is motte kuru, not tsurete kuru.

items.use: Away from the speaker; tsurete itte! = take me with you!

example.romaji: kodomo, byouin ni tsurete iku ne.
example.ja: 子ども、病院に連れて行くね。
example.english: I'll take our kid to the doctor.

examplePolite.romaji: kodomo o byouin ni tsurete ikimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 子どもを病院に連れて行きます。
examplePolite.english: I'm taking my child to the doctor.

items.notes: Taking a thing is motte iku. Often shortened to tsureteku.

blocks.label: Trains and buses
blocks.rationale: Get on, get off, change lines and grumble about the crowds.
blocks.interference: noru takes ni (densha ni noru) but oriru takes o (densha o oriru).

items.english: get on, ride (a train, bus, car, bike)
items.use: The vehicle takes ni: densha ni noru.

example.ja: 次の電車に乗ろう。
example.english: Let's get on the next train.

examplePolite.romaji: tsugi no densha ni norimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 次の電車に乗りましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's take the next train.

items.notes: Opposite: oriru (get off).

items.english: get off (a train, bus); go down
items.use: The vehicle takes o: densha o oriru.

example.romaji: tsugi no eki de oriru yo.
example.ja: 次の駅で降りるよ。
example.english: We're getting off at the next station.

examplePolite.romaji: tsugi no eki de orimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 次の駅で降ります。
examplePolite.english: I'm getting off at the next station.

items.notes: Opposite: noru. On a packed train, orimasu! gets people to let you out.

items.use: Usually as konde iru / konderu (is crowded).

example.ja: 今日、電車すごい混んでるね。
example.english: The train's really packed today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa densha ga totemo konde imasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は電車がとても混んでいますね。
examplePolite.english: The train's very crowded today.

items.notes: Not crowded = suite iru (from suku).

items.use: The line you switch to takes ni.

example.ja: 新宿で乗り換えるよ。
example.english: We change at Shinjuku.

examplePolite.romaji: shinjuku de norikaemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 新宿で乗り換えます。
examplePolite.english: We change trains at Shinjuku.

items.notes: norikae = a transfer. Also used casually for switching phones or partners.

blocks.label: Getting dressed and washed
blocks.rationale: Covers shoes off at the door, putting shoes on, showering and brushing teeth.
blocks.interference: Haku is only for feet and legs; tops use kiru, though nugu takes everything off.

example.ja: ここで靴脱いでね。
example.english: Take your shoes off here, okay?

examplePolite.romaji: koko de kutsu o nuide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: ここで靴を脱いでください。
examplePolite.english: Please take your shoes off here.

items.notes: One verb takes everything off, but putting on splits: kiru (tops), haku (shoes, trousers), kaburu (hats).

items.english: put on, wear (shoes, socks, trousers, skirts)
items.use: For anything on the feet or legs; haite iru (haiteru) = be wearing.

example.ja: 今日はスカート履いていく。
example.english: I'm wearing a skirt today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa sukaato o haite ikimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はスカートを履いていきます。
examplePolite.english: I'm wearing a skirt today.

items.notes: Tops take kiru and hats kaburu. Same sound as haku 'throw up'.

items.use: Almost always shawaa o abiru; also sunlight or criticism pouring onto you.

example.romaji: saki ni shawaa abite kuru ne.
example.ja: 先にシャワー浴びてくるね。
example.english: I'll go take a shower first.

examplePolite.romaji: saki ni shawaa o abite kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 先にシャワーを浴びてきます。
examplePolite.english: I'll go take a shower first.

items.notes: A bath is ofuro ni hairu, not abiru.

items.use: Above all ha o migaku, brushing your teeth; also shoes, or a skill (ude o migaku).

example.ja: 寝る前に歯磨いた?
example.english: Did you brush your teeth before bed?

examplePolite.romaji: neru mae ni ha o migakimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 寝る前に歯を磨きましたか?
examplePolite.english: Did you brush your teeth before bed?

items.notes: Hamigaki = brushing your teeth, or toothpaste.

blocks.label: Laundry and wiping
blocks.rationale: Covers wiping up, hanging out the washing and folding it.
blocks.interference: Fuku (wipe) sounds like fuku (clothes) and fuku (blow).

items.use: With a cloth or towel: tables, hands, tears, a wet body.

example.ja: ちょっとテーブル拭いてくれる?
example.english: Can you wipe the table?

examplePolite.romaji: chotto teeburu o fuite moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ちょっとテーブルを拭いてもらえますか?
examplePolite.english: Could you wipe the table?

items.notes: Same sound as fuku 'clothes' and fuku 'blow'.

items.english: hang out to dry; air (a futon)

example.ja: 洗濯物、外に干してくれた?
example.english: Did you hang the washing outside?

examplePolite.romaji: sentakumono o soto ni hoshite kuremashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 洗濯物を外に干してくれましたか?
examplePolite.english: Did you hang the washing outside?

items.notes: Bringing it back in is torikomu. Futon o hosu = air the futon in the sun.

example.ja: 乾いたら洗濯物畳んでおいてね。
example.english: Fold the laundry once it's dry, okay?

examplePolite.romaji: kawaitara sentakumono o tatande oite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 乾いたら洗濯物を畳んでおいてください。
examplePolite.english: Please fold the laundry once it's dry.

items.notes: Also mise o tatamu = close a shop for good.

blocks.label: Sleep habits
blocks.rationale: Lets you explain oversleeping, naps, early mornings and late nights.
blocks.interference: Hayaoki (getting up early) and yofukashi (staying up late) are easy to swap.

items.use: The classic excuse for being late.

example.ja: ごめん、今朝寝坊しちゃった!
example.english: Sorry, I overslept this morning!

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, kesa nebou shimashita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、今朝寝坊しました。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry, I overslept this morning.

items.use: A daytime nap, often after lunch.

example.romaji: gohan no ato, chotto hirune suru.
example.ja: ご飯の後、ちょっと昼寝する。
example.english: I'm going to take a quick nap after lunch.

examplePolite.romaji: gohan no ato, sukoshi hirune shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: ご飯の後、少し昼寝します。
examplePolite.english: I'm going to take a short nap after lunch.

items.notes: Also a noun: hirune no jikan = nap time.

example.romaji: ashita hayaoki shinakya ikenai n da.
example.ja: 明日早起きしなきゃいけないんだ。
example.english: I have to get up early tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa hayaoki shinai to ikenai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 明日は早起きしないといけないんです。
examplePolite.english: I have to get up early tomorrow.

items.notes: Also a noun for the habit: hayaoki da ne = you're an early riser.

example.ja: 昨日また夜更かししちゃったよ。
example.english: I stayed up late again last night.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou mata yofukashi shite shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日また夜更かししてしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I stayed up late again last night.

items.notes: The opposite habit is hayaoki, getting up early.

blocks.label: Heating and cooking
blocks.rationale: Covers reheating food, the microwave, boiling water and basic cooking.
blocks.interference: Wakasu boils the water; yuderu boils food in it.

items.use: Convenience store staff ask atatamemasu ka? about your bento.

example.ja: 昨日のカレー、温めようか?
example.english: Shall I heat up yesterday's curry?

examplePolite.romaji: kinou no karee o atatamemashou ka?
examplePolite.ja: 昨日のカレーを温めましょうか?
examplePolite.english: Shall I heat up yesterday's curry?

items.notes: Written 暖める for rooms and air; same sound.

items.use: From the microwave's ding; the everyday word at home.

example.ja: これ、3分ぐらいチンして。
example.english: Microwave this for about three minutes.

examplePolite.romaji: kore o sanpun gurai chin shite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: これを3分ぐらいチンしてください。
examplePolite.english: Please microwave this for about three minutes.

items.notes: The neutral way to say it is renji de atatameru.

example.ja: お茶入れるから、お湯沸かして。
example.english: I'll make tea, so boil some water.

examplePolite.romaji: ocha o ireru node, oyu o wakashite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: お茶を入れるので、お湯を沸かしてください。
examplePolite.english: I'll make tea, so please boil some water.

items.notes: Ofuro o wakasu = heat the bath. Water boiling by itself is waku: oyu ga waita.

items.use: Cooking food in boiling water — pasta, eggs, vegetables.

example.ja: パスタ、10分ぐらい茹でて。
example.english: Boil the pasta for about ten minutes.

examplePolite.romaji: pasuta o juppun gurai yudete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: パスタを10分ぐらい茹でてください。
examplePolite.english: Please boil the pasta for about ten minutes.

items.notes: Yudetamago = a boiled egg. Just heating water is wakasu.

example.romaji: yasai to niku, issho ni itameru dake da yo.
example.ja: 野菜と肉、一緒に炒めるだけだよ。
example.english: You just stir-fry the veg and meat together.

examplePolite.romaji: yasai to niku o issho ni itameru dake desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 野菜と肉を一緒に炒めるだけですよ。
examplePolite.english: You just stir-fry the vegetables and meat together.

items.notes: Itamemono = a stir-fry. Deep-frying is ageru.

blocks.label: Break, dirty, fix
blocks.rationale: Lets you say something broke, cracked, got dirty or went off, and that you fixed it.
blocks.interference: Kowareru is for machines that stop working, wareru for glass and screens that crack.

items.use: Machines and objects breaking down by themselves.

example.ja: エアコン壊れちゃった。
example.english: The AC's broken.

examplePolite.romaji: eakon ga kowarete shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: エアコンが壊れてしまいました。
examplePolite.english: The air conditioner has broken.

items.notes: Kowasu is 'break it' (you do it). For glass or a cracked screen, wareru is the word.

items.use: Repairing things and correcting mistakes or habits; after a verb stem, -naosu means 'redo' (kakinaosu).

example.ja: 自転車、自分で直した。
example.english: I fixed my bike myself.

examplePolite.romaji: jitensha o jibun de naoshimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 自転車を自分で直しました。
examplePolite.english: I fixed my bike myself.

items.notes: Naoru is 'be fixed, get better'. Same sound as naosu 治す, cure (an illness).

items.use: Glass, plates, screens and eggs cracking or smashing.

example.ja: スマホの画面が割れた。
example.english: My phone screen cracked.

examplePolite.romaji: sumaho no gamen ga waremashita.
examplePolite.ja: スマホの画面が割れました。
examplePolite.english: My phone screen cracked.

items.notes: Waru is 'break it' (you do it). A machine that stops working is kowareru.

items.use: Clothes, hands or rooms getting dirty; yogorete iru = is dirty.

example.ja: 服汚れちゃった。
example.english: I got my clothes dirty.

examplePolite.romaji: fuku ga yogorete shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 服が汚れてしまいました。
examplePolite.english: My clothes got dirty.

items.notes: Yogosu is 'make it dirty' (you do it). The adjective 'dirty' is kitanai.

items.use: Mostly heard as kusatteru, 'it's gone off'.

example.ja: この牛乳、腐ってるかも。
example.english: This milk might be off.

examplePolite.romaji: kono gyuunyuu, kusatte iru kamo shiremasen.
examplePolite.ja: この牛乳、腐っているかもしれません。
examplePolite.english: This milk may have gone off.

items.notes: Said of a person, it means sulk or lose heart.

blocks.label: When I was little
blocks.rationale: Lets you start a story about your childhood or the past.
blocks.interference: Touji (at the time) and toujitsu (on the day) sound alike.

items.english: when I was a kid; childhood
items.use: The standard opener for a childhood memory.

example.romaji: kodomo no koro, yoku koko de asonda
example.ja: 子供の頃、よくここで遊んだ
example.english: When I was a kid, I played here a lot.

examplePolite.romaji: kodomo no koro, yoku koko de asobimashita
examplePolite.ja: 子供の頃、よくここで遊びました
examplePolite.english: When I was a kid, I played here a lot.

items.notes: Kodomo no koro kara = ever since I was a kid. Chiisai koro means the same.

items.use: A soft, everyday way to talk about early childhood.

example.romaji: chiisai koro wa yasai kirai datta
example.ja: 小さい頃は野菜嫌いだった
example.english: I hated vegetables when I was little.

examplePolite.romaji: chiisai koro wa yasai ga kirai deshita
examplePolite.ja: 小さい頃は野菜が嫌いでした
examplePolite.english: I hated vegetables when I was little.

items.notes: Same as kodomo no koro. Chiisai here means young, not small.

items.use: Points to a time both of you know, often with nostalgia.

example.ja: あの頃は楽しかったな
example.english: Those were good times.

examplePolite.romaji: ano koro wa tanoshikatta desu ne
examplePolite.ja: あの頃は楽しかったですね
examplePolite.english: Those were good times, weren't they?

items.notes: Sono koro = at that time, in a story you're telling the listener.

items.use: Sets the scene when explaining past events: touji wa, touji no ~ (the ~ of that time).

example.ja: 当時はまだ学生だった
example.english: I was still a student at the time.

examplePolite.romaji: touji wa mada gakusei deshita
examplePolite.ja: 当時はまだ学生でした
examplePolite.english: I was still a student at the time.

items.notes: More factual than ano koro. Don't mix it up with toujitsu (on the day).

blocks.label: Worth and purpose
blocks.rationale: Lets you say whether something is worth doing, or that you've got something on.
blocks.interference: You in you ga aru means business or an errand, not use.

items.english: pointless; no use; makes no sense
items.use: Casually shortened to imi nai, often as imi nai jan (that's pointless).

example.romaji: imasara itte mo imi nai yo.
example.ja: 今さら言っても意味ないよ。
example.english: There's no point saying it now.

examplePolite.romaji: imasara itte mo imi ga arimasen yo.
examplePolite.ja: 今さら言っても意味がありませんよ。
examplePolite.english: There's no point saying it now.

items.notes: Imi wakannai = I don't get it, that makes no sense.

items.english: there's a point; worth it, meaningful
items.use: Often asked with doubt: sore, imi aru? (is there any point?).

example.ja: それ、やる意味あるの？
example.english: Is there any point doing that?

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa yaru imi ga aru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: それはやる意味があるんですか？
examplePolite.english: Is there any point doing that?

items.english: have something to do; want someone for something
items.use: Used to excuse yourself (I've got something on) or about why someone came to see you.

example.romaji: gomen, kyou wa chotto you ga aru n da.
example.ja: ごめん、今日はちょっと用があるんだ。
example.english: Sorry, I've got something on today.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, kyou wa chotto you ga aru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、今日はちょっと用があるんです。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I've got something on today.

items.notes: Nan no you? = What do you want? (can sound curt). Youji is the noun for an errand.

items.use: Usually 'X suru kachi ga aru' (worth doing).

example.romaji: ano mise, ikkai iku kachi aru yo.
example.ja: あの店、一回行く価値あるよ。
example.english: That place is worth going to at least once.

examplePolite.romaji: ano mise wa ikkai iku kachi ga arimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの店は一回行く価値がありますよ。
examplePolite.english: That place is worth going to at least once.

items.notes: Kachikan = values, what you believe in.

blocks.label: Eating and drinking out
blocks.rationale: Lets you suggest a place to eat, drink or take a break.
blocks.interference: Resutoran means a sit-down, usually Western place, not any eatery.

example.romaji: tsukareta ne. ano kafe de chotto yasumou.
example.ja: 疲れたね。あのカフェでちょっと休もう。
example.english: I'm worn out. Let's take a break in that café.

examplePolite.romaji: tsukaremashita ne. ano kafe de sukoshi yasumimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 疲れましたね。あのカフェで少し休みましょう。
examplePolite.english: I'm worn out. Let's take a break in that café.

items.notes: Kissaten is the older word for a traditional coffee shop.

items.use: A casual bar with lots of small dishes, the usual place for drinks after work.

example.ja: 仕事のあと、居酒屋行かない?
example.english: Want to go to an izakaya after work?

examplePolite.romaji: shigoto no ato, izakaya ni ikimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 仕事のあと、居酒屋に行きませんか?
examplePolite.english: Would you like to go to an izakaya after work?

items.use: Usually a sit-down, often Western-style place; a casual eatery is just a mise or shokudou.

example.romaji: ashita no yoru, resutoran yoyaku shita yo.
example.ja: 明日の夜、レストラン予約したよ。
example.english: I booked a restaurant for tomorrow night.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita no yoru, resutoran o yoyaku shimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 明日の夜、レストランを予約しました。
examplePolite.english: I booked a restaurant for tomorrow night.

blocks.label: Meeting points
blocks.rationale: Lets you arrange where to meet.
blocks.interference: Iriguchi (entrance) is easy to swap with deguchi (exit).

example.romaji: iriguchi no mae de matteru ne.
example.ja: 入り口の前で待ってるね。
example.english: I'll wait outside the entrance.

examplePolite.romaji: iriguchi no mae de matte imasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 入り口の前で待っていますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll wait outside the entrance.

items.notes: The opposite is deguchi, exit. A home's front entrance is the genkan.

items.english: in front of the station; the station area
items.use: The shops and square outside a station, the standard place to meet.

example.romaji: jaa, rokuji ni ekimae de ii?
example.ja: じゃあ、六時に駅前でいい?
example.english: So, six o'clock outside the station, okay?

examplePolite.romaji: jaa, rokuji ni ekimae de ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: じゃあ、六時に駅前でいいですか?
examplePolite.english: So, is six o'clock outside the station okay?

example.romaji: chuushajou, doko ni aru ka wakaru?
example.ja: 駐車場、どこにあるかわかる?
example.english: Do you know where the car park is?

examplePolite.romaji: chuushajou wa doko ni aru ka wakarimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 駐車場はどこにあるかわかりますか?
examplePolite.english: Do you know where the car park is?

items.notes: Bike parking is chuurinjou.

items.use: Where an event happens: a concert, wedding, exam or party.

example.ja: 会場までどれぐらいかかる?
example.english: How long does it take to get to the venue?

examplePolite.romaji: kaijou made dore gurai kakarimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 会場までどれぐらいかかりますか?
examplePolite.english: How long does it take to get to the venue?

blocks.label: Errands in town
blocks.rationale: Lets you say where you're popping out to.
blocks.interference: Biyouin (hair salon) sounds close to byouin (hospital).

example.romaji: saki ni ginkou yotte kara iku ne.
example.ja: 先に銀行寄ってから行くね。
example.english: I'll stop at the bank first, then come.

examplePolite.romaji: saki ni ginkou ni yotte kara ikimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 先に銀行に寄ってから行きます。
examplePolite.english: I'll stop at the bank first, then come.

items.use: Where you get a cut or colour; a traditional men's barber is a tokoya.

example.ja: 明日美容院行ってくる。
example.english: I'm going to the hairdresser's tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita biyouin ni itte kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 明日美容院に行ってきます。
examplePolite.english: I'm going to the hairdresser's tomorrow.

items.notes: Don't mix up bi-you-in (salon) with byou-in (hospital).

example.romaji: kore, yuubinkyoku de dashite kite kureru?
example.ja: これ、郵便局で出してきてくれる?
example.english: Could you post this at the post office for me?

examplePolite.romaji: kore, yuubinkyoku de dashite kite moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: これ、郵便局で出してきてもらえますか?
examplePolite.english: Could you post this at the post office for me?

items.notes: Posting something is dasu: tegami o dasu.

items.use: Short for hyaku-en kin'itsu; fine in any register.

example.romaji: kore, hyakkin de katta n da.
example.ja: これ、百均で買ったんだ。
example.english: I got this at the 100-yen shop.

examplePolite.romaji: kore, hyakkin de kaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: これ、百均で買いました。
examplePolite.english: I got this at the 100-yen shop.

blocks.label: Living room things
blocks.rationale: Lets you turn the TV and lights on and off and find a seat.
blocks.interference: Denki in a room means the light, not electricity.

example.ja: テレビつけてもいい?
example.english: Can I put the TV on?

examplePolite.romaji: terebi o tsukete mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: テレビをつけてもいいですか?
examplePolite.english: May I put the TV on?

items.notes: Turn on = tsukeru, turn off = kesu; watch = miru.

items.use: In a room it usually means the light: denki o tsukeru / kesu.

example.romaji: neru mae ni denki keshite ne.
example.ja: 寝る前に電気消してね。
example.english: Turn the light off before you go to sleep.

examplePolite.romaji: neru mae ni denki o keshite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 寝る前に電気を消してください。
examplePolite.english: Please turn the light off before you go to sleep.

items.notes: The electricity bill is denkidai.

example.romaji: kagi, teeburu no ue ni oita yo.
example.ja: 鍵、テーブルの上に置いたよ。
example.english: I left the keys on the table.

examplePolite.romaji: kagi wa teeburu no ue ni okimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 鍵はテーブルの上に置きました。
examplePolite.english: I left the keys on the table.

items.notes: A desk for working or studying is a tsukue.

example.ja: この椅子、使ってもいい?
example.english: Can I use this chair?

examplePolite.romaji: kono isu, tsukatte mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: この椅子、使ってもいいですか?
examplePolite.english: May I use this chair?

items.notes: Sit on a chair = isu ni suwaru.

blocks.label: Bags and boxes
blocks.rationale: Lets you name what you carry things in and turn down a shop bag.
blocks.interference: Three bag words: kaban is general, baggu a fashion bag, fukuro a soft carrier bag.

items.use: A soft carrier bag or pouch; cashiers ask fukuro wa goriyou desu ka? (Do you need a bag?).

example.romaji: fukuro iranai yo, eko baggu aru kara.
example.ja: 袋いらないよ、エコバッグあるから。
example.english: I don't need a bag, I've got my own.

examplePolite.romaji: fukuro wa ii desu. eko baggu ga arimasu kara.
examplePolite.ja: 袋はいいです。エコバッグがありますから。
examplePolite.english: No bag, thanks. I've brought my own.

items.notes: In compounds it becomes -bukuro: rejibukuro (carrier bag), kamibukuro (paper bag).

items.use: The general word for a bag you carry your things in.

example.ja: カバン、ここに置いていい?
example.english: Can I put my bag here?

examplePolite.romaji: kaban o koko ni oite mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: カバンをここに置いてもいいですか?
examplePolite.english: May I put my bag here?

items.use: Mostly a handbag or fashion bag; kaban is the general word.

example.ja: そのバッグ、かわいいね。
example.english: That bag's cute.

examplePolite.romaji: sono baggu, kawaii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: そのバッグ、かわいいですね。
examplePolite.english: That's a cute bag.

items.notes: A reusable shopping bag is an eko baggu.

example.ja: これ、箱に入れておいて。
example.english: Put these in the box, would you?

examplePolite.romaji: kore o hako ni irete oite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: これを箱に入れておいてください。
examplePolite.english: Please put these in the box.

items.notes: A cardboard box is a danbooru.

blocks.label: Cleaning and chores
blocks.rationale: Lets you share the cleaning and take the rubbish out.
blocks.interference: Souji is cleaning a room; washing clothes is sentaku.

items.use: Sweeping, wiping or vacuuming; washing clothes is sentaku and washing dishes is arau.

example.romaji: shuumatsu wa heya no souji suru tsumori.
example.ja: 週末は部屋の掃除するつもり。
example.english: I'm planning to clean my room this weekend.

examplePolite.romaji: shuumatsu wa heya no souji o suru tsumori desu.
examplePolite.ja: 週末は部屋の掃除をするつもりです。
examplePolite.english: I'm planning to clean my room this weekend.

items.notes: Also a plain noun: souji ga owatta = the cleaning's done.

items.use: Sorted strictly, with moeru gomi (burnable), moenai gomi and recycling collected on set days.

example.romaji: ashita, moeru gomi no hi da yo.
example.ja: 明日、燃えるごみの日だよ。
example.english: Tomorrow's burnable rubbish day.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa moeru gomi no hi desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 明日は燃えるごみの日ですよ。
examplePolite.english: Tomorrow is burnable rubbish day.

items.notes: Take the rubbish out = gomi o dasu; a bin is a gomibako. Often written ゴミ.

example.romaji: kaji, hanbun zutsu ni shiyou yo.
example.ja: 家事、半分ずつにしようよ。
example.english: Let's split the housework half and half.

examplePolite.romaji: kaji wa hanbun zutsu ni shimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 家事は半分ずつにしましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's split the housework half and half.

items.notes: Sounds the same as kaji, a fire; context sorts it out.

items.use: Anything you use for a job: cleaning things, sports gear, art supplies.

example.romaji: souji no dougu, doko ni aru?
example.ja: 掃除の道具、どこにある?
example.english: Where are the cleaning things?

examplePolite.romaji: souji no dougu wa doko ni arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 掃除の道具はどこにありますか?
examplePolite.english: Where are the cleaning things?

blocks.label: Clothes and shoes
blocks.rationale: Lets you name what you wear and take your shoes off.
blocks.interference: Fuku goes on with kiru, but shoes, socks and trousers with haku.

example.romaji: sono fuku, doko de katta no?
example.ja: その服、どこで買ったの?
example.english: Where did you get that outfit?

examplePolite.romaji: sono fuku, doko de kaimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: その服、どこで買いましたか?
examplePolite.english: Where did you get that outfit?

items.notes: Put clothes on = kiru; take them off = nugu.

example.ja: この靴、歩きやすくていいよ。
example.english: These shoes are really easy to walk in.

examplePolite.romaji: kono kutsu wa arukiyasukute ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: この靴は歩きやすくていいですよ。
examplePolite.english: These shoes are easy to walk in.

items.notes: Shoes go on with haku, like socks and trousers, not kiru.

example.romaji: kutsushita, katahou nai n da kedo.
example.ja: 靴下、片方ないんだけど。
example.english: One of my socks is missing.

examplePolite.romaji: kutsushita ga katahou nai n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: 靴下が片方ないんですけど。
examplePolite.english: One of my socks seems to be missing.

items.notes: Put on with haku, like shoes.

example.ja: このズボン、ちょっときつい。
example.english: These trousers are a bit tight.

examplePolite.romaji: kono zubon, sukoshi kitsui desu.
examplePolite.ja: このズボン、少しきついです。
examplePolite.english: These trousers are a little tight.

items.notes: Put on with haku. Pantsu usually means underpants, so zubon is the safe word.

blocks.label: Bath and toilet
blocks.rationale: Lets you ask for the toilet and talk about bathing.
blocks.interference: Ofuro takes hairu but shawaa takes abiru.

items.use: Taking a bath is ofuro ni hairu, literally 'go into the bath'.

example.romaji: saki ni ofuro haitte ii yo.
example.ja: 先にお風呂入っていいよ。
example.english: You can have the bath first.

examplePolite.romaji: saki ni ofuro ni haitte mo ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 先にお風呂に入ってもいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Please go ahead and have the bath first.

items.notes: Furo without the o sounds blunt. The toilet is a separate room, the toire.

example.ja: ちょっとトイレ行ってくる。
example.english: I'm just popping to the toilet.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto toire ni itte kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっとトイレに行ってきます。
examplePolite.english: I'm just going to the toilet.

items.notes: Otearai is a politer word, often heard in shops and seen on signs.

example.romaji: natsu wa shawaa dake de sumaseru.
example.ja: 夏はシャワーだけで済ませる。
example.english: In summer I just have a shower, no bath.

examplePolite.romaji: natsu wa shawaa dake de sumasemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 夏はシャワーだけで済ませます。
examplePolite.english: In summer I just have a shower instead of a bath.

items.notes: The verb is abiru, not hairu (hairu is for the bath).

example.romaji: taoru, koko ni oite oku ne.
example.ja: タオル、ここに置いておくね。
example.english: I'll leave a towel here for you.

examplePolite.romaji: taoru o koko ni oite okimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: タオルをここに置いておきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll leave a towel here for you.

example.ja: ティッシュある?鼻水止まらない。
example.english: Got a tissue? My nose won't stop running.

examplePolite.romaji: tisshu, arimasu ka? hanamizu ga tomaranakute.
examplePolite.ja: ティッシュ、ありますか?鼻水が止まらなくて。
examplePolite.english: Do you have a tissue? My nose won't stop running.

items.notes: Toilet paper is toiretto peepaa, a different word.

blocks.label: Bed and sleep
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about going to bed and where people sleep.
blocks.interference: None.

items.use: Laid out on the floor at night and folded away by day.

example.romaji: kyakuyou no futon, shiite oku ne.
example.ja: 客用の布団、敷いておくね。
example.english: I'll lay out the spare futon for you.

examplePolite.romaji: kyakuyou no futon o shiite okimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 客用の布団を敷いておきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll lay out the guest futon for you.

items.notes: Lay out = shiku; put away = tatamu; airing it in the sun = futon o hosu.

example.romaji: kinou wa tsukarete sugu beddo ni haitta.
example.ja: 昨日は疲れてすぐベッドに入った。
example.english: I was tired last night, so I went straight to bed.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou wa tsukarete sugu beddo ni hairimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日は疲れてすぐベッドに入りました。
examplePolite.english: I was tired last night, so I went straight to bed.

items.notes: Go to bed is usually just neru; the traditional floor bed is a futon.

example.ja: ホテルの枕、高すぎて寝れなかった。
example.english: The hotel pillow was too high, I couldn't sleep.

examplePolite.romaji: hoteru no makura ga takasugite, nemuremasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: ホテルの枕が高すぎて、眠れませんでした。
examplePolite.english: The hotel pillow was too high, so I couldn't sleep.

items.notes: Pillows are takai (high) or hikui (low), not thick or thin.

example.ja: もうパジャマに着替えたよ。
example.english: I've already changed into my pyjamas.

examplePolite.romaji: mou pajama ni kigaemashita.
examplePolite.ja: もうパジャマに着替えました。
examplePolite.english: I've already changed into my pyjamas.

blocks.label: Kitchen and table
blocks.rationale: Lets you set the table and find things in the fridge.
blocks.interference: Reizouko (fridge) and reitouko (freezer) differ by one sound.

example.ja: ビール、冷蔵庫に入ってるよ。
example.english: There's beer in the fridge.

examplePolite.romaji: biiru wa reizouko ni haitte imasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: ビールは冷蔵庫に入っていますよ。
examplePolite.english: There's beer in the fridge.

items.notes: The freezer is reitouko, one sound away.

items.use: Most people say ohashi in everyday speech.

example.romaji: ohashi no tsukaikata, jouzu da ne.
example.ja: お箸の使い方、上手だね。
example.english: You're good with chopsticks.

examplePolite.romaji: ohashi no tsukaikata, jouzu desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: お箸の使い方、上手ですね。
examplePolite.english: You're very good with chopsticks.

items.notes: Same sounds as hashi, bridge, and hashi, edge; pitch and context tell them apart.

items.use: Most people say osara; doing the dishes is osara o arau.

example.ja: お皿、私が洗うよ。
example.english: I'll do the dishes.

examplePolite.romaji: osara wa watashi ga araimasu.
examplePolite.ja: お皿は私が洗います。
examplePolite.english: I'll wash the dishes.

items.notes: In compounds it becomes -zara: kozara (small plate), haizara (ashtray).

items.use: A drinking glass or plastic cup; a mug for hot drinks is a magu kappu.

example.ja: コップ、もう一つもらっていい?
example.english: Can I get another glass?

examplePolite.romaji: koppu o mou hitotsu itadakemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: コップをもう一ついただけますか?
examplePolite.english: Could I have another glass?

items.notes: Gurasu also means a glass, especially for wine.

blocks.label: Doing the laundry
blocks.rationale: Lets you do the washing and hang it out.
blocks.interference: Sentaku (the chore), sentakumono (the clothes) and sentakuki (the machine) sound alike.

items.use: Only for clothes and linen; washing dishes or hands is arau.

example.romaji: kyou wa tenki ii kara sentaku suru.
example.ja: 今日は天気いいから洗濯する。
example.english: It's nice out today, so I'm doing the washing.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa tenki ga ii kara sentaku shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は天気がいいから洗濯します。
examplePolite.english: It's nice out today, so I'm doing the washing.

items.notes: The clothes themselves are sentakumono; the machine is a sentakuki.

items.use: The clothes themselves, dirty or drying.

example.romaji: ame da kara sentakumono torikomu ne.
example.ja: 雨だから洗濯物取り込むね。
example.english: It's raining, so I'll bring the washing in.

examplePolite.romaji: ame na node, sentakumono o torikomimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 雨なので、洗濯物を取り込みますね。
examplePolite.english: It's raining, so I'll bring the washing in.

items.notes: Hang it out = hosu; fold it = tatamu.

items.use: Where most Japanese flats hang their washing out to dry.

example.ja: 洗濯物、ベランダに干したよ。
example.english: I hung the washing out on the balcony.

examplePolite.romaji: sentakumono wa beranda ni hoshimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 洗濯物はベランダに干しました。
examplePolite.english: I hung the washing out on the balcony.

example.ja: 洗濯機、まだ回ってるから待って。
example.english: The washing machine's still going, so hang on.

examplePolite.romaji: sentakuki ga mada mawatte iru node, matte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 洗濯機がまだ回っているので、待ってください。
examplePolite.english: The washing machine is still running, so please wait.

items.notes: Running it is sentakuki o mawasu, literally 'turn' it.

blocks.label: Chores at home
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about cooking, cleaning up and daily routines at home.
blocks.interference: Ryouri is any cooking; jisui is cooking your own meals instead of eating out.

example.romaji: ryouri kekkou tokui na n da
example.ja: 料理けっこう得意なんだ
example.english: I'm actually pretty good at cooking.

examplePolite.romaji: ryouri wa kekkou tokui na n desu
examplePolite.ja: 料理はけっこう得意なんです
examplePolite.english: I'm actually quite good at cooking.

items.notes: Ryouri suru means to cook. As cuisine: nihon ryouri is Japanese food.

items.use: Mostly as hamigaki suru, to brush your teeth.

example.ja: 寝る前に歯磨きした?
example.english: Did you brush your teeth before bed?

examplePolite.romaji: neru mae ni hamigaki shimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 寝る前に歯磨きしましたか?
examplePolite.english: Did you brush your teeth before going to bed?

items.notes: Toothpaste is hamigakiko.

items.use: Usually dirty dishes; goes with suru or yaru.

example.romaji: araimono wa ato de yattoku ne
example.ja: 洗い物はあとでやっとくね
example.english: I'll do the dishes later.

examplePolite.romaji: araimono wa ato de yatte okimasu
examplePolite.ja: 洗い物はあとでやっておきます
examplePolite.english: I'll take care of the dishes later.

items.notes: Can also mean laundry waiting to be washed.

items.use: Courier delivery to your door; you hear 'takuhaibin desu' at the intercom.

example.ja: さっき宅配便来てたよ
example.english: A parcel came for you earlier.

examplePolite.romaji: sakki takuhaibin ga kite imashita yo
examplePolite.ja: さっき宅配便が来ていましたよ
examplePolite.english: A delivery came earlier.

items.notes: Takkyuubin is heard for the same thing.

items.english: cook for yourself; make your own meals
items.use: Said of people living alone who cook instead of eating out or buying ready meals.

example.romaji: hitorigurashi da kedo mainichi jisui shiteru yo
example.ja: 一人暮らしだけど毎日自炊してるよ
example.english: I live alone, but I cook for myself every day.

examplePolite.romaji: hitorigurashi desu ga mainichi jisui shite imasu
examplePolite.ja: 一人暮らしですが毎日自炊しています
examplePolite.english: I live alone, but I cook my own meals every day.

items.notes: The opposite of gaishoku (eating out).

blocks.label: Home appliances
blocks.rationale: Lets you ask for and use the everyday machines at home.
blocks.interference: Renji is the microwave, never a stove or cooker.

items.use: Wall units both cool and heat, so it's on in winter too.

example.ja: 暑いからエアコンつけて
example.english: It's hot, turn on the air con.

examplePolite.romaji: atsui node eakon o tsukete kudasai
examplePolite.ja: 暑いのでエアコンをつけてください
examplePolite.english: It's hot, so please turn on the air conditioning.

items.notes: Tsukeru turns it on, kesu turns it off.

items.use: Short for denshi renji; it means the microwave, not a stove.

example.romaji: sore renji de atatamereba ii yo
example.ja: それレンジで温めればいいよ
example.english: Just heat it up in the microwave.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa renji de atatamereba ii desu yo
examplePolite.ja: それはレンジで温めればいいですよ
examplePolite.english: You can just heat that in the microwave.

items.notes: Chin suru is a casual way to say microwave something.

example.ja: テレビのリモコンどこ行った?
example.english: Where'd the TV remote go?

examplePolite.romaji: terebi no rimokon wa doko desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: テレビのリモコンはどこですか?
examplePolite.english: Where's the TV remote?

items.use: To vacuum is soujiki o kakeru.

example.ja: 部屋に掃除機かけといたよ
example.english: I vacuumed the room.

examplePolite.romaji: heya ni soujiki o kakete okimashita
examplePolite.ja: 部屋に掃除機をかけておきました
examplePolite.english: I've vacuumed the room.

items.notes: Souji is cleaning; soujiki is the machine.

blocks.label: Beer, wine and juice
blocks.rationale: Lets you order or offer drinks at a meal or party.
blocks.interference: Juusu covers any sweet soft drink, not only fruit juice.

example.romaji: shigoto no ato no biiru wa saikou
example.ja: 仕事のあとのビールは最高
example.english: Beer after work is the best.

examplePolite.romaji: shigoto no ato no biiru wa saikou desu
examplePolite.ja: 仕事のあとのビールは最高です
examplePolite.english: A beer after work is the best.

items.notes: At a bar, nama or nama biiru is draft beer.

example.romaji: aka wain to shiro, dotchi ga ii?
example.ja: 赤ワインと白、どっちがいい?
example.english: Red wine or white, which do you want?

examplePolite.romaji: aka wain to shiro, dochira ga ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 赤ワインと白、どちらがいいですか?
examplePolite.english: Would you prefer red wine or white?

items.use: Covers sweet soft drinks like cola too, not just fruit juice.

example.romaji: kodomo ni wa juusu de ii?
example.ja: 子どもにはジュースでいい?
example.english: Is juice okay for the kids?

examplePolite.romaji: kodomo ni wa juusu de ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 子どもにはジュースでいいですか?
examplePolite.english: Is juice all right for the children?

blocks.label: Taste and seasoning
blocks.rationale: Lets you say how food tastes and what goes on it.
blocks.interference: Shio (salt) and shouyu (soy sauce) start with the same sound.

example.ja: この味ちょっと薄くない?
example.english: Isn't this a bit bland?

examplePolite.romaji: kono aji, chotto usukunai desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: この味、ちょっと薄くないですか?
examplePolite.english: Isn't the flavour a little weak?

items.notes: Aji ga koi is strong-tasting, aji ga usui mild or bland. Nan no aji? asks what flavour it is.

items.use: Raw food, a draft beer at a bar, or something seen live and in person.

example.ja: これ生で食べられるの?
example.english: Can you eat this raw?

examplePolite.romaji: kore wa nama de taberaremasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: これは生で食べられますか?
examplePolite.english: Can this be eaten raw?

items.notes: Toriaezu nama is the classic bar order: a draft beer to start. Nama de mita means saw it live.

example.ja: ごめん、そこの塩取って
example.english: Sorry, can you pass me the salt?

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, soko no shio o totte kudasai
examplePolite.ja: すみません、そこの塩を取ってください
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, could you pass the salt?

items.notes: Shio ramen is salt-flavoured ramen.

example.ja: 醤油かけすぎじゃない?
example.english: Isn't that too much soy sauce?

examplePolite.romaji: shouyu o kakesugi ja nai desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 醤油をかけすぎじゃないですか?
examplePolite.english: Aren't you putting on too much soy sauce?

items.notes: Shouyu o kakeru is pour it on; shouyu ni tsukeru is dip in it.

blocks.label: Sweets and snacks
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about desserts, sweets and snacks.
blocks.interference: Okashi is the snack food itself; oyatsu is the snack between meals or snack time.

example.romaji: tanjoubi no keeki katte kita yo
example.ja: 誕生日のケーキ買ってきたよ
example.english: I picked up a birthday cake.

examplePolite.romaji: tanjoubi no keeki o katte kimashita
examplePolite.ja: 誕生日のケーキを買ってきました
examplePolite.english: I bought a birthday cake.

items.use: Covers candy, chips and biscuits, anything packaged to snack on.

example.ja: お菓子ばっかり食べないの
example.english: Stop eating nothing but snacks.

examplePolite.romaji: okashi bakari tabenaide kudasai
examplePolite.ja: お菓子ばかり食べないでください
examplePolite.english: Please don't eat only snacks.

items.notes: Wagashi are traditional Japanese sweets.

items.use: Means ice cream, not ice; ice cubes are koori.

example.ja: 暑いからアイス食べたい
example.english: It's so hot, I want ice cream.

examplePolite.romaji: atsui node aisu ga tabetai desu
examplePolite.ja: 暑いのでアイスが食べたいです
examplePolite.english: It's hot, so I'd like some ice cream.

items.notes: Before a drink it means iced: aisu koohii.

items.use: Short for chokoreeto; the short form is what people usually say.

example.ja: そのチョコ一個もらっていい?
example.english: Can I have one of those chocolates?

examplePolite.romaji: sono choko ikko moratte mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: そのチョコ一個もらってもいいですか?
examplePolite.english: May I have one of those chocolates?

items.notes: On Valentine's Day women give choko; giri choko is the obligation chocolate for coworkers.

items.use: The afternoon snack between meals, especially for kids.

example.ja: おやつにプリンあるよ
example.english: There's pudding for a snack.

examplePolite.romaji: oyatsu ni purin ga arimasu yo
examplePolite.ja: おやつにプリンがありますよ
examplePolite.english: There's some pudding for a snack.

blocks.label: Popular dishes
blocks.rationale: Lets you name the dishes people go out for most.
blocks.interference: None.

items.use: Usually Japanese curry over rice, a standard home dinner.

example.romaji: kyou no bangohan karee da yo
example.ja: 今日の晩ご飯カレーだよ
example.english: We're having curry for dinner tonight.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou no bangohan wa karee desu
examplePolite.ja: 今日の晩ご飯はカレーです
examplePolite.english: Tonight's dinner is curry.

items.notes: The full name is kareeraisu.

example.ja: 帰りにラーメン食べてかない?
example.english: Want to grab ramen on the way home?

examplePolite.romaji: kaeri ni raamen o tabete ikimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 帰りにラーメンを食べていきませんか?
examplePolite.english: Would you like to get ramen on the way home?

example.romaji: oiwai da kara sushi tabe ni ikou
example.ja: お祝いだから寿司食べに行こう
example.english: It's a celebration, let's go for sushi.

examplePolite.romaji: oiwai na node sushi o tabe ni ikimashou
examplePolite.ja: お祝いなので寿司を食べに行きましょう
examplePolite.english: Since it's a celebration, let's go out for sushi.

items.notes: Often said osushi. Kaitenzushi is conveyor-belt sushi.

example.romaji: kaze no toki wa udon ga ii yo
example.ja: 風邪の時はうどんがいいよ
example.english: Udon is good when you've got a cold.

examplePolite.romaji: kaze no toki wa udon ga ii desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 風邪の時はうどんがいいですよ
examplePolite.english: Udon is good when you have a cold.

blocks.label: Japanese home food
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about everyday Japanese meals and packed lunches.
blocks.interference: Nabe is both the cooking pot and the hot-pot meal.

items.use: Home-made or bought at a convenience store; usually said obentou.

example.ja: 今日お弁当持ってきた?
example.english: Did you bring a lunch today?

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa obentou o motte kimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今日はお弁当を持ってきましたか?
examplePolite.english: Did you bring a packed lunch today?

items.notes: Convenience store staff ask 'atatamemasu ka?': do you want it heated?

items.use: Most often the shared hot-pot meal cooked at the table in winter.

example.romaji: samui shi kon'ya wa nabe ni shiyou yo
example.ja: 寒いし今夜は鍋にしようよ
example.english: It's cold, let's have hot pot tonight.

examplePolite.romaji: samui node kon'ya wa nabe ni shimashou
examplePolite.ja: 寒いので今夜は鍋にしましょう
examplePolite.english: It's cold, so let's have hot pot tonight.

items.notes: Also the cooking pot or saucepan itself.

example.romaji: konbini de onigiri katte kuru ne
example.ja: コンビニでおにぎり買ってくるね
example.english: I'll go grab some rice balls from the convenience store.

examplePolite.romaji: konbini de onigiri o katte kimasu ne
examplePolite.ja: コンビニでおにぎりを買ってきますね
examplePolite.english: I'll go and buy some rice balls at the convenience store.

items.notes: Also called omusubi in some places.

example.ja: 味噌汁飲むとほっとする
example.english: Miso soup always makes me feel at home.

examplePolite.romaji: misoshiru o nomu to hotto shimasu
examplePolite.ja: 味噌汁を飲むとほっとします
examplePolite.english: Drinking miso soup makes me relax.

items.notes: Often said omisoshiru. You drink it from the bowl, so the verb is nomu.

blocks.label: Eating out
blocks.rationale: Lets you handle restaurants, lunch out and takeaway.
blocks.interference: Gaishoku is the habit of eating out; ranchi is one lunch, usually out.

example.ja: メニュー見てから決めよう
example.english: Let's look at the menu and then decide.

examplePolite.romaji: menyuu o mite kara kimemashou
examplePolite.ja: メニューを見てから決めましょう
examplePolite.english: Let's decide after looking at the menu.

items.notes: Also a list of options outside food, like a workout menu.

items.use: Mostly for lunch out; lunch at home is hirugohan.

example.ja: 明日一緒にランチ行かない?
example.english: Want to go to lunch together tomorrow?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita issho ni ranchi ni ikimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日一緒にランチに行きませんか?
examplePolite.english: Would you like to have lunch together tomorrow?

items.notes: Restaurants offer cheap ranchi sets at midday.

items.use: Talks about the habit of eating out rather than one restaurant meal.

example.ja: 最近外食ばっかりだな
example.english: I've been eating out way too much lately.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin gaishoku bakari desu
examplePolite.ja: 最近外食ばかりです
examplePolite.english: Lately I've been eating out all the time.

items.notes: Gaishoku suru means eat out. The opposite is jisui (cooking for yourself).

items.use: A set price, usually with a time limit.

example.ja: 焼肉の食べ放題行こうよ
example.english: Let's go to an all-you-can-eat barbecue place.

examplePolite.romaji: yakiniku no tabehoudai ni ikimashou
examplePolite.ja: 焼肉の食べ放題に行きましょう
examplePolite.english: Let's go for all-you-can-eat barbecue.

items.notes: All-you-can-drink is nomihoudai.

items.use: Staff ask 'omochikaeri desu ka?': is it to go?

example.ja: 混んでるし持ち帰りにしない?
example.english: It's packed, want to get it to go?

examplePolite.romaji: konde iru node mochikaeri ni shimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 混んでいるので持ち帰りにしませんか?
examplePolite.english: It's crowded, so shall we get it to go?

items.notes: Eating in is tennai or kochira de. Teikuauto is also used.

blocks.label: Meetings and deadlines
blocks.rationale: Handle the office calendar: meetings, papers, trips and deadlines.
blocks.interference: Uchiawase is a working meeting; kaigi is a formal one.

items.use: A working meeting to go over details, often small and with a client or colleague.

example.romaji: gogo kara uchiawase ga aru n da.
example.ja: 午後から打ち合わせがあるんだ。
example.english: I've got a meeting this afternoon.

examplePolite.romaji: gogo kara uchiawase ga arimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 午後から打ち合わせがあります。
examplePolite.english: I have a meeting this afternoon.

items.notes: Kaigi is a bigger, more formal meeting. Uchiawase suru = to meet and sort out plans.

items.use: Your plans for a day or week, or the timetable for a project or trip.

example.ja: 来週のスケジュール、どうなってる？
example.english: What's your schedule like next week?

examplePolite.romaji: raishuu no sukejuuru wa dou natte imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 来週のスケジュールはどうなっていますか？
examplePolite.english: What does your schedule look like next week?

items.notes: Yotei is the everyday word for one plan: ashita yotei aru? = got plans tomorrow?

items.use: Official papers such as forms, contracts and applications.

example.romaji: sono shorui, tsukue no ue ni oitoite.
example.ja: その書類、机の上に置いといて。
example.english: Just leave those papers on my desk.

examplePolite.romaji: sono shorui wa tsukue no ue ni oite oite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: その書類は机の上に置いておいてください。
examplePolite.english: Please leave those papers on the desk.

items.notes: A plain sheet of paper is kami; shorui is papers that matter, like an application.

example.romaji: raishuu, oosaka ni shutchou nan da.
example.ja: 来週、大阪に出張なんだ。
example.english: I've got a business trip to Osaka next week.

examplePolite.romaji: raishuu, oosaka ni shutchou desu.
examplePolite.ja: 来週、大阪に出張です。
examplePolite.english: I'm going to Osaka on business next week.

items.notes: Shutchou ni iku or shutchou suru = go on a business trip; shutchou chuu = away on business.

example.ja: 締め切り、明日までだよ。
example.english: The deadline's tomorrow, you know.

examplePolite.romaji: shimekiri wa ashita made desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 締め切りは明日までですよ。
examplePolite.english: The deadline is tomorrow.

items.notes: Shimekiri ni maniau = make the deadline; maniawanai = miss it.

blocks.label: Work hours and time off
blocks.rationale: Talk about your workday, overtime and days off.
blocks.interference: Kyuukei (a short break), yuukyuu (paid leave) and renkyuu (days off in a row) all sound alike.

items.use: A short pause from work, study or a long drive; used with suru.

example.ja: ちょっと休憩しようか。
example.english: Shall we take a quick break?

examplePolite.romaji: chotto kyuukei shimashou ka.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと休憩しましょうか。
examplePolite.english: Shall we take a short break?

items.notes: Yasumi is the wider word for time off or a day off. Kyuukei chuu = on a break.

items.use: Staying late at work after normal hours; zangyou suru = to work overtime.

example.romaji: kyou mo zangyou de osoku naru.
example.ja: 今日も残業で遅くなる。
example.english: I'll be home late again, working overtime.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou mo zangyou de osoku narimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日も残業で遅くなります。
examplePolite.english: I'll be late again today because of overtime.

items.notes: Saabisu zangyou = unpaid overtime.

example.romaji: tsuukin ni ichijikan kakaru n da.
example.ja: 通勤に一時間かかるんだ。
example.english: My commute takes an hour.

examplePolite.romaji: tsuukin ni ichijikan kakarimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 通勤に一時間かかります。
examplePolite.english: My commute takes an hour.

items.notes: Tsuugaku is commuting to school. Tsuukin suru = to commute; densha de tsuukin = commute by train.

items.use: Short for yuukyuu kyuuka; you 'take' it: yuukyuu o toru.

example.romaji: raishuu, yuukyuu totte ryokou suru n da.
example.ja: 来週、有給取って旅行するんだ。
example.english: I'm taking paid leave next week to go on a trip.

examplePolite.romaji: raishuu, yuukyuu o totte ryokou shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 来週、有給を取って旅行します。
examplePolite.english: I'm taking paid leave next week for a trip.

items.english: days off in a row; long weekend
items.use: Two or more days off in a row, especially around public holidays.

example.romaji: kondo no renkyuu, doko ka iku?
example.ja: 今度の連休、どこか行く？
example.english: Going anywhere over the long weekend?

examplePolite.romaji: kondo no renkyuu wa doko ka ikimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今度の連休はどこか行きますか？
examplePolite.english: Are you going anywhere over the long weekend?

items.notes: Sanrenkyuu = a three-day weekend. Golden Week in early May is the big one.

blocks.label: Staying healthy
blocks.rationale: Talk about health habits, exercise, weight and check-ups.
blocks.interference: Daietto only means trying to lose weight, never your normal diet.

items.use: Health in general; kenkou ni ii = good for you.

example.romaji: sore, kenkou ni ii n da yo.
example.ja: それ、健康にいいんだよ。
example.english: That's actually good for your health.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa kenkou ni ii n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: それは健康にいいんですよ。
examplePolite.english: That's good for your health, you know.

items.notes: Also a na-adjective: kenkou na = healthy. 'Take care of yourself' is usually karada ni ki o tsukete.

items.use: Exercise for your health; undou suru = to work out.

example.romaji: motto undou shinai to dame da na.
example.ja: もっと運動しないとダメだな。
example.english: I really need to get more exercise.

examplePolite.romaji: motto undou shinai to ikemasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: もっと運動しないといけませんね。
examplePolite.english: I really should exercise more.

items.notes: Undou busoku = not getting enough exercise. It can also mean a political or social movement.

items.use: Always about losing weight; daietto chuu = on a diet.

example.romaji: ima daietto chuu dakara, amai mono wa ii ya.
example.ja: 今ダイエット中だから、甘いものはいいや。
example.english: I'm on a diet, so I'll pass on sweets.

examplePolite.romaji: ima daietto chuu na node, amai mono wa kekkou desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今ダイエット中なので、甘いものは結構です。
examplePolite.english: I'm on a diet, so no sweets for me, thanks.

items.notes: Daietto suru = go on a diet. What you normally eat is shokuji, not daietto.

items.use: Weight goes up (fueru) or down (heru); taijuu o hakaru = weigh yourself.

example.romaji: saikin, taijuu ga sankiro mo fueta.
example.ja: 最近、体重が3キロも増えた。
example.english: I've put on a whole three kilos lately.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin, taijuu ga sankiro mo fuemashita.
examplePolite.ja: 最近、体重が3キロも増えました。
examplePolite.english: I've gained three kilos recently.

items.notes: Taijuukei = bathroom scales.

items.use: The yearly check-up most companies and schools require.

example.romaji: raishuu, kaisha no kenkou shindan ga aru.
example.ja: 来週、会社の健康診断がある。
example.english: We've got the company health check next week.

examplePolite.romaji: raishuu, kaisha no kenkou shindan ga arimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 来週、会社の健康診断があります。
examplePolite.english: There's a company health check next week.

items.notes: Often shortened to kenshin. Kenkou shindan o ukeru = have a check-up.

blocks.label: Symptoms and seasonal ills
blocks.rationale: Describe common symptoms and the seasonal ills everyone talks about.
blocks.interference: Netchuushou (heatstroke) shares its first sound with netsu (fever) but is a different thing.

items.use: Hanamizu ga deru = have a runny nose.

example.ja: 風邪かな、鼻水が止まらない。
example.english: Maybe it's a cold; my nose won't stop running.

examplePolite.romaji: kaze kamo shiremasen. hanamizu ga tomaranai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 風邪かもしれません。鼻水が止まらないんです。
examplePolite.english: It might be a cold. My nose won't stop running.

items.notes: Hana o kamu = blow your nose; hanazumari = a blocked nose.

items.use: Seki ga deru = to cough; seki ga tomaranai = can't stop coughing.

example.romaji: kinou kara seki ga zenzen tomaranai.
example.ja: 昨日から咳が全然止まらない。
example.english: I haven't stopped coughing since yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou kara seki ga tomaranai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日から咳が止まらないんです。
examplePolite.english: I've been coughing nonstop since yesterday.

items.notes: Seki o suru also works. A sneeze is kushami.

items.use: A common summer warning in Japan; netchuushou ni naru = get heatstroke.

example.romaji: kyou atsui kara, netchuushou ni ki o tsukete ne.
example.ja: 今日暑いから、熱中症に気をつけてね。
example.english: It's hot today, so watch out for heatstroke.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa atsui node, netchuushou ni ki o tsukete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は暑いので、熱中症に気をつけてください。
examplePolite.english: It's hot today, so please watch out for heatstroke.

items.use: Very common in Japan each spring; kafunshou nan da = I've got hay fever.

example.romaji: kafunshou de, me ga kayukute tamaranai.
example.ja: 花粉症で、目がかゆくてたまらない。
example.english: My hay fever's making my eyes itch like crazy.

examplePolite.romaji: kafunshou de, me ga totemo kayui n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 花粉症で、目がとてもかゆいんです。
examplePolite.english: My eyes are really itchy from hay fever.

items.notes: Kafun = pollen; sugi (cedar) is the main culprit.

blocks.label: News and emergencies
blocks.rationale: Talk about the news, earthquakes and urgent situations.
blocks.interference: Jishin (earthquake) sounds like jishin (confidence).

example.ja: 今朝の新聞読んだ？
example.english: Did you read this morning's paper?

examplePolite.romaji: kesa no shinbun yomimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今朝の新聞読みましたか？
examplePolite.english: Did you read this morning's paper?

items.notes: Goes with yomu (read); shinbun o toru means to subscribe.

example.romaji: ima no jishin, kekkou yureta ne.
example.ja: 今の地震、結構揺れたね。
example.english: That earthquake just now really shook.

examplePolite.romaji: ima no jishin, kekkou yuremashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今の地震、結構揺れましたね。
examplePolite.english: That earthquake just now really shook.

items.notes: Goes with yureru (shake). Jishin also means self-confidence; context tells them apart.

items.use: Sounds serious, like an alarm or the news; for an everyday rush people often say isogi.

example.romaji: kinkyuu no youji ga dekita kara, saki ni kaeru ne.
example.ja: 緊急の用事ができたから、先に帰るね。
example.english: Something urgent came up, so I'm heading home first.

examplePolite.romaji: kinkyuu no youji ga dekita node, saki ni kaerimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 緊急の用事ができたので、先に帰ります。
examplePolite.english: Something urgent came up, so I'll head home first.

items.notes: Kinkyuu jishin sokuhou is the earthquake alert that blares on phones.

items.use: In daily talk it mostly means calm, nothing going on.

example.romaji: kyou wa nanimo nakute heiwa da ne.
example.ja: 今日は何もなくて平和だね。
example.english: Nothing's going on today, it's nice and peaceful.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa nanimo nakute heiwa desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は何もなくて平和ですね。
examplePolite.english: Nothing's going on today, it's nice and peaceful.

items.notes: Also the noun peace, as in sekai heiwa (world peace).

blocks.label: Contracts and paperwork
blocks.rationale: Deal with contracts, personal details and official forms.
blocks.interference: Kojin is individual, not private life (puraibeeto).

items.use: Phone plans, apartments, jobs; anything you sign up to.

example.romaji: kinou, atarashii heya no keiyaku shite kita.
example.ja: 昨日、新しい部屋の契約してきた。
example.english: I signed the contract for my new place yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou, atarashii heya no keiyaku o shite kimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日、新しい部屋の契約をしてきました。
examplePolite.english: I signed the contract for my new apartment yesterday.

items.notes: Keiyaku suru = sign a contract; keiyaku ga kireru = it runs out.

items.use: Mostly heard in kojinteki ni (personally, for me) and kojin jouhou (personal data).

example.romaji: sore wa kojin jouhou da kara, oshierarenai yo.
example.ja: それは個人情報だから、教えられないよ。
example.english: That's personal information, so I can't tell you.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa kojin jouhou na node, oshieraremasen.
examplePolite.ja: それは個人情報なので、教えられません。
examplePolite.english: That's personal information, so I'm afraid I can't share it.

items.notes: For your private life, say puraibeeto, not kojin.

items.use: The forms and steps for official things: moving, banks, visas, cancelling.

example.ja: 区役所で手続きしなきゃ。
example.english: I have to do the paperwork at the ward office.

examplePolite.romaji: kuyakusho de tetsuzuki o shinai to ikenai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 区役所で手続きをしないといけないんです。
examplePolite.english: I have to do the paperwork at the ward office.

items.notes: Goes with suru (tetsuzuki suru) and often with mendoukusai (a pain).

blocks.label: Out and back home
blocks.rationale: Talk about heading out, getting home and being picked up.
blocks.interference: None.

items.use: Kaeri ni = on the way home.

example.romaji: kaeri ni konbini yotte kuru ne.
example.ja: 帰りにコンビニ寄ってくるね。
example.english: I'll stop at the convenience store on the way home.

examplePolite.romaji: kaeri ni konbini ni yotte kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 帰りにコンビニに寄ってきます。
examplePolite.english: I'll stop at the convenience store on the way home.

items.notes: Kaeri wa nanji? asks what time someone will be back. The verb is kaeru.

items.use: Picking up kids from daycare or someone from the station; omukae ni iku = go and pick up.

example.romaji: gogo, kodomo no omukae ni ikanakya.
example.ja: 午後、子どものお迎えに行かなきゃ。
example.english: I have to go pick up my kid this afternoon.

examplePolite.romaji: gogo wa kodomo no omukae ni ikanai to ikenai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 午後は子どものお迎えに行かないといけないんです。
examplePolite.english: I have to go pick up my child this afternoon.

items.notes: Plain mukae means the same: eki made mukae ni iku yo (I'll come get you at the station). The verb is mukaeru.

items.use: A soft word for an outing, often with kids or a partner; odekake suru = go out.

example.romaji: kyou wa tenki ii kara, odekake shiyou ka.
example.ja: 今日は天気いいから、お出かけしようか。
example.english: The weather's nice today, shall we go out somewhere?

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa tenki ga ii node, odekake shimashou ka.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は天気がいいので、お出かけしましょうか。
examplePolite.english: The weather's nice today, so shall we go out somewhere?

items.notes: Neighbours greet you with odekake desu ka? (heading out?). The verb is dekakeru.

example.ja: やばい、終電逃しちゃったかも。
example.english: Oh no, I think I missed the last train.

examplePolite.romaji: shuuden o nogashite shimatta kamo shiremasen.
examplePolite.ja: 終電を逃してしまったかもしれません。
examplePolite.english: I may have missed the last train.

items.notes: Goes with nogasu (miss) and ni maniau (make it in time).

blocks.label: Traffic and crowds
blocks.rationale: Describe lights, jams and packed trains on the way somewhere.
blocks.interference: None.

items.use: Directions are given by them: tsugi no shingou (the next light).

example.romaji: tsugi no shingou o migi ni magatte.
example.ja: 次の信号を右に曲がって。
example.english: Turn right at the next light.

examplePolite.romaji: tsugi no shingou o migi ni magatte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 次の信号を右に曲がってください。
examplePolite.english: Please turn right at the next light.

items.notes: The green light is called ao (blue): shingou ga ao ni natta.

example.ja: 渋滞で全然動かない。
example.english: We're stuck in traffic, not moving at all.

examplePolite.romaji: juutai de zenzen ugokimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 渋滞で全然動きません。
examplePolite.english: We're stuck in traffic and not moving at all.

items.notes: Also juutai suru (be jammed): michi ga juutai shiteru.

items.use: The rush-hour train where you can't move; man'in alone means full to capacity.

example.romaji: maiasa man'in densha de tsukareru yo.
example.ja: 毎朝満員電車で疲れるよ。
example.english: The packed train every morning wears me out.

examplePolite.romaji: maiasa man'in densha de tsukaremasu.
examplePolite.ja: 毎朝満員電車で疲れます。
examplePolite.english: The packed train every morning wears me out.

blocks.label: Free and extras
blocks.rationale: Say something costs nothing or comes as a bonus.
blocks.interference: Tada is casual, muryou is what signs say; saabisu often means free, not service.

items.use: The casual word; muryou is what signs and staff say.

example.romaji: kono ibento, tada de haireru n datte.
example.ja: このイベント、タダで入れるんだって。
example.english: Apparently you can get into this event for free.

examplePolite.romaji: kono ibento wa tada de haireru sou desu.
examplePolite.ja: このイベントはタダで入れるそうです。
examplePolite.english: I hear you can get into this event for free.

items.notes: The same sound also means just or only: tada no tomodachi (just a friend).

items.use: The standard word on signs, menus and from staff; tada is the casual one.

example.romaji: koko no waifai, muryou da yo.
example.ja: ここのWi-Fi、無料だよ。
example.english: The Wi-Fi here is free.

examplePolite.romaji: koko no waifai wa muryou desu.
examplePolite.ja: ここのWi-Fiは無料です。
examplePolite.english: The Wi-Fi here is free.

items.notes: The opposite is yuuryou (paid). Free refills read okawari muryou.

items.use: Store points come up at almost every till: pointo kaado wa omochi desu ka?

example.romaji: pointo tamatta kara, tada de kaeta.
example.ja: ポイント貯まったから、タダで買えた。
example.english: I'd saved up points, so I got it for free.

examplePolite.romaji: pointo ga tamatta node, tada de kaemashita.
examplePolite.ja: ポイントが貯まったので、タダで買えました。
examplePolite.english: I'd saved up points, so I got it for free.

items.notes: Also the key part: koko ga pointo (this is what matters).

items.english: service; something free, on the house
items.use: In shops and restaurants it often means a freebie.

example.ja: このコーヒー、サービスだって。
example.english: They said this coffee's on the house.

examplePolite.romaji: kono koohii wa saabisu da sou desu.
examplePolite.ja: このコーヒーはサービスだそうです。
examplePolite.english: I'm told this coffee is on the house.

items.notes: Staff say kore, saabisu desu (this one's on us). Saabisu zangyou is unpaid overtime.

blocks.label: Shopping and prices
blocks.rationale: Talk about going shopping, what things cost and getting them cheaper.
blocks.interference: Seeru is a sale event, waribiki is a discount on an item.

items.use: Both grocery runs and fun shopping; kaimono ni iku = go shopping.

example.ja: ちょっと買い物行ってくるね。
example.english: I'm just popping out to do some shopping.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto kaimono ni itte kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと買い物に行ってきます。
examplePolite.english: I'm just going out to do some shopping.

items.notes: Kaimono suru also works.

example.romaji: kore, nedan no wari ni oishii ne.
example.ja: これ、値段の割においしいね。
example.english: This is really good for the price.

examplePolite.romaji: kore wa nedan no wari ni oishii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: これは値段の割においしいですね。
examplePolite.english: This is really good for the price.

items.notes: To ask a price you just say ikura? Nedan ga takai / yasui = pricey / cheap.

items.use: Shop and business talk; for stuff you bought, people just say mono.

example.ja: この商品、もう売り切れだって。
example.english: They said this item's already sold out.

examplePolite.romaji: kono shouhin wa mou urikire desu.
examplePolite.ja: この商品はもう売り切れです。
examplePolite.english: This item is already sold out.

items.notes: Shinshouhin (new product) is all over menus and packaging.

items.use: A shop's bargain period; never 'sale' as in selling something.

example.romaji: ima seeru chuu da kara, yasui yo.
example.ja: 今セール中だから、安いよ。
example.english: There's a sale on now, so it's cheap.

examplePolite.romaji: ima seeru chuu na node, yasui desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 今セール中なので、安いですよ。
examplePolite.english: There's a sale on now, so it's cheap.

items.use: A set amount or percent off; gakusei waribiki = student discount.

example.romaji: gakuseishou misetara waribiki ni naru yo.
example.ja: 学生証見せたら割引になるよ。
example.english: You get a discount if you show your student ID.

examplePolite.romaji: gakuseishou o miseru to waribiki ni narimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 学生証を見せると割引になります。
examplePolite.english: You get a discount if you show your student ID.

items.notes: Percent off is counted in tenths: sanwaribiki = 30% off. A store-wide sale is a seeru.

blocks.label: Booking, ordering, paying
blocks.rationale: Book a table, order, pay and split the bill.
