blocks.interference: Shiharai is the formal noun; with friends you use harau or warikan.

items.use: For restaurants, hotels, doctors, haircuts; the noun yoyaku is the booking itself.

example.romaji: mise, shichiji ni yoyaku shitoita yo.
example.ja: 店、7時に予約しといたよ。
example.english: I booked the restaurant for seven.

examplePolite.romaji: omise, shichiji ni yoyaku shite okimashita.
examplePolite.ja: お店、7時に予約しておきました。
examplePolite.english: I've booked the restaurant for seven.

items.notes: On arrival you say yoyaku shita tanaka desu (I'm Tanaka, I have a booking).

items.use: At a restaurant or online; the noun chuumon is the order itself.

example.ja: もう何か注文した？
example.english: Have you ordered anything yet?

examplePolite.romaji: mou nanika chuumon shimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: もう何か注文しましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you ordered anything yet?

items.notes: Staff ask gochuumon wa okimari desu ka? (ready to order?). When ordering, people mostly just say X onegai shimasu.

items.use: Common on bills and with shop staff; with friends you'd more often use the verb harau.

example.ja: 支払いはカードでいい？
example.english: Okay if I pay by card?

examplePolite.romaji: shiharai wa kaado de ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 支払いはカードでいいですか？
examplePolite.english: Can I pay by card?

items.notes: Staff say oshiharai, as in oshiharai houhou wa? (how will you pay?).

items.use: The default among friends; warikan ni suru = split it.

example.ja: 今日は割り勘にしよう。
example.english: Let's split the bill today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa warikan ni shimashou ka.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は割り勘にしましょうか。
examplePolite.english: Shall we split the bill today?

items.notes: The opposite is ogoru (to treat someone).

items.use: Money owed, to a bank or a person.

example.romaji: kare, kekkou shakkin aru rashii yo.
example.ja: 彼、結構借金あるらしいよ。
example.english: Apparently he's got quite a lot of debt.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa kekkou shakkin ga aru rashii desu.
examplePolite.ja: 彼は結構借金があるらしいです。
examplePolite.english: Apparently he has quite a lot of debt.

items.notes: Shakkin suru = borrow money; shakkin o kaesu = pay it back. A small loan from a friend is just kariru.

example.ja: それ、絶対詐欺だよ。
example.english: That's definitely a scam.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa zettai sagi desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: それは絶対詐欺ですよ。
examplePolite.english: That's definitely a scam.

items.notes: Casually also for anything misleading: shashin sagi is a photo far better than the real thing.

blocks.label: Paying at the till
blocks.rationale: Handle the checkout: card or cash, change, receipt.
blocks.interference: Reshiito is the till slip, not the formal ryoushuusho receipt.

items.use: At a till it usually means a credit card; kaado de = by card.

example.ja: ここってカード使えるかな？
example.english: Do you think they take cards here?

examplePolite.romaji: kaado wa tsukaemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: カードは使えますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you take cards?

items.notes: The full word is kurejitto kaado.

example.ja: ここ、現金しか使えないよ。
example.english: This place only takes cash.

examplePolite.romaji: koko wa genkin shika tsukaemasen.
examplePolite.ja: ここは現金しか使えません。
examplePolite.english: This place only takes cash.

items.notes: Genkin na hito is someone who only helps when there's something in it for them.

example.ja: あ、おつりもらってないかも。
example.english: Oh, I don't think I got my change.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, otsuri o moratte inai n desu ga.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、おつりをもらっていないんですが。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, I didn't get my change.

items.notes: Staff hand it over saying otsuri desu. There's no tipping, so you always take it.

items.use: Where you pay in any shop; reji bukuro is the plastic bag you get at the till.

example.ja: レジすごい並んでるね。
example.english: There's a huge line at the checkout.

examplePolite.romaji: reji ga sugoku konde imasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: レジがすごく混んでいますね。
examplePolite.english: The checkout is really busy.

items.notes: Serufu reji is a self-checkout.

items.use: The till slip; a formal receipt for expenses is a ryoushuusho.

example.romaji: reshiito mada aru? henpin shitai n da.
example.ja: レシートまだある？返品したいんだ。
example.english: Do you still have the receipt? I want to return it.

examplePolite.romaji: reshiito wa mada arimasu ka? henpin shitai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: レシートはまだありますか？返品したいんです。
examplePolite.english: Do you still have the receipt? I'd like to return it.

items.notes: To decline one at the till, say reshiito wa ii desu.

blocks.label: Videos, manga, social media
blocks.rationale: Talk about what you watch, read and post.
blocks.interference: Douga is an online video; a TV show is bangumi.

items.use: Any video clip, especially online; a TV show is bangumi.

example.romaji: kono douga mita? chou omoshiroi yo.
example.ja: この動画見た？超おもしろいよ。
example.english: Did you see this video? It's so funny.

examplePolite.romaji: kono douga, mimashita ka? totemo omoshiroi desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: この動画、見ましたか？とてもおもしろいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Have you seen this video? It's really funny.

items.notes: Douga o toru = film a video; bideo sounds dated.

example.romaji: manga yomu no ga shumi nan da.
example.ja: 漫画読むのが趣味なんだ。
example.english: Reading manga is my hobby.

examplePolite.romaji: manga o yomu no ga shumi nan desu.
examplePolite.ja: 漫画を読むのが趣味なんです。
examplePolite.english: My hobby is reading manga.

items.notes: Any comic or cartoon drawing; the animated version is anime.

items.use: Japanese says SNS where English says 'social media'.

example.romaji: esu enu esu ni shashin ageta yo.
example.ja: SNSに写真あげたよ。
example.english: I put the photos on social media.

examplePolite.romaji: esu enu esu ni shashin o agemashita.
examplePolite.ja: SNSに写真をあげました。
examplePolite.english: I posted the photos on social media.

items.notes: To post is ageru (casual) or toukou suru.

items.english: character (in a story or game); someone's persona
items.use: Also the role someone plays among friends: sonna kyara ja nai = that's not like me.

example.ja: あのキャラ、かわいいよね。
example.english: That character's cute, isn't it?

examplePolite.romaji: ano kyara, kawaii desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: あのキャラ、かわいいですよね。
examplePolite.english: That character is cute, isn't it?

items.notes: Short for kyarakutaa. Kyara ga koi = has a big personality.

example.ja: コンビニで雑誌買ってくる。
example.english: I'm going to buy a magazine at the convenience store.

examplePolite.romaji: konbini de zasshi o katte kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: コンビニで雑誌を買ってきます。
examplePolite.english: I'll go buy a magazine at the convenience store.

blocks.label: Songs and gigs
blocks.rationale: Talk about music you like and nights out singing or at shows.
blocks.interference: Kyoku is a song you listen to; uta is a song as sung.

items.use: The usual word for a song you listen to or play.

example.ja: この曲、好きなんだ。
example.english: I love this song.

examplePolite.romaji: kono kyoku, suki nan desu.
examplePolite.ja: この曲、好きなんです。
examplePolite.english: I really like this song.

items.notes: Uta is the song as sung, with words. Also counts songs: sankyoku = three songs.

example.ja: 来週、ライブ行くんだ。
example.english: I'm going to a gig next week.

examplePolite.romaji: raishuu, raibu ni iku n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 来週、ライブに行くんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm going to a concert next week.

items.notes: Used for any pop or rock show, big or small; konsaato sounds more formal or classical.

items.use: Usually a private room you rent by the hour with friends.

example.ja: 今日カラオケ行かない？
example.english: Want to go to karaoke today?

examplePolite.romaji: kyou karaoke ni ikimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今日カラオケに行きませんか？
examplePolite.english: Would you like to go to karaoke today?

items.notes: Said ka-ra-o-ke, four even beats, not 'carry-oh-key'.

blocks.label: Sport and exercise
blocks.rationale: Say what sports you play, watch or train for.
blocks.interference: Taikai is the whole tournament; a single game is shiai.

example.ja: なんかスポーツやってる？
example.english: Do you play any sports?

examplePolite.romaji: nanika supootsu o yatte imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 何かスポーツをやっていますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you do any sports?

items.notes: You yaru or suru a sport; asobu is for playing around.

example.ja: 昨日野球見に行った。
example.english: I went to see a baseball game yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou yakyuu o mi ni ikimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日野球を見に行きました。
examplePolite.english: I went to watch baseball yesterday.

items.notes: Japan's most-watched sport; a game is shiai.

example.ja: 仕事のあとジム行く。
example.english: I'm going to the gym after work.

examplePolite.romaji: shigoto no ato, jimu ni ikimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 仕事のあと、ジムに行きます。
examplePolite.english: I go to the gym after work.

items.notes: A fitness gym; a school sports hall is taiikukan.

example.romaji: raigetsu, sakkaa no taikai ga aru.
example.ja: 来月、サッカーの大会がある。
example.english: There's a football tournament next month.

examplePolite.romaji: raigetsu, sakkaa no taikai ga arimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 来月、サッカーの大会があります。
examplePolite.english: There's a football tournament next month.

items.notes: Also a big gathering or convention; a single match is shiai.

items.use: For organised, ongoing activity like a club or a band, not one fun thing you did.

example.ja: 最近、ボランティア活動してる。
example.english: I've been doing volunteer work lately.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin, borantia katsudou o shite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 最近、ボランティア活動をしています。
examplePolite.english: Recently I've been doing volunteer work.

items.notes: Bukatsu (school club activities) is short for bukatsudou.

blocks.label: Walks and holidays
blocks.rationale: Talk about strolls, summer break and spring outings.
blocks.interference: Sanpo is walking for pleasure; walking somewhere is aruku.

items.use: A walk for its own sake, often with a dog: sanpo suru or sanpo ni iku.

example.ja: ちょっと散歩してくる。
example.english: I'm going out for a little walk.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto sanpo shite kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと散歩してきます。
examplePolite.english: I'm just going out for a walk.

items.notes: Walking to get somewhere is aruku, not sanpo.

example.ja: 夏休み、どこか行く？
example.english: Going anywhere for the summer holidays?

examplePolite.romaji: natsuyasumi wa doko ka ikimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 夏休みはどこか行きますか？
examplePolite.english: Are you going anywhere for the summer break?

items.notes: For workers it's usually a few days off around Obon in mid-August.

items.use: A spring picnic with food and drinks under the cherry trees.

example.ja: 週末、お花見しようよ。
example.english: Let's do hanami this weekend.

examplePolite.romaji: shuumatsu, ohanami o shimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 週末、お花見をしませんか？
examplePolite.english: Shall we go cherry-blossom viewing this weekend?

items.notes: Usually said with o in front: ohanami.

blocks.label: Phone and messages
blocks.rationale: Talk about your phone, apps and LINE messages.
blocks.interference: Rain here means the LINE app, not a drawn line.

items.use: The everyday word for your mobile phone.

example.ja: スマホ忘れちゃった。
example.english: I forgot my phone.

examplePolite.romaji: sumaho o wasurete shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: スマホを忘れてしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I've forgotten my phone.

items.notes: Short for sumaato fon. Keitai is the older word, still heard.

items.english: LINE (messaging app); a LINE message; line
items.use: Japan's main messaging app; rain suru means 'message someone on LINE'.

example.ja: あとでLINEするね。
example.english: I'll message you on LINE later.

examplePolite.romaji: ato de rain shimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あとでLINEしますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll message you on LINE later.

items.notes: Also 'line' in general, like a limit: rain o koeru = cross the line.

example.romaji: kono apuri, mechakucha benri da yo.
example.ja: このアプリ、めちゃくちゃ便利だよ。
example.english: This app is super handy.

examplePolite.romaji: kono apuri, totemo benri desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: このアプリ、とても便利ですよ。
examplePolite.english: This app is really handy.

items.notes: Short for apurikeeshon. You 'put in' an app: apuri o ireru.

items.use: The 'Read' mark LINE shows once someone opens your message.

example.romaji: kidoku ni natteru noni henji nai.
example.ja: 既読になってるのに返事ない。
example.english: It says read, but there's no reply.

examplePolite.romaji: kidoku ni natte iru noni, henji ga arimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 既読になっているのに、返事がありません。
examplePolite.english: It shows as read, but there's no reply.

items.notes: Kidoku suruu = reading a message and not replying.

example.ja: それ、スクショして送って。
example.english: Screenshot that and send it to me.

examplePolite.romaji: sore o sukusho shite okutte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: それをスクショして送ってください。
examplePolite.english: Please take a screenshot of that and send it.

items.notes: Short for sukuriinshotto; sukusho suru = take a screenshot.

blocks.label: Computer and charging
blocks.rationale: Handle everyday device trouble: battery, charger, wifi, screen.
blocks.interference: Juuden is the charge; juudenki is the charger.

example.ja: パソコン固まっちゃった。
example.english: My computer froze.

examplePolite.romaji: pasokon ga katamatte shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: パソコンが固まってしまいました。
examplePolite.english: My computer has frozen.

items.notes: Short for paasonaru konpyuutaa; a laptop is a nooto pasokon.

items.use: Also the battery level itself: juuden ga nai = my battery's dead.

example.ja: やばい、充電がもうない。
example.english: Oh no, my battery's almost dead.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, juuden ga mou nai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、充電がもうないんです。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, my battery's nearly dead.

items.notes: Juuden suru = to charge; juudengire = out of battery.

example.ja: 充電器貸してくれない？
example.english: Can you lend me a charger?

examplePolite.romaji: juudenki o kashite moraemasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 充電器を貸してもらえませんか？
examplePolite.english: Could I borrow a charger?

items.notes: Juuden is the charge; juudenki is the cable or plug that gives it.

example.ja: ここWi-Fiある？
example.english: Is there wifi here?

examplePolite.romaji: koko wa waifai ga arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ここはWi-Fiがありますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you have wifi here?

items.notes: Connecting is tsunagaru: waifai ga tsunagaranai = the wifi won't connect.

example.ja: 画面割れちゃった。
example.english: My screen cracked.

examplePolite.romaji: gamen ga warete shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 画面が割れてしまいました。
examplePolite.english: My screen has cracked.

items.notes: A device's screen; a cinema screen is sukuriin.

blocks.label: Size, look and limits
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about size and look when choosing things, and set a limit like 'under 1,000 yen'.
blocks.interference: Saizu (clothes and shop sizes) vs ookisa (how big); ika (or less) vs ijou (or more).

items.use: -sa turns an adjective into a 'how much' noun: ookii (big) becomes ookisa (size).

example.ja: ちょうどいい大きさだね。
example.english: It's just the right size.

examplePolite.romaji: choudo ii ookisa desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: ちょうどいい大きさですね。
examplePolite.english: It's just the right size.

items.notes: Saizu is for clothes and shop sizes; ookisa is how big anything is.

items.use: The shop word for S, M, L and shoe sizes.

example.ja: この靴、サイズが合わない。
example.english: These shoes are the wrong size.

examplePolite.romaji: kono kutsu wa saizu ga aimasen.
examplePolite.ja: この靴はサイズが合いません。
examplePolite.english: These shoes are the wrong size.

items.notes: Usually with au (fit): saizu ga au / awanai.

items.use: Often just means how something looks: 'dezain ga kawaii' = it looks cute.

example.romaji: kono kutsu, dezain ga ii ne.
example.ja: この靴、デザインがいいね。
example.english: I like the look of these shoes.

examplePolite.romaji: kono kutsu wa dezain ga ii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この靴はデザインがいいですね。
examplePolite.english: These shoes have a nice design.

items.notes: Dezain suru = to design.

items.use: Goes after a number and includes it: 'sen'en ika' = 1,000 yen or less.

example.romaji: sen'en ika no purezento ni shiyou.
example.ja: 千円以下のプレゼントにしよう。
example.english: Let's keep presents to 1,000 yen or less.

examplePolite.romaji: sen'en ika no purezento ni shimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 千円以下のプレゼントにしましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's keep presents to 1,000 yen or less.

items.notes: Opposite is ijou (or more). Also 'the following' in announcements and writing.

blocks.label: Favourites and treats
blocks.rationale: Lets you name a favourite, say 'both', treat yourself and keep a list.
blocks.interference: Dochira mo becomes 'neither' with a negative verb.

items.use: A noun: 'okiniiri no mise' = my favourite shop; also the favourites button in apps.

example.romaji: koko, watashi no okiniiri no kafe.
example.ja: ここ、私のお気に入りのカフェ。
example.english: This is my favourite café.

examplePolite.romaji: koko wa watashi no okiniiri no kafe desu.
examplePolite.ja: ここは私のお気に入りのカフェです。
examplePolite.english: This is my favourite café.

items.notes: Ichiban suki (like best) is the everyday way to say which one is your favourite.

items.use: With a positive it means both; with a negative it means neither: 'dochira mo shiranai' = I don't know either one.

example.ja: どちらもおいしそうだね。
example.english: They both look delicious.

examplePolite.romaji: dochira mo oishisou desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: どちらもおいしそうですね。
examplePolite.english: They both look delicious.

items.notes: In casual talk it's usually dotchi mo.

items.use: Often a treat you give yourself: 'jibun e no gohoubi' = a little reward for me.

example.ja: 頑張ったから、自分にご褒美。
example.english: I worked hard, so I'm treating myself.

examplePolite.romaji: ganbatta node, jibun ni gohoubi desu.
examplePolite.ja: 頑張ったので、自分にご褒美です。
examplePolite.english: I worked hard, so this is a treat for myself.

items.notes: Also for rewarding kids or pets.

example.ja: 買い物リスト、作った？
example.english: Did you make a shopping list?

examplePolite.romaji: kaimono risuto wa tsukurimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 買い物リストは作りましたか？
examplePolite.english: Did you make the shopping list?

items.notes: Usually with tsukuru (make) or ni ireru (add to the list).

blocks.label: How your body feels
blocks.rationale: Lets you say you're sleepy, sick, run-down or itchy, or that something feels good.
blocks.interference: Kimochi warui is both 'gross' and 'I feel sick'; darui (heavy body) gets mixed with nemui (sleepy).

example.ja: 昨日遅くまで起きてて、眠い。
example.english: I stayed up late last night, so I'm sleepy.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou osoku made okite ita node, nemui desu.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日遅くまで起きていたので、眠いです。
examplePolite.english: I stayed up late last night, so I'm sleepy.

items.notes: Tsukareta is worn out from effort; nemui only means you want to sleep.

items.use: Covers both something disgusting and your own nausea: on its own, 'kimochi warui' often means 'I feel sick'.

example.ja: 飲みすぎて気持ち悪い。
example.english: I drank too much, I feel sick.

examplePolite.romaji: nomisugite kimochi warui desu.
examplePolite.ja: 飲みすぎて気持ち悪いです。
examplePolite.english: I drank too much, I feel sick.

items.notes: Slang short form kimoi is rude when aimed at a person. Opposite: kimochi ii.

items.use: For physical comfort: a breeze, a hot bath, a massage, a good stretch.

example.ja: 風が気持ちいいね。
example.english: The breeze feels nice.

examplePolite.romaji: kaze ga kimochi ii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 風が気持ちいいですね。
examplePolite.english: The breeze feels nice.

items.notes: Past is kimochi yokatta, not kimochi iikatta.

items.use: Your body feels heavy and slow, often before a cold or after bad sleep.

example.ja: なんか体がだるい。
example.english: My body feels kind of heavy.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto karada ga darui desu.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと体がだるいです。
examplePolite.english: I feel a bit run-down.

items.notes: Young people also use it like mendokusai: gakkou darui = school is such a drag.

example.ja: 蚊に刺されて、すごくかゆい。
example.english: A mosquito bit me and it's really itchy.

examplePolite.romaji: ka ni sasarete, totemo kayui desu.
examplePolite.ja: 蚊に刺されて、とてもかゆいです。
examplePolite.english: A mosquito bit me and it's really itchy.

items.notes: Kaku = to scratch: kakanaide = don't scratch it.

blocks.label: Kind and close
blocks.rationale: Lets you describe kind, dependable people and close relationships.
blocks.interference: Naka ii (get along) vs shitashii (close); shinsetsu (kind acts) vs yasashii (kind nature).

items.use: Mostly for kind acts, often by strangers: 'shinsetsu ni oshiete kureta' = kindly showed me.

example.romaji: michi o kiitara, shinsetsu ni oshiete kureta.
example.ja: 道を聞いたら、親切に教えてくれた。
example.english: I asked for directions and they kindly showed me.

examplePolite.romaji: michi o kiitara, shinsetsu ni oshiete kuremashita.
examplePolite.ja: 道を聞いたら、親切に教えてくれました。
examplePolite.english: I asked for directions and they kindly showed me.

items.notes: Yasashii is kind as a personality; shinsetsu is kind in what someone does.

items.use: Short for naka ga ii; describes a relationship, not one person.

example.romaji: ano futari, honto ni naka ii yo ne.
example.ja: あの二人、ほんとに仲いいよね。
example.english: Those two really get along, don't they?

examplePolite.romaji: ano futari wa hontou ni naka ga ii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの二人は本当に仲がいいですね。
examplePolite.english: Those two really get along, don't they?

items.notes: Opposite: naka ga warui. Nakayoku shite = play nicely (to kids).

items.english: reliable; someone you can count on
items.use: Praise for a person you can lean on: 'tayori ni naru senpai' = a senior I can count on.

example.romaji: ane wa itsumo tayori ni naru n da.
example.ja: 姉はいつも頼りになるんだ。
example.english: I can always count on my big sister.

examplePolite.romaji: ane wa itsumo tayori ni narimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 姉はいつも頼りになります。
examplePolite.english: I can always count on my older sister.

items.notes: Opposite: tayorinai (unreliable). Tayoru = to rely on.

items.use: Describes how close people are: 'shitashii tomodachi' = a close friend.

example.romaji: kare to wa sonna ni shitashikunai yo.
example.ja: 彼とはそんなに親しくないよ。
example.english: I'm not that close with him.

examplePolite.romaji: kare to wa sonna ni shitashikunai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 彼とはそんなに親しくないです。
examplePolite.english: I'm not that close with him.

items.notes: In speech naka ga ii is more common; shitashii sounds slightly more careful.

blocks.label: Calling things bad
blocks.rationale: Give a blunt or soft negative opinion.
blocks.interference: Mashi sounds like praise but only means 'less bad'.

items.english: the worst, awful; at least, minimum
items.use: 'Saitei!' about a person means 'You're the worst!'

example.ja: 嘘つくなんて最低。
example.english: Lying? That's the lowest.

examplePolite.romaji: uso o tsuku nante saitei desu.
examplePolite.ja: 嘘をつくなんて最低です。
examplePolite.english: Lying is the worst.

items.notes: 'Saitei demo' means at the very least: 'saitei demo ichijikan'. Opposite: 'saikou' (the best).

items.use: For jokes, shows or arguments not worth your time.

example.romaji: sonna kudaranai koto de kenka shinaide.
example.ja: そんなくだらないことでけんかしないで。
example.english: Don't fight over something so stupid.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna kudaranai koto de kenka shinaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: そんなくだらないことでけんかしないでください。
examplePolite.english: Please don't argue over something so trivial.

items.notes: Often said 'kudannai'. About a silly joke it can be affectionate: 'Kudaranai!' (So dumb!).

items.use: 'X yori mashi' means better than X; never real praise.

example.romaji: kinou yori wa mashi da yo.
example.ja: 昨日よりはマシだよ。
example.english: It's better than yesterday, at least.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou yori wa mashi desu.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日よりはマシです。
examplePolite.english: It's better than yesterday, at least.

items.notes: 'Mashi na X' is a decent X: 'Mashi na mise nai?' (Anywhere decent around?).

items.english: iffy, so-so; hard to say; subtle
items.use: A soft way to say 'not great' or 'not sure' without saying no.

example.ja: あの映画、微妙だった。
example.english: That movie was so-so.

examplePolite.romaji: ano eiga wa chotto bimyou deshita.
examplePolite.ja: あの映画はちょっと微妙でした。
examplePolite.english: That movie was kind of meh.

items.notes: 'Bimyou ni' means slightly: 'bimyou ni chigau' (a little different).

items.use: For clothes, style and try-hard behaviour.

example.ja: その帽子、ダサくない？
example.english: Isn't that hat kind of tacky?

examplePolite.romaji: kono shashin no fuku, ima miru to dasai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この写真の服、今見るとダサいですね。
examplePolite.english: The clothes in this photo look so lame now.

items.notes: Opposite: 'kakkoii' or 'oshare'.

blocks.label: Strong, weak, detailed
blocks.rationale: Talk about detail, and how strong food, drink or colour is.
blocks.interference: Kuwashii is detailed knowledge; komakai is small or fussy detail.

items.use: About a person: 'X ni kuwashii' means knows X well.

example.ja: 彼、車に詳しいよ。
example.english: He knows a lot about cars.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa kuruma ni kuwashii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 彼は車に詳しいですよ。
examplePolite.english: He knows a lot about cars.

items.notes: 'Kuwashiku' means in detail: 'kuwashiku oshiete' (tell me the details).

example.romaji: sonna komakai koto, ki ni shinaide.
example.ja: そんな細かいこと、気にしないで。
example.english: Don't worry about little things like that.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna komakai koto wa ki ni shinaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: そんな細かいことは気にしないでください。
examplePolite.english: Please don't worry about small details like that.

items.notes: 'Komakai no' is small change. About a person it means fussy or stingy.

items.use: For drinks and food it means bland or watered down.

example.ja: このコーヒー、ちょっと薄いね。
example.english: This coffee's a bit weak.

examplePolite.romaji: kono koohii, chotto usui desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: このコーヒー、ちょっと薄いですね。
examplePolite.english: This coffee is a little weak.

items.notes: Opposite for taste and colour: 'koi'; for thickness: 'atsui'.

items.use: For strong coffee, rich flavours, dark colours, heavy makeup.

example.romaji: kono raamen, aji ga koi ne.
example.ja: このラーメン、味が濃いね。
example.english: This ramen has a strong flavour.

examplePolite.romaji: kono raamen wa aji ga koi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: このラーメンは味が濃いですね。
examplePolite.english: This ramen is richly flavoured.

items.notes: Opposite: 'usui'. Same sound as 'koi' (love); context tells them apart.

blocks.label: Quick gut reactions
blocks.rationale: Lets you react out loud to food, drinks and gross things.
blocks.interference: Mazui usually means 'this is bad', not just bad taste.

items.use: Blunt slang for anything that disgusts or creeps you out, people included.

example.ja: うわ、この虫キモい!
example.english: Ugh, this bug is gross!

items.notes: Short for kimochi warui, the safer way to say it, which also means 'I feel sick'. Calling a person kimoi is a real insult.

items.use: A hearty, casual 'delicious', said more by men; also praises someone's skill.

example.ja: このラーメン、うまい!
example.english: This ramen is great!

examplePolite.romaji: kono raamen, umai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: このラーメン、うまいですね。
examplePolite.english: This ramen is really good.

items.notes: Umee is the rough, drawn-out version you hear in dramas. Oishii is the safe default for food; jouzu is politer for skill.

items.use: For drinks, food or bathwater that should be hot or cold but isn't.

example.ja: コーヒー、ぬるくなっちゃった。
example.english: My coffee's gone lukewarm.

examplePolite.romaji: koohii ga nuruku natte shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: コーヒーがぬるくなってしまいました。
examplePolite.english: My coffee has gone lukewarm.

items.notes: Also means soft or lax, as in a lenient rule or an easy-going approach.

blocks.label: Quietly and by accident
blocks.rationale: Lets you say how something was done: carelessly, vaguely, gently, secretly or without moving.
blocks.interference: Sotto means gently; kossori means without being seen.

items.use: A slip you didn't mean, often with -te shimau.

example.ja: うっかり乗り過ごしちゃった。
example.english: I accidentally missed my stop.

examplePolite.romaji: ukkari norikoshite shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: うっかり乗り過ごしてしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I carelessly rode past my stop.

items.notes: Ukkari shiteta = I wasn't paying attention.

items.use: Moving carefully so as not to disturb anyone or anything.

example.romaji: akachan neteru kara, sotto doa shimete.
example.ja: 赤ちゃん寝てるから、そっとドア閉めて。
example.english: The baby's asleep, so close the door gently.

examplePolite.romaji: akachan ga nete iru node, sotto doa o shimete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 赤ちゃんが寝ているので、そっとドアを閉めてください。
examplePolite.english: The baby is sleeping, so please close the door quietly.

items.notes: Sotto shite oite = just leave me be for now.

items.use: Doing something so others won't notice.

example.ja: 授業中にこっそりお菓子食べた。
example.english: I snuck a snack during class.

examplePolite.romaji: jugyouchuu ni kossori okashi o tabemashita.
examplePolite.ja: 授業中にこっそりお菓子を食べました。
examplePolite.english: I secretly ate snacks during class.

items.notes: Sotto is about being gentle; kossori is about not being seen.

items.use: Not moving, or staring hard: jitto shite (hold still), jitto miru.

example.ja: じっとして、すぐ終わるから。
example.english: Hold still, it'll be over soon.

examplePolite.romaji: jitto shite ite kudasai, sugu owarimasu kara.
examplePolite.ja: じっとしていてください、すぐ終わりますから。
examplePolite.english: Please stay still, it'll be over in a moment.

items.notes: Jitto mitsumeru = stare intently at.

blocks.label: Grumbles and hassles
blocks.rationale: Lets you complain about fussing, bad timing and hassle.
blocks.interference: Fuben is for things and places, not for a time that doesn't suit you.

items.english: every single time; one by one
items.use: Mostly a complaint about fussing over every little thing.

example.ja: いちいち聞かなくていいよ。
example.english: You don't have to ask me every single time.

examplePolite.romaji: ichiichi kikanakute mo ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: いちいち聞かなくてもいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You don't need to ask me every time.

items.notes: Ichiichi urusai! 'stop nitpicking!' is a stock retort.

items.english: now (when it's too late); after all this time
items.use: Complains that something comes far too late to matter.

example.ja: 今更謝っても遅いよ。
example.english: It's too late to apologize now.

examplePolite.romaji: imasara ayamatte mo osoi desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 今更謝っても遅いですよ。
examplePolite.english: Apologizing now is too late.

items.notes: Imasara kikenai means it's too awkward to ask now, for things you should already know.

items.use: For things that are a tangle to follow or sort out, like rules, plans or who's dating whom.

example.ja: この説明、ややこしいな。
example.english: These instructions are confusing.

examplePolite.romaji: kono setsumei wa chotto yayakoshii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この説明はちょっとややこしいですね。
examplePolite.english: These instructions are a bit confusing.

items.notes: Fukuzatsu also means complicated but is neutral; yayakoshii adds a note of annoyance.

items.use: For places, tools or setups that make life harder; the opposite of benri.

example.romaji: koko, eki kara tookute fuben da yo.
example.ja: ここ、駅から遠くて不便だよ。
example.english: It's far from the station here, so it's a pain.

examplePolite.romaji: koko wa eki kara tookute fuben desu.
examplePolite.ja: ここは駅から遠くて不便です。
examplePolite.english: It's inconvenient here because it's far from the station.

items.notes: Not for a time that doesn't suit you; for that, say tsugou ga warui.

blocks.label: Giving it everything
blocks.rationale: Lets you say you'll go all out, together, and manage somehow.
blocks.interference: Seiippai is careful best effort; omoikkiri is holding nothing back.

items.english: as hard as you can; your very best
items.use: Full effort within your limits; seiippai ganbaru.

example.ja: 精いっぱい頑張るよ。
example.english: I'll do my very best.

examplePolite.romaji: seiippai ganbarimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 精いっぱい頑張ります。
examplePolite.english: I'll give it my all.

items.notes: Kore ga seiippai = this is all I can manage.

items.english: with all your might; to your heart's content
items.use: Holding nothing back: omoikkiri asobu, omoikkiri naku.

example.ja: 今日は思いっきり遊ぼう！
example.english: Let's have all the fun we can today!

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa omoikkiri asobimashou!
examplePolite.ja: 今日は思いっきり遊びましょう！
examplePolite.english: Let's enjoy ourselves to the full today!

items.notes: Casual form of omoikiri.

items.use: Often otagai ni (to each other), or alone meaning 'we both'.

example.ja: お互い頑張ろうね。
example.english: Let's both hang in there.

examplePolite.romaji: otagai ganbarimashou.
examplePolite.ja: お互い頑張りましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's both do our best.

items.notes: Otagaisama desu = we're in the same boat (reply to thanks or an apology).

items.use: Managing despite difficulty: dou ni ka naru (it'll work out).

example.romaji: dou ni ka ma ni atta.
example.ja: どうにか間に合った。
example.english: Somehow I made it in time.

examplePolite.romaji: dou ni ka ma ni aimashita.
examplePolite.ja: どうにか間に合いました。
examplePolite.english: I managed to make it in time.

items.notes: Dou ni ka shite! = do something about it! Nantoka is a close, very common synonym.

items.english: I was sure (but wrong); I just assumed
items.use: Always a belief that turned out wrong, usually tekkiri ... to omotta.

example.ja: てっきり休みだと思った。
example.english: I was sure it was a day off.

examplePolite.romaji: tekkiri yasumi da to omoimashita.
examplePolite.ja: てっきり休みだと思いました。
examplePolite.english: I was certain it was a holiday.

items.notes: Often followed by the correction: ...kedo, chigatta (...but I was wrong).

blocks.label: As usual, basically
blocks.rationale: Lets you describe your normal routine and habits.
blocks.interference: Shotchuu means 'often', not 'always' (itsumo).

items.use: Things go, or should go, the normal way: itsumo doori de ii (the usual is fine).

example.ja: 今日もいつもどおり忙しかった。
example.english: Busy as usual today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou mo itsumo doori isogashikatta desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日もいつもどおり忙しかったです。
examplePolite.english: Today was busy, as usual.

items.notes: -doori means 'just as': yotei doori (as planned).

items.use: A casual 'often', usually hinting 'too often'.

example.romaji: kare, shotchuu chikoku suru yo ne.
example.ja: 彼、しょっちゅう遅刻するよね。
example.english: He's always late, isn't he?

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa shotchuu chikoku shimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼はしょっちゅう遅刻しますね。
examplePolite.english: He's late all the time.

items.notes: More casual and stronger than yoku (often).

items.use: States the general rule while leaving room for exceptions.

example.romaji: doyoubi wa kihonteki ni yasumi da yo.
example.ja: 土曜日は基本的に休みだよ。
example.english: I'm basically off on Saturdays.

examplePolite.romaji: doyoubi wa kihonteki ni yasumi desu.
examplePolite.ja: 土曜日は基本的に休みです。
examplePolite.english: Saturdays are generally my day off.

items.notes: -teki ni makes adverbs from nouns: jikanteki ni (time-wise).

blocks.label: Just now, in no time
blocks.rationale: Lets you say when something happened or must be done.
blocks.interference: Itsu no ma ni is about not noticing; atto iu ma ni is about speed.

items.use: Stronger than ima: it happened a moment ago.

example.ja: たった今着いたところ。
example.english: I literally just got here.

examplePolite.romaji: tatta ima tsuita tokoro desu.
examplePolite.ja: たった今着いたところです。
examplePolite.english: I've just this moment arrived.

items.notes: Often with -ta tokoro (have just done): tatta ima deta tokoro (just left).

items.english: in no time; in the blink of an eye
items.use: For time flying or something happening fast, often with -te shimau.

example.romaji: natsuyasumi, atto iu ma ni owatchatta ne.
example.ja: 夏休み、あっという間に終わっちゃったね。
example.english: Summer break was over in no time.

examplePolite.romaji: natsuyasumi wa atto iu ma ni owatte shimaimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: 夏休みはあっという間に終わってしまいましたね。
examplePolite.english: The summer holidays flew by.

items.notes: Atto iu ma datta = it flew by.

items.english: when did...?; before I knew it
items.use: Surprise that something happened without you noticing.

example.romaji: itsu no ma ni kami kitta no?
example.ja: いつの間に髪切ったの？
example.english: When did you cut your hair?

examplePolite.romaji: itsu no ma ni kami o kitta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: いつの間に髪を切ったんですか？
examplePolite.english: When did you get your hair cut?

items.notes: Add ka for a statement: itsu no ma ni ka nete ita (I fell asleep before I knew it).

items.english: by the end of today; sometime today
items.use: Sets a deadline for today.

example.ja: 今日中に返事するね。
example.english: I'll get back to you by the end of today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyoujuu ni ohenji shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日中にお返事します。
examplePolite.english: I'll reply by the end of today.

items.notes: Same pattern for this week: konshuuchuu ni.

blocks.label: Asking how much
blocks.rationale: Lets you ask how much or how long, and push a question with surprise.
blocks.interference: Dore gurai is neutral; dore dake and donna ni are usually emotional.

items.english: how much; how long; how many
items.use: The everyday question for any amount, time or distance; dore kurai is the same word.

example.ja: 駅までどれぐらいかかる？
example.english: How long does it take to get to the station?

examplePolite.romaji: eki made dore gurai kakarimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 駅までどれぐらいかかりますか？
examplePolite.english: How long does it take to get to the station?

items.notes: For a rough answer, put gurai after the number: juppun gurai (about ten minutes).

items.use: Usually emotional: how much someone worried, waited or cared, not a neutral measurement.

example.romaji: dore dake shinpai shita to omotteru no?
example.ja: どれだけ心配したと思ってるの？
example.english: Do you know how worried I was?

examplePolite.romaji: dore dake shinpai shita to omotte iru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: どれだけ心配したと思っているんですか？
examplePolite.english: Do you have any idea how worried I was?

items.notes: For a plain question about amount or time, dore gurai is more usual.

items.use: Usually with -te mo: donna ni ganbatte mo (no matter how hard I try).

example.romaji: donna ni isogashikute mo, asagohan wa taberu yo.
example.ja: どんなに忙しくても、朝ごはんは食べるよ。
example.english: No matter how busy I am, I eat breakfast.

examplePolite.romaji: donna ni isogashikute mo, asagohan wa tabemasu.
examplePolite.ja: どんなに忙しくても、朝ごはんは食べます。
examplePolite.english: No matter how busy I am, I eat breakfast.

items.notes: Also in exclamations: donna ni ureshikatta ka (you can't imagine how happy I was).

blocks.label: So-so and fairly
blocks.rationale: Lets you give a modest, middle-of-the-road answer.
blocks.interference: Maamaa works alone as a reply; sorenari ni and aru teido modify a verb.

items.use: The reply to 'how was it?' when it was OK but not great.

example.ja: 試験どうだった？—まあまあかな。
example.english: How was the exam? — So-so, I guess.

examplePolite.romaji: shiken wa dou deshita ka? — maamaa deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 試験はどうでしたか？—まあまあでした。
examplePolite.english: How was the exam? — It was all right.

items.notes: Said softly to calm someone: maamaa, ochitsuite (now, now, calm down).

items.use: Neither bad nor great; often modest about your own skills or things.

example.ja: あの店、そこそこおいしいよ。
example.english: That place is pretty decent.

examplePolite.romaji: ano mise wa sokosoko oishii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの店はそこそこおいしいですよ。
examplePolite.english: That restaurant is fairly good.

items.notes: Sokosoko no = decent, okay-ish: sokosoko no kyuuryou (a decent salary).

items.english: reasonably; in its own way; as you'd expect
items.use: Usually sorenari ni: decent enough given the situation, effort or price.

example.romaji: renshuu shita kara, sorenari ni dekita.
example.ja: 練習したから、それなりにできた。
example.english: I'd practiced, so it went reasonably well.

examplePolite.romaji: renshuu shita node, sorenari ni dekimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 練習したので、それなりにできました。
examplePolite.english: I had practiced, so it went fairly well.

items.notes: Sorenari no = fitting, matching: sorenari no riyuu (a good enough reason).

items.english: to some extent; a certain amount
items.use: Hedges a claim so you don't overstate it.

example.romaji: nihongo wa aru teido wakaru yo.
example.ja: 日本語はある程度わかるよ。
example.english: I understand Japanese to some extent.

examplePolite.romaji: nihongo wa aru teido wakarimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 日本語はある程度わかります。
examplePolite.english: I understand Japanese to a certain degree.

items.notes: A bit more neutral and work-friendly than sokosoko.

blocks.label: Just right
blocks.rationale: Lets you say something fits, works or feels just right.
blocks.interference: Sukkiri is about feeling clear, not about fit.

items.english: exactly; a perfect fit; just right
items.use: A perfect match in size, timing or suitability: pittari no hito (the perfect person).

example.ja: この靴、サイズぴったり！
example.english: These shoes fit perfectly!

examplePolite.romaji: kono kutsu wa saizu ga pittari desu.
examplePolite.ja: この靴はサイズがぴったりです。
examplePolite.english: These shoes are exactly my size.

items.notes: Also exact amounts or times: pittari sen'en (exactly 1,000 yen).

items.use: Casual 'perfectly done' or 'fully ready': junbi batchiri.

example.ja: 準備はバッチリだよ。
example.english: I'm all set.

examplePolite.romaji: junbi wa batchiri desu.
examplePolite.ja: 準備はバッチリです。
examplePolite.english: Everything's ready.

items.notes: Pittari is about fit; batchiri is about things going or looking just right.

items.english: feel refreshed; feel better; look neat
items.use: Relief once something is off your chest or out of the way; also a tidy, uncluttered look.

example.ja: 全部話したらすっきりした。
example.english: I feel so much better after telling you everything.

examplePolite.romaji: zenbu hanashitara sukkiri shimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 全部話したらすっきりしました。
examplePolite.english: I feel much better now that I've said it all.

items.notes: Don't mix with sukkari (completely). Heya ga sukkiri shita = the room looks neat now.

blocks.label: Feelings as sounds
blocks.rationale: Lets you say you're nervous, excited, annoyed, let down or relieved.
blocks.interference: Dokidoki includes nerves; wakuwaku is pure happy excitement.

items.english: heart pounding; be nervous; be thrilled
items.use: A racing heart from nerves, excitement or a crush.

example.romaji: happyou no mae, sugoi dokidoki shita.
example.ja: 発表の前、すごいドキドキした。
example.english: My heart was pounding before the presentation.

examplePolite.romaji: happyou no mae wa totemo dokidoki shimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 発表の前はとてもドキドキしました。
examplePolite.english: I was really nervous before the presentation.

items.notes: Wakuwaku is pure happy excitement; dokidoki includes nerves.

items.use: Happy anticipation of something coming up.

example.romaji: ashita no ryokou, wakuwaku suru ne!
example.ja: 明日の旅行、ワクワクするね！
example.english: So excited for tomorrow's trip!

examplePolite.romaji: ashita no ryokou, wakuwaku shimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 明日の旅行、ワクワクしますね。
examplePolite.english: I'm really looking forward to tomorrow's trip.

items.notes: Wakuwaku shite nemurenai = too excited to sleep.

items.use: Ongoing irritation or impatience from people, waiting or stress.

example.ja: 電車が来なくてイライラする。
example.english: The train isn't coming and it's driving me nuts.

examplePolite.romaji: densha ga konakute iraira shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 電車が来なくてイライラします。
examplePolite.english: The train isn't coming, and it's frustrating.

items.notes: Iraira shinaide = don't get so worked up.

items.use: When something falls short of what you hoped.

example.romaji: ame de shiai ga chuushi ni natte, gakkari shita.
example.ja: 雨で試合が中止になって、がっかりした。
example.english: The game got rained off. What a letdown.

examplePolite.romaji: ame de shiai ga chuushi ni natte, gakkari shimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 雨で試合が中止になって、がっかりしました。
examplePolite.english: I was disappointed the game was cancelled for rain.

items.notes: Said to someone's face (anata ni gakkari shita) it's a harsh rebuke.

items.use: The relief when a worry ends, or the calm of feeling at home.

example.ja: 無事でほっとしたよ。
example.english: I'm so relieved you're okay.

examplePolite.romaji: buji de hotto shimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 無事でほっとしました。
examplePolite.english: I was relieved you were safe.

items.notes: Hotto suru basho = a place where you can relax.

blocks.label: Early, last-minute, hectic
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about timing and pace: early, cutting it close, rushed or relaxed.
blocks.interference: Girigiri is about the limit; batabata is about being busy.

items.english: a bit early; earlier than usual
items.use: Mostly hayame ni: doing something ahead of time to be safe.

example.ja: 混むから、早めに出よう。
example.english: It'll be crowded, so let's leave a bit early.

examplePolite.romaji: komimasu kara, hayame ni demashou.
examplePolite.ja: 混みますから、早めに出ましょう。
examplePolite.english: It gets crowded, so let's leave a little early.

items.notes: The opposite is osome (a bit late). -me after an adjective means 'on the X side': ookime (biggish).

items.english: just barely; at the last minute; cutting it close
items.use: Right at the limit of time, space or money: girigiri ma ni atta (just made it).

example.ja: 終電、ギリギリ間に合った！
example.english: I just barely made the last train!

examplePolite.romaji: shuuden ni girigiri ma ni aimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 終電にギリギリ間に合いました。
examplePolite.english: I just made the last train.

items.notes: Girigiri made = until the last possible moment: girigiri made neru (sleep till the last minute).

items.use: A common excuse for being out of touch: batabata shiteta (things have been crazy).

example.ja: 今週はバタバタしてた。
example.english: This week's been crazy.

examplePolite.romaji: konshuu wa batabata shite imashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今週はバタバタしていました。
examplePolite.english: This week has been hectic.

items.notes: Also the sound of flapping, or of feet running around.

items.english: take it easy; relax; be laid-back
items.use: Relaxing with no rush; also describes an easygoing person or place.

example.romaji: shuumatsu wa ie de nonbiri shitai.
example.ja: 週末は家でのんびりしたい。
example.english: I want to take it easy at home this weekend.

examplePolite.romaji: shuumatsu wa ie de nonbiri shitai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 週末は家でのんびりしたいです。
examplePolite.english: I'd like to relax at home this weekend.

items.notes: Nonbiri shita hito = an easygoing (or slow-moving) person.

blocks.label: Moods at a glance
blocks.rationale: Lets you describe a mood you can see or feel.
blocks.interference: Moyamoya (nagging unease) and bootto (blank mind) both sound vague but differ.

items.use: Usually bootto suru (zone out) or bootto shite ita (wasn't paying attention).

example.ja: ごめん、ちょっとぼーっとしてた。
example.english: Sorry, I zoned out for a sec.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, chotto bootto shite imashita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、ちょっとぼーっとしていました。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I zoned out for a moment.

items.notes: Also feeling dazed from fever or heat: atama ga bootto suru.

items.use: Usually nikoniko suru or nikoniko shite iru: a warm, steady smile.

example.ja: 今日ずっとニコニコしてるね。
example.english: You've been smiling all day.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa zutto nikoniko shite imasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はずっとニコニコしていますね。
examplePolite.english: You've been smiling all day.

items.notes: Niyaniya is a smirk with something behind it; nikoniko is always pleasant.

items.use: Usually moyamoya suru: a nagging feeling you can't put your finger on.

example.romaji: nanka moyamoya suru n da yo ne.
example.ja: なんかモヤモヤするんだよね。
example.english: Something just doesn't sit right with me.

examplePolite.romaji: nan da ka moyamoya shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: なんだかモヤモヤします。
examplePolite.english: Something just doesn't sit right with me.

items.notes: Literally hazy or misty, like a blur in your vision.

items.use: Usually ukiuki suru: light, bouncy happiness before something nice, like a trip.

example.romaji: ashita ryokou da kara ukiuki shiteru.
example.ja: 明日旅行だからウキウキしてる。
example.english: I'm all excited because I'm going on a trip tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita ryokou na node ukiuki shite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 明日旅行なのでウキウキしています。
examplePolite.english: I'm all excited because I'm going on a trip tomorrow.

items.notes: Close to wakuwaku; ukiuki is a lighter mood that shows on the outside.

blocks.label: How well it's done
blocks.rationale: Lets you say how well, how roughly or how steadily something is done.
blocks.interference: None.

items.use: For a quick once-over (zatto miru) or a ballpark figure.

example.ja: ざっと目を通しておいて。
example.english: Give it a quick look-over.

examplePolite.romaji: zatto me o tooshite oite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: ざっと目を通しておいてください。
examplePolite.english: Please give it a quick look-over.

items.notes: With numbers it means 'about': zatto sanjuu nin (roughly thirty people).

items.use: Usually X-go ga perapera (fluent in a language).

example.romaji: kanojo, eigo perapera da yo ne.
example.ja: 彼女、英語ペラペラだよね。
example.english: She speaks fluent English, doesn't she?

examplePolite.romaji: kanojo wa eigo ga perapera desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼女は英語がペラペラですね。
examplePolite.english: Her English is fluent, isn't it.

items.notes: Also talking too much or blabbing secrets (perapera shaberu), and thin flimsy paper.

items.use: For patient, unglamorous effort over time, like saving or studying.

example.romaji: mainichi kotsukotsu benkyou shiteru n da.
example.ja: 毎日コツコツ勉強してるんだ。
example.english: I study a little bit every day.

examplePolite.romaji: mainichi kotsukotsu benkyou shite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 毎日コツコツ勉強しています。
examplePolite.english: I study a little bit every day.

items.notes: Also the sound of tapping or heels on a hard floor.

blocks.label: Lazing and wandering
blocks.rationale: Lets you say you lazed around or wandered about.
blocks.interference: Burabura is strolling for fun; urouro is aimless or suspicious.

items.use: Usually gorogoro suru: lying around at home doing nothing.

example.romaji: kyuujitsu wa uchi de gorogoro shiteta.
example.ja: 休日はうちでゴロゴロしてた。
example.english: I just lazed around at home on my day off.

examplePolite.romaji: kyuujitsu wa ie de gorogoro shite imashita.
examplePolite.ja: 休日は家でゴロゴロしていました。
examplePolite.english: I just lazed around at home on my day off.

items.notes: Also thunder rumbling (kaminari ga gorogoro), a cat purring, or lots of something lying about.

items.use: For slacking with no purpose, or something that drags on too long, like a meeting.

example.ja: 今日一日ダラダラしちゃった。
example.english: I wasted the whole day lazing about.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa ichinichi daradara shite shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は一日ダラダラしてしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I wasted the whole day lazing about.

items.notes: Gorogoro is lying around; daradara is slack and unfocused. Also sweat or blood running: ase ga daradara.

items.use: Moving back and forth in one area, lost or loitering; can sound suspicious.

example.romaji: hen na hito ga ie no mae o urouro shiteta.
example.ja: 変な人が家の前をうろうろしてた。
example.english: Some weird guy was hanging around outside the house.

examplePolite.romaji: hen na hito ga ie no mae o urouro shite imashita.
examplePolite.ja: 変な人が家の前をうろうろしていました。
examplePolite.english: A suspicious person was hanging around outside the house.

items.notes: Burabura is strolling for fun; urouro is aimless, lost or up to no good.

items.use: Usually burabura suru: wandering with no plan, or idling without a job.

example.ja: 駅前をぶらぶらして帰った。
example.english: I wandered around near the station, then went home.

examplePolite.romaji: ekimae o burabura shite kaerimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 駅前をぶらぶらして帰りました。
examplePolite.english: I wandered around near the station, then went home.

items.notes: Also something dangling or swinging, like legs from a high chair.

blocks.label: Empty, packed, messy
blocks.rationale: Lets you describe crowded, empty and messy places.
blocks.interference: Gyutto (squeeze tight) vs gyuugyuu (packed full).

items.use: For trains, shops or roads with hardly anyone in them.

example.romaji: kyou no densha, garagara datta ne.
example.ja: 今日の電車、ガラガラだったね。
example.english: The train was nearly empty today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou no densha wa garagara deshita ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日の電車はガラガラでしたね。
examplePolite.english: The train was nearly empty today.

items.notes: Also a hoarse voice (koe ga garagara) and a rattling sound, like a sliding door. Opposite: gyuugyuu or konde iru.

items.use: For a room, hair or thoughts in a mess, or food gone soggy.

example.ja: 部屋がぐちゃぐちゃだよ。
example.english: The room's a total mess.

examplePolite.romaji: heya ga guchagucha de sumimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 部屋がぐちゃぐちゃですみません。
examplePolite.english: Sorry the room's such a mess.

items.notes: Feelings too: atama no naka ga guchagucha (my head's a mess). Close to mechakucha.

items.use: With squeezing or holding verbs: gyutto dakishimeru (hug tight), gyutto nigiru (grip tight).

example.ja: 手をぎゅっと握ってくれた。
example.english: She squeezed my hand tight.

examplePolite.romaji: te o gyutto nigitte kuremashita.
examplePolite.ja: 手をぎゅっと握ってくれました。
examplePolite.english: She squeezed my hand tight.

items.notes: Gyuu alone is a hug in casual talk (gyuu shite = hug me).

items.use: For a train, bag or schedule crammed full.

example.romaji: asa no densha, gyuugyuu da yo.
example.ja: 朝の電車、ぎゅうぎゅうだよ。
example.english: The morning train is packed.

examplePolite.romaji: asa no densha wa gyuugyuu desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 朝の電車はぎゅうぎゅうですね。
examplePolite.english: The morning train is packed, isn't it.

items.notes: Gyuugyuu zume = crammed in like sardines.

blocks.label: Food textures
blocks.rationale: Lets you praise food by its texture.
blocks.interference: Sakusaku is light and airy-crisp, paripari thin and snappy.

items.use: Praise for fluffy food, hair, towels or bedding.

example.ja: このパンケーキ、ふわふわだね!
example.english: This pancake is so fluffy!

examplePolite.romaji: kono pankeeki, fuwafuwa desu ne!
examplePolite.ja: このパンケーキ、ふわふわですね!
examplePolite.english: This pancake is so fluffy!

items.notes: Also floating, or a dreamy, light-headed mood (fuwafuwa suru).

items.english: light and crispy; quickly and smoothly
items.use: For light, crisp food like tempura or cookies.

example.ja: この天ぷら、サクサクでおいしい。
example.english: This tempura is nice and crispy.

examplePolite.romaji: kono tenpura wa sakusaku de oishii desu.
examplePolite.ja: この天ぷらはサクサクでおいしいです。
examplePolite.english: This tempura is nice and crispy.

items.notes: Second sense: things moving fast and smoothly, like work (shigoto ga sakusaku susumu) or an app.

items.use: Praise for soft, bouncy food like mochi, bread or noodles.

example.romaji: kono udon, mochimochi de oishii ne.
example.ja: このうどん、もちもちでおいしいね。
example.english: These udon are nice and chewy.

examplePolite.romaji: kono udon wa mochimochi de oishii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: このうどんはもちもちでおいしいですね。
examplePolite.english: These udon are nice and chewy.

items.notes: Always a compliment, unlike English 'chewy'. Also soft, plump skin: mochimochi hada.

items.use: Usually kotteri shita: rich, oily or thick flavour, like ramen broth.

example.romaji: kyou wa kotteri shita raamen ga tabetai.
example.ja: 今日はこってりしたラーメンが食べたい。
example.english: I want some rich, heavy ramen today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa kotteri shita raamen ga tabetai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はこってりしたラーメンが食べたいです。
examplePolite.english: I'd like some rich, heavy ramen today.

items.notes: The opposite is assari (light, plain). Kotteri shiborareta = got a real chewing out.

items.use: For thin, crackly things: seaweed, chips, fresh lettuce, crisp chicken skin.

example.ja: 海苔がパリパリでおいしい。
example.english: The seaweed's nice and crisp.

examplePolite.romaji: nori ga paripari de oishii desu.
examplePolite.ja: 海苔がパリパリでおいしいです。
examplePolite.english: The seaweed's nice and crisp.

items.notes: Sakusaku is light and airy; paripari is thin and snappy; a hard crunch is karikari.

blocks.label: Sleep and tiredness
blocks.rationale: Lets you say how you slept and how tired you are.
blocks.interference: Utouto is light dozing, gussuri deep sleep; furafura is dizzy, kutakuta worn out.

items.use: Almost always with neru or nemuru.

example.ja: 昨日はぐっすり寝た。
example.english: I slept like a log last night.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou wa gussuri nemuremashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日はぐっすり眠れました。
examplePolite.english: I slept really well last night.

items.notes: Gussuri nemureta? (Did you sleep well?) is a common morning question.

items.use: Usually furafura suru: feeling faint from hunger, fever or tiredness.

example.romaji: netsu ga atte, chotto furafura suru.
example.ja: 熱があって、ちょっとフラフラする。
example.english: I've got a fever and feel a bit dizzy.

examplePolite.romaji: netsu ga atte, chotto furafura shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 熱があって、ちょっとフラフラします。
examplePolite.english: I have a fever and feel a bit dizzy.

items.notes: Also drifting about with no aim, or someone who won't commit. A spinning dizziness is memai.

items.use: Usually kutakuta da or kutakuta ni naru, after a long day.

example.ja: 一日歩いて、もうくたくた。
example.english: I walked all day and I'm totally worn out.

examplePolite.romaji: ichinichi aruite, mou kutakuta desu.
examplePolite.ja: 一日歩いて、もうくたくたです。
examplePolite.english: I walked all day and I'm totally worn out.

items.notes: Stronger than tsukareta. Also clothes or vegetables gone limp.

items.use: Usually utouto suru: drifting into light sleep, like on a train.

example.ja: 電車でうとうとしちゃった。
example.english: I nodded off on the train.

examplePolite.romaji: densha de utouto shite shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 電車でうとうとしてしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I nodded off on the train.

items.notes: Light sleep, the opposite of gussuri.

blocks.label: Hunger, thirst and aches
blocks.rationale: Lets you describe hunger, thirst, nausea, pain and shivering.
blocks.interference: Karakara (parched) vs garagara (nearly empty).

items.use: Almost always onaka ga pekopeko (I'm starving).

example.ja: もうお腹ペコペコだよ。
example.english: I'm already starving.

examplePolite.romaji: mou onaka ga pekopeko desu.
examplePolite.ja: もうお腹がペコペコです。
examplePolite.english: I'm already starving.

items.notes: Pekopeko suru = bow repeatedly, often meaning to grovel.

items.use: Usually nodo ga karakara (my throat's parched); also dry air or weather.

example.ja: 喉カラカラ、なんか飲もう。
example.english: I'm parched, let's get something to drink.

examplePolite.romaji: nodo ga karakara desu. nani ka nomimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 喉がカラカラです。何か飲みましょう。
examplePolite.english: I'm parched. Let's get something to drink.

items.notes: Also a rattling sound, and karakara warau (laugh heartily). A nearly empty place is garagara.

items.english: queasy, sick to your stomach; seething (angry)
items.use: Usually mukamuka suru, for nausea or for anger building up.

example.ja: 飲みすぎて、胸がムカムカする。
example.english: I drank too much and I feel sick.

examplePolite.romaji: nomisugite, mune ga mukamuka shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 飲みすぎて、胸がムカムカします。
examplePolite.english: I drank too much and I feel sick.

items.notes: Anger sense: kao o miru dake de mukamuka suru (just seeing his face makes me mad). Related: mukatsuku (to get pissed off).

items.use: Usually X ga zukizuki suru, for a headache, toothache or wound.

example.romaji: asa kara atama ga zukizuki suru n da.
example.ja: 朝から頭がズキズキするんだ。
example.english: My head's been throbbing since this morning.

examplePolite.romaji: asa kara atama ga zukizuki suru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 朝から頭がズキズキするんです。
examplePolite.english: My head's been throbbing since this morning.

items.notes: Handy at a clinic; a sharp stabbing pain is kirikiri, a dull ache shikushiku.

items.use: Shaking from cold or fear, often buruburu furueru.

example.ja: 寒くてぶるぶる震えたよ。
example.english: It was so cold I was shivering.

examplePolite.romaji: samukute buruburu furuemashita.
examplePolite.ja: 寒くてぶるぶる震えました。
examplePolite.english: It was so cold I was shivering.

items.notes: Also a phone vibrating.

blocks.label: Surfaces and wetness
blocks.rationale: Lets you describe how things look and feel to the touch.
blocks.interference: Sarasara is dry-smooth; tsurutsuru is slick or slippery.

items.use: For something polished or brand new; often pikapika ni suru (make it spotless).

example.ja: 車、ピカピカにしたよ。
example.english: I got the car sparkling clean.

examplePolite.romaji: kuruma o pikapika ni shimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 車をピカピカにしました。
examplePolite.english: I got the car sparkling clean.

items.notes: Pikapika no ichinensei = a brand-new first-grader. Also lights flashing (pikapika hikaru).

items.use: For hair, sand or skin that's smooth and dry, not sticky.

example.ja: 髪、さらさらだね。
example.english: Your hair is so silky.

examplePolite.romaji: kami ga sarasara desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 髪がさらさらですね。
examplePolite.english: Your hair is so silky.

items.notes: Also a stream flowing, or writing without effort (sarasara kaku). Opposite of betobeto.

items.use: For clothes, hair or people soaked by rain or a spill.

example.ja: 雨でびしょびしょになった。
example.english: I got soaked in the rain.

examplePolite.romaji: ame de bishobisho ni narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 雨でびしょびしょになりました。
examplePolite.english: I got soaked in the rain.

items.notes: Bishonure means the same.

items.use: For slick surfaces like an icy road, and very smooth skin.

example.romaji: michi ga tsurutsuru da kara ki o tsukete.
example.ja: 道がつるつるだから気をつけて。
example.english: The road is slippery, so be careful.

examplePolite.romaji: michi ga tsurutsuru desu kara ki o tsukete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 道がつるつるですから気をつけてください。
examplePolite.english: The road is slippery, so please be careful.

items.notes: Also slurping noodles: soba o tsurutsuru taberu.

items.use: For sticky hands, sweaty skin or a greasy table.

example.romaji: te ga betobeto da, aratte kuru.
example.ja: 手がベトベトだ、洗ってくる。
example.english: My hands are sticky, I'll go wash them.

examplePolite.romaji: te ga betobeto na node, aratte kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 手がベトベトなので、洗ってきます。
examplePolite.english: My hands are sticky, so I'll go wash them.

items.notes: Nebaneba is gooey and stringy, like natto; betobeto is unpleasantly sticky.

blocks.label: Warm, muggy, rainy weather
blocks.rationale: Lets you talk about warm, damp and rainy days.
blocks.interference: Mushimushi is hot and muggy; jimejime is damp.

items.use: For gentle sunshine, or warmth spreading through your body after a bath.

example.romaji: kyou wa pokapoka shite kimochi ii ne.
example.ja: 今日はぽかぽかして気持ちいいね。
example.english: It's nice and warm today, feels great.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa pokapoka shite kimochi ii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はぽかぽかして気持ちいいですね。
examplePolite.english: It's nice and warm today, isn't it.

items.notes: Always a pleasant warmth, never too hot.

items.use: Usually jimejime suru, for the rainy season or a damp room.

example.romaji: tsuyu wa jimejime shite iya da ne.
example.ja: 梅雨はじめじめして嫌だね。
example.english: The rainy season is so damp and gross.

examplePolite.romaji: tsuyu wa jimejime shite iya desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 梅雨はじめじめして嫌ですね。
examplePolite.english: The rainy season is so damp and unpleasant.

items.notes: Mushimushi is hot and muggy; jimejime stresses damp. Also a gloomy, brooding personality.

items.use: For heavy rain: ame ga zaazaa futte iru.

example.ja: 外、雨ザーザー降ってるよ。
example.english: It's pouring outside.

examplePolite.romaji: soto wa ame ga zaazaa futte imasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 外は雨がザーザー降っていますよ。
examplePolite.english: It's pouring outside.

items.notes: Zaazaa buri = a downpour. Light rain is potsupotsu (a few drops) or shitoshito (drizzle).

items.use: Usually mushimushi suru, for sticky summer heat.

example.romaji: kyou wa honto mushimushi suru ne.
example.ja: 今日はほんと蒸し蒸しするね。
example.english: It's really muggy today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa mushimushi shimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は蒸し蒸ししますね。
examplePolite.english: It's muggy today, isn't it.

items.notes: Mushiatsui (hot and muggy) is the i-adjective version.
